title: Texas Late Fee Rules
bodyText:
You may collect a late fee only if (1) notice of the fee is in a written lease, (2) the fee is reasonable, and (3) any portion of the rent has remained unpaid two full days after the date it was originally due. A fee is reasonable if it is not more than 12% of the rent for the rental period in a structure with four or fewer units, or 10% in a structure with more than four units.

A higher fee is still reasonable if it is not more than your uncertain damages from late payment (direct or indirect expenses, costs, or collection overhead) - but you would have to prove that. An initial fee plus daily fees count together as one late fee. Charging a fee that breaks these rules costs you $100 plus three times the fee collected plus the tenant's attorney's fees, and a lease term waiving these rules is void.

On request, you must tell a tenant in writing whether a late fee is owed and how much, using the communication method you normally use.

title: Texas Security Deposit Rules
bodyText:
A security deposit is any advance of money, other than a rental application deposit or advance rent, intended primarily to secure performance under the lease. Refund it within 30 days after the tenant surrenders the unit, with a written itemized list of deductions (not needed if the tenant owes rent and the amount is undisputed). You may deduct damages and charges the tenant is legally liable for, never normal wear and tear.

Your duty waits for the tenant's written forwarding address, but the tenant never forfeits the deposit for failing to give one. A refund or accounting postmarked by the deadline counts as on time. Missing the 30-day deadline creates a presumption of bad faith; bad-faith retention costs $100 plus three times the amount wrongfully withheld plus attorney's fees, and bad-faith failure to itemize forfeits your right to keep any of the deposit and to sue for damage.

Keep accurate deposit records. A requirement that the tenant give advance notice of move-out as a condition of refund works only if it is underlined or in conspicuous bold in the lease. A tenant may not withhold the last month's rent against the deposit (treble rent if in bad faith). If a tenant fails to move in and a satisfactory replacement tenant occupies by the start date, you may keep only an agreed lease cancellation fee or your actual re-letting expenses.

A new owner is liable for deposits from the date of acquiring title and must give each tenant a signed statement acknowledging responsibility and stating the exact deposit amount; the seller stays liable until the buyer receives or assumes the deposits, unless the parties' written contract says otherwise (a foreclosing mortgage lender is excepted). If you took no deposit, you must notify the tenant in writing of any damage claim before reporting it to a credit bureau or debt collector, or you forfeit the claim; the notice is not needed if the tenant has not given you a forwarding address (§ 92.110(b)).

Deposit notices may go by e-mail if you have previously e-mailed with the tenant. That rule applies to leases signed or renewed on or after September 1, 2025; for a month-to-month tenancy that began earlier, whether each month counts as a renewal is unsettled, so use mail for those tenants. None of these duties can be waived.

title: No Deposit Cap or Interest Requirement in Chapter 92
bodyText: Chapter 92 of the Texas Property Code, which contains Texas's security deposit law, sets no maximum amount for a security deposit and does not require you to pay interest on it or hold it in a separate or interest-bearing account. This finding is limited to Chapter 92.

title: No Entry-Notice Statute in Chapter 92
bodyText: Chapter 92 of the Texas Property Code contains no rule on when or with how much notice a landlord may enter a rented dwelling. Your right of entry comes from the lease, so state it there. This finding is limited to Chapter 92.

title: Texas Repair Duty and Tenant Remedies
bodyText:
You must make a diligent effort to repair a condition that materially affects the physical health or safety of an ordinary tenant (or a failure to keep hot water at 120 degrees Fahrenheit) once the tenant gives notice to the person or place where rent is normally paid and is not behind on rent. You have no duty during the lease to repair conditions caused by the tenant, an occupant, family, or guests, other than normal wear and tear.

Seven days is presumed reasonable. If you do not give a written explanation for delay within five days of the tenant's written demand, you bear the burden of proving diligence. Repair-and-deduct is limited to the greater of one month's rent or $500 per month and has condition-specific waiting periods: none for sewage backup or flooding inside the unit, three days for a total loss of water you agreed in the lease to furnish, or for inadequate heat or cooled air from heating or cooling equipment you agreed in the lease to furnish, once a local official has certified in writing that it affects health or safety (listing water or a heating or cooling unit among the utilities or appliances you provide is that agreement); seven days for other conditions a local official has certified in writing.

You can delay a tenant's repair with a sworn affidavit for 15 days (parts delay) or 30 days (post-disaster labor or material shortage), up to six months total. Court remedies include repair orders, rent reduction, one month's rent plus $500, actual damages, and fees; knowingly contracting to waive the repair duty costs one month's rent plus $2,000. The duty cannot be waived except by the specific bold or underlined agreements the statute allows (tenant repairs at your expense; a tenant paying for drain stoppages from foreign objects, door/window/screen damage and windows left open; or a full shift only if you own a single rental dwelling that is defect-free at lease start).

The lease must tell the tenant of these remedies in bold or underlined print. After an insured casualty the repair period starts when you receive insurance proceeds. If a natural disaster makes the unit unusable and you move the tenant to another of your units, you cannot require a longer term than was left on the old lease. If a city or county revokes the certificate of occupancy because you failed to maintain the property, you owe a non-defaulting tenant the full deposit, prepaid rent, moving and other actual damages, and fees.

You may close a unit by certified-mail notice to the tenant and local officials, but after a repair notice you must pay moving expenses and refund rent pro rata.

title: Lockouts, Utility Cutoffs, and Removal of Fixtures
bodyText:
You may not cut off a utility the tenant pays for directly, or one you furnish, except for bona fide repairs, construction, or an emergency (the only exception is interrupting submetered or allocated electricity for nonpayment, under strict notice, weather, medical, and reconnection rules and only if the lease allows it). Violations let the tenant recover possession or terminate, plus actual damages, one month's rent plus $1,000, and fees, and the tenant can get an ex parte writ restoring service.

You may not remove doors, windows, locks, or furnished appliances except for prompt bona fide repair. You may lock a tenant out of the unit (never common areas) only by judicial process, for repairs or emergencies, to remove an abandoned tenant's contents, or by changing the locks for delinquent rent if the lease allows it. A rent lockout needs advance written notice (mailed at least 5 days, or hand-delivered or posted inside the main door at least 3 days, before) stating the earliest date, the amount to pay, where to pay, and, underlined or in bold, the tenant's right to a new key at any hour.

On the day of the change you must post a notice on the front door with a 24-hour key location or phone number (key delivered within two hours) and the amount owed. You must give the key whether or not the tenant pays; cannot change locks while anyone lawful is inside, more than once per rental period, or when no one is available to take payment.

Violations: possession or termination plus one month's rent plus $1,000, actual damages, costs and fees; refusing the key adds another month's rent. The tenant can get an ex parte writ of reentry. A lease term waiving any of this is void.

title: Texas Security Device Duties
bodyText:
Without being asked, you must equip each unit with window latches on exterior windows; a doorknob lock or keyed dead bolt on each exterior door; a pin lock and a handle latch or security bar on each exterior sliding glass door; and a keyless bolting device and a door viewer on each exterior door, at your expense, operable throughout the tenancy. French doors and certain dead bolt configurations have their own rules, and bolt heights, strike plates, and throws are specified.

You must rekey key, card, or combination devices within seven days after each new tenant moves in, at your expense. Tenant requests to rekey or add devices are at the tenant's expense and must be completed within a reasonable time, presumed seven days, or 72 hours if the tenant reports a recent break-in or violent crime at the complex. You may charge tenants only for misuse (and only with an underlined lease provision), never for normal wear and tear, and never more than third-party cost.

If you fail to comply, the tenant may install and deduct, terminate, and sue for actual and punitive damages, one month's rent plus $500, and fees. The keyless bolting device may be omitted in some senior or disability housing, or at a qualifying tenant's separate written request. These duties replace local ordinances (except certain pre-1993 ones) and cannot be waived.

Print the lease's security device section in bold or underlined type: if you do, you have seven days, rather than three, to comply with a tenant's written request before the tenant may terminate or sue under § 92.164(a)(2) or (4); the extra time does not apply where the request reports a recent unauthorized entry or crime of personal violence (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.164(b)-(c)).

title: Texas Smoke Alarm Duties
bodyText:
You must install at least one smoke alarm in each bedroom, one in the corridor serving multiple bedrooms, one on each level, and one inside a studio's single room. Alarms must detect visible and invisible combustion products, be audible in the bedrooms served, and be listed by UL or a named testing lab; on request as a disability accommodation, they must also alert a hearing-impaired person. Units first occupied or certified before September 1, 2011 may use battery power and need not be interconnected, but a replacement must meet the code that applied when the unit was first occupied.

Mount on the ceiling at least six inches from a wall, or on a wall six to twelve inches below the ceiling, unless local officials approve otherwise. Test at move-in. During the lease you must inspect and repair only when the tenant reports a problem or asks, within a reasonable time; you become liable if you have not done so by the seventh day after the tenant's written notice that remedies may be pursued. You need not supply batteries after move-in if the alarm worked when the tenant moved in.

Failure exposes you to a court order, damages, one month's rent plus $100, fees, and lease termination; a tenant who is behind on rent cannot use these remedies. If you have installed a residential fire extinguisher, inspect it at move-in and within a reasonable time after a written request, and repair or replace it at your expense if it is faulty or was used legitimately. Owner-occupied units, units in buildings five or more stories where local ordinance regulates alarms, and licensed nursing homes are exempt.

title: Tenant's Statutory Early Termination Rights
bodyText:
Tenants may end a lease early and avoid future rent in four situations. Family violence: the tenant provides a protective order (or documentation from a licensed health care or mental health provider or a family violence advocate) and gives 30 days' written notice, then moves out; where the abuser is a cotenant or occupant, no 30-day notice is needed. Certain sexual offenses or stalking in the prior six months: the tenant provides specified documentation (for stalking on the premises, a protective order or provider documentation plus a police report), gives 30 days' written notice, and moves out; a parent or guardian must live with the victim; you may not disclose the information except for a legitimate business purpose or as the law requires.

Military service: a tenant entering service, or receiving permanent-change-of-station or 90-day-plus deployment orders, may terminate by written notice with orders; termination takes effect 30 days after the next rent due date (monthly leases) and you must refund prepaid rent within 30 days; a waiver is allowed only in a separate signed document for moves to base housing within 30 miles. Sole-occupant tenant's death: the estate's representative may terminate on 30 days' written notice after removing the property.

Violations cost actual damages, one month's rent plus $500, and fees. If your lease lacks the required statement about these rights, a tenant using the family-violence, sexual-offense/stalking, or military right is released from all delinquent rent.

title: When a Tenant Dies
bodyText:
You may ask a tenant in writing for an emergency contact and a signed authorization to let that person in, remove property, and receive the deposit refund if the tenant dies. If a sole-occupant tenant dies, you may remove and store the property, must release it and refund the deposit (less lawful deductions, including removal and storage costs) to the designated or legally entitled person, and may discard it only after mailing a certified-mail request and waiting 30 days with no claim.

The lease can set a different procedure. The estate's representative may terminate the lease on 30 days' written notice once the property is removed, and on written request you must give that person a copy of the lease; the estate remains liable for rent and damages before termination.

title: Tenant's Right to Summon Police
bodyText: You may not prohibit or limit a tenant's right to call police or emergency assistance based on a reasonable belief that someone needs help, or penalize the tenant for doing so. A lease provision waiving this right is void. Violations cost a civil penalty of one month's rent (fair market rent if subsidized), actual damages, costs, injunctive relief, and attorney's fees.

title: Texas Retaliation Rules
bodyText: For six months after a tenant in good faith exercises a legal right, gives a repair notice, complains to a code agency or utility, or organizes or joins a tenant organization, you may not file an eviction, deprive the tenant of the premises, cut services, raise rent, terminate the lease, or harass the tenant because of it. You are protected if you prove a non-retaliatory reason, for rent increases under a written escalation clause for utilities, taxes, or insurance, and for project-wide increases. Delinquent rent, intentional damage or threats, material breach such as serious misconduct or criminal acts, and certain holdovers are always valid grounds. Retaliation costs one month's rent plus $500, actual damages, costs, and fees, and is a defense to eviction. A tenant who sues in bad faith owes you one month's rent plus $500, costs, and fees.

title: Rental Applications and Screening Notice
bodyText: When you give an applicant an application, you must make available printed notice of your tenant selection criteria and grounds for denial (criminal, rental, and credit history, current income, and inaccurate or incomplete information), and have the applicant sign an acknowledgment containing the statutory statement; it may be part of the application only if the notice is underlined or bold. If you reject an applicant without having made the notice available, you must refund the application fee and any deposit. An applicant not accepted within seven days after submitting a completed application (or after you accept an application deposit without a form) is deemed rejected, and rejecting one co-applicant rejects all. Notice of acceptance or rejection is presumed given by phone or by postmarked mail by the deadline. Bad-faith failure to refund costs $100 plus three times the amount retained plus fees, and any application term waiving these rules is void.

title: Texas Occupancy Limit
bodyText: You may not allow more than three adults (18 or older) per bedroom to occupy a dwelling, unless a fair housing law requires more or an adult is seeking temporary sanctuary from family violence for up to one month. Kitchens, dining and living rooms, bathrooms, utility rooms, closets, and storage areas are not bedrooms. Neighbors within 3,000 feet, or a government entity or civic association on their behalf, can sue to stop a violation and recover $500 per violation plus costs and fees.

title: Cash Rent Payments
bodyText: You must accept a tenant's timely cash rent unless a written lease requires payment by check, money order, or another traceable or negotiable instrument. When you accept cash you must give a written receipt and record the date and amount in a record book. A tenant, or a government entity or civic association, can sue to stop violations; the tenant recovers the greater of one month's rent or $500 per violation, plus costs and fees.

title: Firearms on Leased Premises
bodyText: Unless state or federal law prohibits it on your property, you may not prohibit a tenant or guest from lawfully possessing, carrying, transporting, or storing a firearm, firearm part, or ammunition in the unit, in a vehicle in tenant or guest parking, or in other areas you control as needed to get into or out of the unit, the property, or a vehicle.

title: Giving the Tenant a Copy of the Lease
bodyText: Within three business days after every party signs, you must give at least one tenant a complete copy of the lease; any other tenant on the lease who asks in writing must get one within three business days. Paper, electronic (if the tenant asks), or e-mail (if you have e-mailed about the lease) all work. Failing to do so does not invalidate the lease, but a court must pause your non-rent enforcement action until you provide the copy.

title: Disclosure of Ownership and Management
bodyText:
On a tenant's or government official's request you must disclose the record owner's name and a street or P.O. box address, and, if an off-site company primarily manages the dwelling, its name and street address, within seven days (in writing or by continuous posting), and keep the information current. Putting it in the lease or written rules before any request satisfies the duty.

Liability arises only after a further written notice giving you seven days; willful misstatement is bad faith. Remedies include a court order, the tenant's discovery costs, one month's rent plus $100, fees, and lease termination. A tenant behind on rent cannot use the request remedies. A management company named in writing to the tenant becomes your sole agent for service of process; otherwise your manager or rent collector is, unless your own name and business street address were given to the tenant.

title: Parking and Towing Rules in Multiunit Properties
bodyText:
In a multiunit complex, if you have towing or parking rules at lease signing, give the tenant a copy before signing, signed by the tenant or included in the signed lease or a signed attachment the lease refers to; in the lease the paragraph title must read "Parking" or "Parking Rules" and be capitalized, underlined, or bold. Mid-lease changes need written notice (you bear the burden of proving receipt), must be based on necessity, safety, construction, or other tenants' parking rights (or the tenant's written consent), and cannot take effect for 14 days except in a construction or utility emergency.

You may require only a vehicle's make, model, color, year, license number, and state of registration. Parking permits must run for the full lease term. You are liable for damage caused by an uninsured towing company you contracted with. Violations cost $100 plus towing and storage costs, with fees to the prevailing party. Other rule changes affecting a tenant's property outside the unit also need prior written notice.

title: Guarantors Are Bound Only for the Original Term
bodyText: A guarantor who is not a tenant is liable only for the original lease term unless the original lease states the last date on which a renewal will renew the guarantor's obligation, that the guarantor is liable for a renewal on or before that date, and that the guarantor is liable only if the renewal involves the same parties and does not increase the guarantor's potential rent obligation. A guarantor may separately agree in writing at renewal to guarantee a higher rent.

title: If You Pay the Utilities and Fall Behind
bodyText: If the lease says you furnish and pay for water, gas, or electricity and the utility cuts or threatens to cut service for your nonpayment, the tenant may pay the utility and deduct it from rent, terminate on 30 days' written notice, apply the deposit to rent, recover prepaid rent, actual damages (moving, reconnection, storage, lost wages), costs, and fees. The remedies end if you show written proof of full payment before the tenant terminates or sues. For a master-metered, non-submetered property of 10 or more units, you must notify each tenant in English and Spanish within five days of receiving a disconnection notice, and notify the city by certified mail.

title: Passing Government Fines to Tenants
bodyText: You may not charge a tenant for a fine a government entity imposed on you unless the tenant or another occupant actually caused the damage or condition the fine is based on.

title: Lease Terms Texas Voids
bodyText: These cannot be waived in a Texas lease: security deposit, security device, ownership-disclosure, and utility-cutoff duties and remedies; the duty to install smoke alarms (the duty to inspect and repair them may be waived only in writing); the repair duty (except the specific bold or underlined tenant-repair agreements the statute allows); the family violence and military termination rights; and the tenant's right to a jury trial in an action under Chapter 92. The landlord's duty to mitigate damages when a tenant abandons, and the residential landlord's lien protections and exemptions, also cannot be waived. Terms waiving the utility-interruption, lockout, late-fee, summon-police, and rental-application rules are void. A lease term diverting an unclaimed deposit to you to avoid the state's unclaimed-property process is prohibited. In an apartment complex, lease terms that conflict with the state towing rules for apartment parking are void. Enlarging your security-device, disclosure, or smoke-alarm duties requires a specific written agreement. A void term can cost money, not just fail: knowingly contracting with a tenant to waive the repair duty costs the tenant's actual damages, one month's rent plus $2,000 and attorney's fees (the tenant must prove you knew); charging a late fee the rules do not allow costs $100 plus three times the fee and attorney's fees whether or not you knew; and collecting a charge that a void term provides for can violate the Texas Debt Collection Act and the Deceptive Trade Practices Act. A lease sentence saying nothing limits the tenant's rights does not make a void term safe.

title: Consequence of Skipping the Flood Notice
bodyText: If you fail to give the required flood notices and the tenant then suffers a substantial flood loss to personal property (repair or replacement cost of at least half its market value), the tenant may terminate the lease by written notice within 30 days after the loss, effective on surrender, and you must refund prepaid rent for the period after termination within 30 days. The tenant still owes rent and other sums due before termination. Leases under 30 days and short sale-related occupancies are exempt from the notice.

title: Fees in Lieu of a Security Deposit
bodyText: If you offer a fee instead of a deposit, you must also offer the deposit option, cannot use the tenant's choice in approving the application, and must disclose in writing the right to pay a deposit instead, the right to switch to a deposit at any time, and the charges for each option. The fee must be a recurring equal amount due with rent, set out in a written agreement signed by both sides. It may fund insurance for tenant-caused damage and unpaid rent at no more than its reasonable cost; if it does, the agreement must state that the fee only secures occupancy, is non-refundable, does not limit the tenant's liability for rent and damage beyond normal wear and tear, and is not insurance for the tenant. Otherwise the fee is treated as a security deposit. You must give the tenant an itemized notice within 30 days after move-out before making an insurance claim, withdraw a claim found incorrect, and may not collect from the tenant what the insurer paid you.

title: Liability for Renting to Someone With a Criminal Record
bodyText: You cannot be sued solely for renting to a tenant with a conviction, arrest, or deferred adjudication. You can still face a negligence claim if the tenant was convicted of certain serious offenses or has a reportable sex-offense conviction or adjudication and you knew or should have known.

title: Ending a Month-to-Month Tenancy
bodyText: Either party may end a month-to-month tenancy by giving notice. For a rent period of a month or longer, the tenancy ends on the later of the date stated in the notice or one month after the notice is given; for a shorter rent period, on the later of the stated date or the day after a period equal to the rent period. If it ends mid-period, rent is owed only to the termination date. A different notice period, or no notice, applies if both parties signed an instrument agreeing to it, and none of this applies where there is a breach of contract recognized by law. A fixed-term lease simply ends at its expiration. If you file an eviction for holding over, you must have complied with this termination rule as well as the notice to vacate.

title: Texas Pre-Eviction Notice Rules (from 2026)
bodyText:
Before filing an eviction you must give written notice: at least three days' notice to vacate unless the lease sets a shorter or longer period. For nonpayment by a tenant who was not late before the month you give notice, the notice must be a notice to pay rent or vacate; for a tenant with earlier late payments, either form works. The statute does not say how far back 'earlier' reaches, so the safe practice is to always use a notice to pay rent or vacate when evicting only for nonpayment.

Deliver it by mail, by leaving it inside the unit in a conspicuous place, by handing it to a tenant 16 or older, or by e-mail or other electronic means only if the tenant agreed in writing; actual receipt satisfies the rule regardless. Days are calendar days, excluding the day of delivery; a deadline landing on a weekend or holiday moves to the next business day. A federal notice requirement does not delay your filing, but the writ cannot be served until the federal period has run.

If a lease or law requires a chance to respond to a proposed eviction, that period may run at the same time as the notice. After a foreclosure sale, a purchaser who will not continue the lease must give a tenant who is current at least 30 days' notice. To recover attorney's fees without a lease fee clause, send a certified or registered-mail demand at least 10 days before filing warning that fees may be sought if the tenant does not leave before the 11th day.

title: How a Texas Eviction Runs (from 2026)
bodyText: Eviction suits are filed in the justice court of the precinct where the property is, on a sworn petition; local court rules may not add petition requirements, require mediation or a pretrial proceeding, or allow dismissal of a curable petition, and a court may hold a pretrial conference only if it does not delay trial. Only the Legislature may modify or suspend eviction procedure (the Supreme Court may do so in a disaster only on uniform, public terms). Officers must try to serve within five business days, after which you may use another trained officer. Trial is set 10 to 21 days after filing, not before the fourth day after service, and cannot be postponed more than seven days without written agreement. Your sworn petition must say when and how you gave the pre-suit notice and which form it took and, in a case based only on nonpayment, whether the tenant was late before the month of the notice; it must name every tenant on a written residential lease who lives in the unit and whom you seek to evict, because no writ can be executed against a tenant who was not named and served. Against a person who entered by force (forcible entry and detainer), you may file a sworn motion for summary disposition with the petition, and the court may rule without trial unless the person files a response within four days after service showing a genuine factual dispute. In an ordinary eviction of a tenant (forcible detainer), a summary disposition motion follows the general justice-court rule instead, with no four-day deadline. Either side may appeal within five days by bond, cash, or statement of inability to pay; a tenant who appeals must pay rent into the court registry within five days and each rental period, or a writ issues without a hearing. If you ask for a default judgment, you must give the clerk the tenant's last known e-mail and mailing addresses, serve the judgment yourself (by e-mail if you know an address) and file a certificate of service. The writ of possession cannot issue before the sixth day after judgment, or the day after the tenant's appeal deadline if that is later, unless a possession bond is approved; it cannot issue more than 60 days after judgment (90 if the court extends the deadline for good cause), so ask for it in time, and it cannot be executed after the 90th day. You pay the costs of issuing and executing it. A local court rule, form or standing order counts only if published on the Office of Court Administration's website. You may be represented by a non-lawyer agent in justice court, and multifamily owners may use one on appeal of a nonpayment case. If both parties agree, the justice court may let them appear by videoconference, telephone or other electronic means; some Texas leases record that agreement in advance, but whether a consent signed before any dispute counts has not been tested.

title: Tenant Property After a Writ of Possession
bodyText: When the officer executes a writ, the officer posts a 24-hour warning, delivers possession to you, removes the occupants, and has the tenant's property placed outside the unit at a nearby location that does not block a public way and not while it is raining, sleeting, or snowing. The officer may use a bonded or insured warehouseman at no cost to you, and may not require you to store the property. A city may provide a free container and later dispose of unclaimed contents. You are not liable to the tenant for damages from lawful enforcement of the judgment, including execution of the writ. A warehouseman who stores the property has a lien for reasonable charges and must release listed necessities (clothing, tools of trade, beds, kitchen items, medicine, one car and one truck, and others) within 30 days on payment of the charges attributable to them.

title: Texas Residential Landlord's Lien
bodyText:
A residential landlord has a statutory lien for unpaid rent that is due on the tenant's nonexempt property in the unit or a storage room, but may seize property only if a written lease authorizes it and it can be done without a breach of the peace. A contractual lien is unenforceable unless underlined or in conspicuous bold print in the lease. Exempt property (clothing, tools of a trade, schoolbooks, family library and pictures, basic furniture, beds, kitchen items, food, medicine, one car and one truck, farm implements, children's toys, and goods you know belong to others or are financed) can never be taken.

After seizure leave a notice and itemized list in the unit. You may charge packing and storage only if the lease allows, and sell only if the lease allows, after 30 days' notice by both first-class and certified mail; the tenant may redeem before sale. Willful violation costs actual damages, return of property or proceeds, one month's rent plus $1,000, and attorney's fees. Lease terms waiving these protections are void.

title: Duty to Re-Let After Abandonment
bodyText: If a tenant abandons the unit in violation of the lease, you must mitigate your damages, generally by making reasonable efforts to re-let. A lease term waiving that duty or exempting you from it is void.

title: Your Liability for Breaching the Lease
bodyText: If you fail to comply with the lease while the tenant is not in default, you are liable for the tenant's resulting damages, and the tenant has a lien on your nonexempt property in the tenant's possession and on the rent due to you to secure payment.

title: Termination After a Public Indecency Conviction
bodyText: You may terminate a lease if the tenant or an occupant, or their agent or employee, is convicted under the public indecency chapter of the Penal Code for an activity on the property and has exhausted or abandoned direct appeals. Give written notice within six months after the right arises; possession reverts to you on the 10th day after notice. This right applies regardless of any lease term to the contrary.

title: Texas Fair Housing Act
bodyText: Texas prohibits housing discrimination because of race, color, religion, sex, familial status, national origin, or disability - the same classes as federal law. Race discrimination includes discrimination based on hair texture or protective hairstyles such as braids, locks, and twists. Familial status covers pregnancy, children under 18, and people obtaining custody. You must permit reasonable modifications at the tenant's expense and make reasonable accommodations in rules and policies when needed for a person with a disability, but need not rent to someone whose tenancy would be a direct threat to others' health or safety or would cause substantial physical damage to others' property. Advertising that indicates a discriminatory preference is prohibited even where you are otherwise exempt. Exemptions: first, an owner of no more than three single-family houses who rents one without a licensed broker and without discriminatory advertising. That owner must also rent without the services of anyone in the business of renting dwellings: someone who was the landlord in three or more rentals in the past year or owns a dwelling for five or more families. Whether an owner who is in the business can use this exemption when renting a house personally is not settled by the text; the cautious course is to assume not. Second, an owner-occupant renting rooms or units in a building for four or fewer families. Senior housing is exempt from the familial-status rules. Complaints go to the Texas Workforce Commission within one year; private suits within two years may recover actual and punitive damages and attorney's fees, and state enforcement can add civil penalties up to $50,000, or $100,000 for a repeat violation in a pattern case. Intimidation by force or threat is a Class A misdemeanor.

title: Housing Vouchers and Local Source-of-Income Rules
bodyText: Texas does not require landlords to accept housing choice vouchers or other federal housing assistance, and cities and counties may not adopt or enforce ordinances that would prohibit a landlord from refusing to rent because a person's income includes federal housing assistance. Two exceptions: local rules protecting military veterans' source of income are allowed, and cities and counties may run voluntary incentive programs to encourage voucher acceptance.

title: Rent Control in Texas
bodyText: A Texas city may adopt rent control only by ordinance, only after finding that a housing emergency exists because of a declared disaster, and only with the governor's approval. It continues or ends the same way the governor continues or ends the state of disaster.

title: Billing Tenants for Water
bodyText:
If you own an apartment house of five or more units, a condominium, or a manufactured home rental community, you may bill tenants for water and wastewater only by submetering or by an allocation method under Public Utility Commission rules, after registering with the PUC and meeting water-efficiency fixture and leak-audit requirements.

You may not mark up the water: submetered bills are limited to the utility's cost per gallon plus taxes and surcharges, and allocated bills to actual charges, plus any permitted service charge (at most 9% for submetering, and none for residents of tax-credit units or tenants with Section 8 vouchers). Late fees on water bills are capped at 5%.

The lease must contain the PUC-required disclosures, you must give the tenant a copy of the PUC rules when the lease is discussed, and you must keep records open for tenant inspection. Changing billing methods requires the tenant's signed agreement and 35 days' notice. Raising rent in the 90 days before installing meters, because of utility costs, must be reversed and refunded. The PUC has exclusive jurisdiction and can order refunds of overcharges and assess penalties.

title: Towing From Your Parking Areas
bodyText:
You may have an unauthorized vehicle towed from a parking facility you own or operate, including apartment-complex parking, only if: compliant signs have been posted for the preceding 24 hours; the vehicle owner or operator received actual notice; you attached a windshield notice and then mailed a certified notice warning of towing if the vehicle is not moved before the 15th day after the postmark; or the vehicle blocks a fire lane, traffic aisle, entry, exit, gate, refuse area, or driveway and you identify the towing company and storage facility on request.

Signs must be at every vehicle entrance, facing entering drivers, permanently mounted with the bottom edge 5 to 8 feet above ground, weather-resistant, at least 18 by 24 inches, with the red-and-white towing symbol and wording, a statement of who may park, the days and hours of enforcement, and a 24-hour phone number. At an apartment complex you may not tow a vehicle merely for an expired registration unless the lease provides for 10 days' written notice first, and any apartment lease term that conflicts with these rules is void.

You may not accept anything of value from, or hold an interest in, the towing company. If you tow in compliance with the law using an insured tow company and storage facility, you are not liable for damage from the removal or storage; if you violate the law you are liable for damages and fees, and an intentional or reckless violation costs $1,000 plus three times the fees. The vehicle owner may request a justice-court hearing within 14 days.

title: Service Animals Under Texas Law
bodyText:
A person with a disability who uses a service animal is entitled to full and equal access to housing offered for rent, and a landlord may not charge extra compensation or a deposit for the animal, though the tenant remains liable for damage the animal does beyond reasonable wear and tear. Refusing that access is a misdemeanor (a fine of up to $300 plus 30 hours of community service), and the tenant may also sue, with damages conclusively presumed to be at least $300. It is a separate misdemeanor, punishable by a fine of up to $1,000 and 30 hours of community service, to knowingly represent that an animal is an assistance or service animal when it is not specially trained or equipped to help a person with a disability.

Under these Texas definitions a service animal is a specially trained dog; the housing rule does not apply to a single-family home whose occupants rent out only one room. Emotional support animals are not covered by this statute; their treatment in housing turns on fair-housing accommodation law.

title: State Preemption of City and County Rules
bodyText: Texas law voids city and county ordinances that regulate conduct in a field occupied by the Property Code unless another statute expressly authorizes them, and the occupied field expressly includes local rules that regulate evictions or restrict or delay notices to vacate or eviction filings. Anyone injured, or threatened with injury, by a preempted ordinance, or a trade association representing them, may sue the city or county for a court order and attorney's fees after giving it at least three months' notice of the claim. A 2023 challenge by several cities was dismissed in 2025 for lack of standing, and the law is in force. Do not assume a local tenant-protection ordinance in your area is enforceable, and do not ignore one either: whether a particular ordinance survives is a local, case-by-case question.

title: No Radon Disclosure Required for Rentals
bodyText: No Texas statute requires a landlord to test for radon or to disclose radon to a tenant. The only residential radon disclosure in Texas law is on the seller's disclosure notice for the SALE of a single-dwelling property; it does not apply to leases.

title: No Bed Bug Statute for Rentals
bodyText: No Texas statute requires a landlord to disclose bed bug history or sets a bed bug treatment timeline. An infestation that materially affects the physical health or safety of an ordinary tenant falls under the general repair duty once the tenant gives notice. Separately, state health law treats disease-carrying bedbugs in a place offering sleeping accommodations to the public as a public health nuisance; whether that reaches an ordinary rental dwelling is unsettled.

title: No Mold Disclosure Required for Rentals
bodyText: No Texas statute requires a landlord to disclose mold to a tenant. Texas regulates mold assessors and remediators, and a property owner who sells must hand the buyer any mold remediation certificates from the past five years, but neither rule reaches leases. Mold that materially affects the physical health or safety of an ordinary tenant falls under the general repair duty.

title: No Carbon Monoxide Alarm Statute for Rentals
bodyText: No Texas statute requires a landlord to install carbon monoxide alarms in a rental dwelling. Texas's rental alarm law covers smoke alarms only. Carbon monoxide alarms may still be required for new or remodeled homes by the building code your city has adopted, so check local codes.

title: No Methamphetamine Disclosure Required for Rentals
bodyText: No Texas statute requires a landlord to disclose past methamphetamine manufacture to a tenant. The only such disclosure in Texas law is on the seller's disclosure notice for the SALE of a single-dwelling property. Separately, a person who manufactures methamphetamine is strictly liable for resulting property damage, which a landlord may use against a tenant who did so.

title: Doing Your Own Mold Work
bodyText: Texas licenses mold assessors and remediators. A property owner, or the owner's managing agent or employee, does not need a license to assess or remediate mold at a residential property the owner owns with fewer than 10 dwelling units, as long as the agent or employee is not in the mold business for the public. Anyone may remediate an area of less than 25 contiguous square feet without a license. For larger properties or larger areas, use licensed professionals; one license holder may not do both the assessment and the remediation on the same project. Once a certificate of mold remediation is issued, the owner is not liable for damages related to the remediation that accrued on or before the certificate date, and an owner who sells must give the buyer copies of certificates from the previous five years.

title: Recovering Damage From a Tenant Who Made Methamphetamine
bodyText: A person who manufactures methamphetamine is strictly liable for personal injury, death, or property damage arising from the manufacture, whether or not convicted, and is jointly liable with any other defendant for the entire amount. The usual caps on exemplary damages and the proportionate-responsibility rules do not apply. Anyone exposed to the manufacturing process may recover the greater of actual damages or $20,000 per incident of exposure.

title: Immigration or Citizenship Questions
bodyText: The Texas Property Code neither prohibits nor requires asking a rental applicant or tenant about immigration or citizenship status. Federal fair-housing law still bars national-origin discrimination. A separate 2025 Texas law limits certain foreign governments, companies, and individuals from acquiring interests in Texas real property; it covers leases of one year or more, and a lease acquired in violation is void (see Foreign-Acquisition Law and Leases of One Year or More).

title: No Tenant EV Charging Statute
bodyText: No Texas statute gives tenants a right to install or use electric vehicle charging. Any charging arrangement is a matter for the lease.

title: No Rent-Increase Notice Statute
bodyText: Texas has no statute setting how much notice a landlord must give before raising rent on an ordinary residential tenancy. During a fixed term, rent can change only as the lease allows. For a month-to-month tenancy, an increase works in practice through the termination-notice rule: at least one month's notice for monthly tenancies, unless a signed agreement sets a different period. You may not raise rent to retaliate against a tenant within six months after the tenant exercises a protected right, and a city may impose rent control only during a declared disaster with the governor's approval.

title: Foreign-Acquisition Law and Leases of One Year or More
bodyText: A 2025 Texas law bars certain foreign governments, companies, and individuals from purchasing or otherwise acquiring an interest in Texas real property, and it covers leasehold interests unless the lease runs less than one year. A standard 12-month lease is not less than one year. The restricted individuals are defined by ties to countries designated by federal threat assessments or by the governor: for example, individuals domiciled in a designated country (with a narrow exception for a lawfully present resident buying a residence homestead), citizens of a designated country who are unlawfully present in the United States, agents of a designated country, and members of its ruling party. The law does not apply to U.S. citizens, lawful permanent residents, or companies they own or control. A leasehold acquired in violation is void. The attorney general may bring an action against the real property itself and record notice of it in the county records, and a court-appointed receiver may terminate the leasehold. A restricted individual who knowingly acquires an interest commits a state jail felony, and a violating company faces a civil penalty of the greater of $250,000 or half the interest's market value. The law places the penalties on the person acquiring the interest and states no duty for a landlord to verify anyone's status. Screening applicants by national origin is prohibited by fair-housing law, so any policy on this should be set with legal counsel.

title: Unclaimed Security Deposits
bodyText: If you owe a former tenant a security deposit refund (or any other money) and for more than three years you cannot locate the tenant and the tenant has not claimed it, the money is presumed abandoned. You are the holder: if you hold it on March 1, you must report and deliver it to the Texas Comptroller by the following July 1, and if it is worth more than $250 you must first notify the tenant by mail or e-mail at the last known address at least 60 days before delivery. Once you have filed a report, you must file one every year after that, certifying if you hold nothing. You may not reduce the amount with service or dormancy charges, other than the postage for the required notice, and a lease term or other private arrangement that diverts unclaimed money to you to avoid this process is prohibited. Keep the records for 10 years. Delivering in good faith relieves you of liability to the tenant. Late delivery carries 10 percent annual interest, penalties of 5 percent plus another 5 percent after 30 days, a civil penalty of up to $100 a day, and willful violations are a misdemeanor.

title: When a Tenant Abandons the Unit
bodyText:
Texas has no statute that defines when a residential tenant has abandoned a unit, and no notice-and-storage procedure for belongings a living tenant leaves behind. The Property Code lets you exclude a tenant in order to remove the contents of premises the tenant has abandoned, and lets you remove the contents of an abandoned residence.

If the tenant had not in fact abandoned, the exclusion is an unlawful lockout: the tenant may recover possession or end the lease and recover one month's rent plus $1,000, actual damages, court costs and attorney's fees (less any rent owed), and can get an ex parte writ of reentry. Because 'abandoned' is undefined, a lease definition is your main protection; the optional abandonment Section of this lease supplies one, and Texas's standard apartment-association lease also defines it.

Before you treat a unit as abandoned, document the signs and give written notice with time to respond. Different rules apply when a sole tenant dies (the certified-mail and 30-day procedure unless the lease sets another) and after an eviction (the officer places belongings outside under the writ). Once the tenant has surrendered, the 30-day deposit refund clock runs, and you must try to re-let to limit your damages.

title: Pools at Multiunit Rentals
bodyText: If you own a multiunit rental complex (two or more units under common ownership and management on the same or adjacent lots, including a condominium project, but not a stand-alone single-family home) with a pool, or a rental unit in a condominium, cooperative or town-home project with a pool, Health and Safety Code chapter 757 applies. A pool includes a permanent swimming pool, wading pool, hot tub or spa more than 18 inches deep. The pool yard must be fully enclosed at least 48 inches high, with limits on openings (no chain link on enclosures built after January 1, 1994); gates must self-close and self-latch, open outward, be lockable, and generally have the latch at least 60 inches high. Unit doors may not open directly into the pool yard where the building or pool first got electrical service on or after January 1, 1994; older doors and windows that do must have specified latches and bolts. You must use reasonable care to inspect, maintain and repair the enclosure, gates and self-closing latches, and inspect them at least once every 31 days, and repair pool-yard window and sliding-door latches, pins and bars after a tenant reports a problem. These duties cannot be waived. A tenant may report those problems orally unless the lease requires written notice in a provision printed in capital letters and underlined, or in 10-point bold type. A tenant or anyone else can sue for a compliance order, actual damages, punitive damages for intentional, malicious or grossly negligent failures, and a civil penalty of up to $5,000 if you do not comply within a reasonable time after a tenant's written notice; the attorney general, a city, a county or a local health department can also enforce. Cities generally may not require a different enclosure than the chapter allows. Your security-device duties under the Property Code still apply.

title: Removing a Squatter Without an Eviction
bodyText: Since September 1, 2025, the owner of residential property, or the owner's agent, can ask the sheriff or a constable to remove immediately a person who unlawfully entered and is living in a dwelling without the owner's consent, without filing an eviction suit. It is available only if the property was not open to the public when the person entered, there is no pending lawsuit between you and the person, you have told the person to leave and they have not, and the person is not your current or former tenant under any oral or written lease and not an immediate family member. You submit a sworn complaint in the statutory form, with a copy of your government-issued ID (and, for an agent, proof of authority). In it you also declare that any lease the person produces is fraudulent. You declare too that the person is not an owner or co-owner, and that any title listing them as one is fraudulent. The officer verifies that you are the record owner or agent, then without delay serves a notice to vacate immediately (by hand or by posting on the front door) and puts you in possession; the officer may arrest occupants for trespass or other offenses. You pay the same fee as for executing a writ of possession, plus an hourly rate if you ask the officer to stay while you change the locks and move the occupants' belongings to your property line. You are not liable for damage to belongings removed under this procedure, but a person wrongfully removed can sue to recover possession plus actual damages, three times the fair market rent, court costs and attorney's fees, and a false complaint is perjury. Anyone who was ever your tenant, including a holdover or a tenant whose lease has ended, must be removed through an eviction suit. Knowingly presenting a fake lease or deed to enter or stay on property is a Class A misdemeanor (Tex. Penal Code § 32.56, as added by S.B. 1333; see the library's trespass row).

title: Crime at Your Property: Nuisance Suits
bodyText:
Under Texas's common-nuisance law, a person who maintains a place where people habitually go to commit listed crimes, knowingly tolerates it, and fails to make reasonable attempts to stop it maintains a common nuisance. The list includes drug dealing, manufacture or possession, prostitution and human trafficking, gambling, reckless or public gunfire, aggravated assault, robbery, sexual assault, murder, criminal trespass, disorderly conduct, arson, graffiti and serious criminal mischief.

A specific rule covers multiunit residential property (three or more units, not a single-family home or duplex). The attorney general, a district, county or city attorney, or a private individual can sue the owner. Frequent crime at the property is prima facie evidence that you tolerated it, and arrests there can be used to show you knew. A court can order you to abate the nuisance, require a bond of $5,000 to $10,000, and order the property closed for one year; if you violate the order it can cut off utilities, revoke the certificate of occupancy, or order you to end a tenant's lease.

For multiunit property found to be a nuisance, it can also appoint a receiver to run it for up to a year. Contempt fines run $1,000 to $10,000 plus jail, and the prevailing party may recover attorney's fees. Your protection is acting promptly: calling the police cannot be used as evidence that you tolerated the activity, anyone deciding whether to sue must consider whether you promptly report crime and cooperate with police, while refusing to cooperate can be used against you, and posting a sign alone does not prove you did not tolerate it. Enforcing the lease against a tenant engaged in the activity is the usual reasonable step.

title: No Eviction Record Sealing in Texas
bodyText: Texas has no statute that seals or expunges eviction records, including under the 2026 eviction overhaul. The court rules add none: the eviction rule (Texas Rule of Civil Procedure 510, rewritten for 2026) has no sealing provision, and the general sealing rule (Rule 76a) never allows a judgment or order to be sealed and allows other court records to be sealed only if the person asking shows a specific, serious and substantial interest that clearly outweighs the presumption that court records are open, after posted public notice and a hearing. A tenant has no statutory right to have an eviction case sealed, and nothing in Texas landlord-tenant law limits your considering a past eviction when you screen, beyond fair-housing law.

title: Returned Payment Fee Limit
bodyText: Texas caps the processing fee for a dishonored payment at $30 (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code 3.506). Use it as a guardrail when you enter the fee. You may not charge it at all if a reimbursement fee was collected for the same payment through the district attorney's hot-check process, and you must refund it at once if one is collected later.

title: Provide an Emergency Repair Phone Number
bodyText:
Give tenants a telephone number for reporting emergencies that materially affect the physical health or safety of an ordinary tenant. If you have an on-site management or superintendent's office for the property, that number must be answered 24 hours a day and must be posted prominently outside the office (Tex. Prop. Code 92.020).

If you have no on-site office, you must still give tenants a number for reporting those emergencies, but it need not be answered around the clock. A city or county rule on 24-hour emergency numbers adopted before January 1, 2008 still applies if it conforms, or is amended to conform, to the state rule, so check for one where you rent. The lease's optional clause is a convenient place to give it.

title: No Just-Cause Eviction Rule
bodyText: Texas has no general just-cause or good-cause eviction rule. A fixed-term lease ends on its end date, and either side may end a month-to-month tenancy without giving a reason on the notice Texas law sets (for a monthly rent period, at least one month, unless both of you signed an agreement setting a different period), however long the tenant has lived there. Cities and counties cannot add a cause requirement: Texas voids local rules that regulate evictions or restrict or delay notices to vacate or eviction filings. The limits are situational. Within six months after a tenant in good faith uses a legal right or remedy, gives a repair notice, makes a good-faith code or utility complaint, or establishes or takes part in a tenant organization, you may not retaliate by filing an eviction, ending the lease, raising the rent or cutting services; retaliation is a defense to an eviction. Some grounds are always valid, including rent delinquency, intentional damage or threats, a material breach other than holding over, and a holdover after your end-of-term termination notice given before the tenant's protected act. After a foreclosure sale, a buyer who will not continue the lease must give a tenant who is current at least 30 days' notice to vacate. Fair-housing law bars ending a tenancy for a discriminatory reason. State law requires good-cause nonrenewal terms in the leases of some tax-advantaged affordable housing (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code §§ 303.0425(i), 394.9026(c)(9); 10 Tex. Admin. Code § 10.613(a)); see the library's Texas good-cause row. Federally assisted housing may carry its own cause and notice rules; a federal notice period does not delay your filing but does delay service of the writ.

title: Sending Notices by E-mail
bodyText:
Texas's electronic-transactions law covers landlord-tenant records and, unlike some states, carves out nothing for eviction, default or cure notices. Three of its rules matter to you. It applies only between parties who have each agreed to deal electronically, judged from the context and their conduct. A tenant who agreed to deal electronically on one matter may still refuse to deal electronically on other matters, and a lease cannot take that right away. And an e-mailed notice that the law requires in writing counts only if the tenant can keep it: if you send it in a form, or through a portal, that stops the tenant from printing or saving it, it cannot be enforced against the tenant, whatever the lease says.

Texas landlord-tenant law adds its own conditions: a notice to vacate or to pay rent or vacate may go by e-mail only if the tenant agreed in writing (the lease's optional e-mail consent clause), though a notice the tenant actually receives counts however it was sent, deposit notices may go by e-mail once you and the tenant have e-mailed each other, and a copy of the lease may be e-mailed if you have e-mailed about the lease.

Because a tenant may argue that a later notice is another matter the tenant can refuse to handle electronically, and a disputed e-mail is hard to prove, also deliver eviction notices by one of the paper methods.

title: Deceptive Trade Practices Act and Rentals
bodyText: Texas's Deceptive Trade Practices Act reaches residential leasing: it defines goods to include real property leased for use, so a tenant is a consumer. Two parts matter. Its list of unlawful practices includes representing that an agreement gives rights, remedies or obligations it does not have or that the law prohibits, and failing to disclose known information to induce a transaction the consumer would otherwise have refused; the list has nothing on blank spaces or on giving the tenant a copy (Texas's lease-copy rule is in the Property Code). Separately, the act lets a consumer sue for any unconscionable action, meaning taking advantage of a consumer's lack of knowledge, ability, experience or capacity to a grossly unfair degree. A consumer who wins recovers economic damages, court costs and attorney's fees, and up to three times the damages if you acted knowingly. A tenant cannot waive the act in a lease unless the tenant is not in a significantly disparate bargaining position, is represented by a lawyer the tenant chose, and signs a waiver in the statute's bold-face form. Separately, Texas's debt-collection act bars collecting a fee or expense incidental to a debt unless the agreement expressly authorizes it or the law otherwise allows it, and makes a violation a deceptive trade practice; whether that act reaches a landlord collecting its own rent is unsettled. So a lease term the law voids is not merely unenforceable: using it can create liability.

title: No Plain-Language Lease Rule
bodyText: Texas has no plain-language or readability statute for residential leases. The plain-language rules in Texas law cover other contracts (home-equity and consumer loans, prepaid funeral contracts). What Texas does require is specific print for specific lease terms (bold or underlined text for the repair-remedies statement and several optional rights), which the library's clauses mark where they apply.

title: When the Tenant Causes Damage
bodyText:
Texas law leaves the cost of tenant-caused damage with the tenant in several places. If a fire or other casualty caused by the negligence or fault of the tenant, the tenant's family or a guest makes the home unusable, the tenant cannot end the lease and gets no rent reduction under the casualty statute; but the same statute's termination right is not available to you either. You have no statutory duty to repair a condition the tenant, an occupant, family or a guest caused (normal wear and tear excepted), so the tenant's repair, repair-and-deduct and termination remedies do not apply to it.

You may deduct the damage from the security deposit, never for normal wear and tear, with an itemized list. Charging for security-device repairs needs an underlined lease term and is limited to misuse or damage by the tenant, family, an occupant or a guest. A specific bold or underlined agreement is needed only to make the tenant pay, whoever caused them (other than your negligence), for drain stoppages from foreign or improper objects in lines serving only the unit, damage to doors, windows or screens, and damage from windows or doors left open.

No Texas statute says what you can recover beyond that, so the library offers an optional clause: no rent reduction while you repair, your right to end the lease if the damage makes the home unusable, and the tenant's liability for repair costs and lost rent less what you get from re-renting. Try to re-rent; Texas requires a landlord to mitigate when a tenant abandons.

title: No Algorithmic Rent-Setting Rule
bodyText: Texas statutes do not regulate using algorithmic or software pricing tools to set residential rents, or sharing rent data with other landlords. Texas's general antitrust law, which makes any contract, combination or conspiracy in restraint of trade unlawful, may still apply, as may federal antitrust law.

title: Fees and Rent
bodyText: Texas's landlord-tenant statutes do not define rent or say whether a fee can be treated as rent, and none lets a lease turn fees into rent. One narrow exception: for a housing-finance-corporation development claiming the property-tax exemption, Tex. Loc. Gov't Code § 394.9026(a)(8) counts recurring mandatory fees as rent. Texas does treat late fees separately: the late-fee statute governs only the fee and does not change your right to end the lease for unpaid rent. The library's lease applies each payment to rent first and does not call any fee rent. When you give a notice to pay rent or vacate, demand only the unpaid rent, so the notice cannot be attacked for including amounts that are not rent.

title: No Statute on Fixing a Tenant's Neglect
bodyText: Texas has no statute letting a landlord fix a tenant's failure to maintain the property and bill the cost as rent. Any such right comes from the lease. Keep two Texas limits in mind: you have no duty to repair conditions the tenant, an occupant, family or a guest caused (other than normal wear and tear), but a lease can make the tenant pay for repairs you would otherwise owe only through the narrow bold or underlined agreements the statute allows. Entering to do the work is governed by the lease, since Texas has no entry-notice statute.

title: No Rule on Blank Spaces in a Lease
bodyText: Texas has no statute barring a landlord from having a tenant sign a residential lease with blank spaces, or requiring the lease to be complete at signing, and the Deceptive Trade Practices Act's list of unlawful practices has no blank-space item. You must give at least one tenant a complete copy of the signed lease within three business days, and another tenant on request; until you do, a court will pause your suit to enforce the lease (other than for unpaid rent) if the tenant raises it. Fill in every blank before anyone signs.

title: No Separate Quiet-Enjoyment Statute
bodyText: Texas's landlord-tenant statutes have no separate quiet-enjoyment covenant; any covenant comes from the common law and the lease. The statutes protect the tenant's possession directly instead: you may change the locks only in the narrow cases the statute allows, may interrupt utilities only as it allows, and may not, in retaliation for a protected act, engage in bad faith in a course of conduct that materially interferes with the tenant's rights under the lease. Each carries money penalties.

title: Statutory Forms
bodyText: Texas prescribes only a few forms a residential landlord uses. The floodplain notice, and the prior-flooding notice where you know of flood damage in the last five years, must be substantially in the statute's words, with its check boxes, and signed by you and the tenant (the library's flood disclosure clause). The lease must contain language substantially equivalent to the statute's statement on the tenant's special rights to end the lease early for family violence, certain sex offenses or stalking, or military service, or you lose the right to collect unpaid rent from a tenant who leaves under those rights (the library's statement clause). A homeowner removing an unauthorized occupant uses the complaint the statute sets out. Other notices (the electricity termination notice, the smoke-alarm notice, the repair-remedies statement) have required content and print, not a fixed text.

title: No Tenant Security-Camera Rule
bodyText: Texas statutes do not address tenant-installed security cameras or video doorbells. The lease's alteration and installation terms govern, subject to the tenant's statutory rights to rekey and to have security devices installed. A separate statute stops a homeowners' association from barring an owner's security camera on the owner's own property; it protects owners, not tenants.

title: No Accessory Dwelling Unit Statute
bodyText: No Texas statute deals with accessory dwelling units (a second, smaller home on the same lot, such as a garage apartment, backyard cottage or in-law suite). Nothing in state law requires a city to allow one, protects renting one out, or bars a city from requiring the owner to live on the lot (all Texas codes searched). Whether you may build and rent a second unit is left to the city's zoning ordinance: a city may regulate "the location and use of buildings, other structures, and land for business, industrial, residential, or other purposes" (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code § 211.003(a)(5)). So before you rent out a second unit, check the city's zoning and building rules, and any deed restrictions or owners' association rules on the lot. A second unit you rent is a dwelling like any other, and the Texas landlord-tenant rules in Chapter 92 of the Property Code apply to it.

title: Agreed Notice Methods and Actual Receipt
bodyText:
For a notice to vacate or a notice to pay rent or vacate, Texas lets you and the tenant agree in writing on one extra delivery method. A notice to vacate or a notice to pay rent or vacate must go by mail (including a delivery service), by delivery to the inside of the premises in a conspicuous place, by hand to a tenant 16 or older, or, "if the parties have agreed in writing, electronic communication, including e-mail or other electronic means" (Tex. Prop. Code § 24.005(f-3)).

The lease's optional e-mail consent clause is that written agreement. Whatever method you use, the delivery rules do not apply "if the tenant actually receives the notice" (§ 24.005(f-4)), but you must be able to prove that receipt, so use a listed method. No Texas statute defines actual notice for tenancies generally. For other notices the law requires in writing, an electronic record satisfies the writing rule only between parties who have each agreed to deal electronically, and where the other statute prescribes its own delivery method the notice must still go by that method, except that a first-class mail requirement may be varied by agreement where the other law permits (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §§ 322.005(b), 322.008(a), (b)(2), (d)(2); the library's electronic notices row); for a lease entered into or renewed on or after September 1, 2025, deposit notices may go by e-mail once you and the tenant have e-mailed each other (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.113; H.B. 2037, 89th Leg., R.S., SECTION 5).

Where a statute sets its own method, follow it. For the repair statute's timing rules, you are treated as having received a tenant's repair notice when you, your agent or employee actually receive it or when the Postal Service attempts delivery (§ 92.056(b)(4)-(5), (c)).

title: Notice of Foreclosure and Other Proceedings
bodyText:
No Texas statute requires you to tell a tenant or applicant that the property is in foreclosure, is the subject of a city substandard-building case, or faces another proceeding that could end the tenancy. The notices Texas does require run elsewhere. Before a foreclosure sale, the foreclosing lender "may" give the tenant written notice of the sale date. After a tax or trustee's foreclosure sale under a lien superior to the lease, a buyer who chooses not to continue the lease must give a residential tenant who is paying rent and not otherwise in default at least 30 days' written notice to vacate (Tex. Prop. Code § 24.005(b)).

A city's substandard-building ordinance must give notice to the owner, and the hearing order goes to the owner, lienholders and mortgagees, not the tenants, although the city may order the occupants relocated (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code § 214.001(b), (d), (g)). A buyer at foreclosure also takes subject to some of a tenant's pending repair remedies (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.0562(g)).

Because your tenant may first learn of a problem from a stranger, keep the lease clause asking the tenant to forward any notice of a proceeding to you, and tell tenants promptly yourself. Federal law (e.g. the Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act) may also apply; not reviewed here.

title: Charging a Tenant Who Disables a Smoke Alarm
bodyText: Texas sets its own remedies for a tenant who disables a smoke alarm, and no Texas statute authorizes a flat lease fee for it (all Texas codes searched). A tenant is liable if the tenant removes a battery without immediately replacing it with a working one, or knowingly disconnects or intentionally damages the alarm (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.2611(a)). You may sue for your actual damages, but not for damage caused by your own failure to repair the alarm within a reasonable time after the tenant asked (§ 92.2611(b), (c)). The stronger remedies need two things: the bold or underlined notice in the lease (the Smoke Alarms clause has it), and a separate written notice, given after you discover the problem, that you will use your remedies if the tenant does not fix it within seven days. If the tenant still does not comply, a court may order compliance and award a civil penalty of one month's rent plus $100, court costs and reasonable attorney's fees (§ 92.2611(d)-(e)). These are court judgments, not charges you may add to the rent. For damage the tenant or the tenant's household or guests cause, you need not repair the alarm unless the tenant pays the reasonable cost in advance (§ 92.258(c)). A fixed fee larger than your real cost risks being treated as an unenforceable penalty under Texas case law, so charge only the documented cost.

title: No Duty to Provide Alternate Housing
bodyText: No Texas statute requires you to move a tenant to another unit, pay for a hotel or provide substitute housing while repairs are made or after a fire, flood or other casualty (all Texas codes searched). What the law does instead: if a casualty not caused by the tenant's household or guests makes the unit totally unusable, either of you may end the lease by written notice before repairs are completed, with a pro rata rent refund and the deposit refund (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.054(b)). If a natural disaster makes the unit totally unusable and you choose to let the tenant move to another of your units, you may not require a lease longer than the term that was left on the old lease (§ 92.062). If a city or county revokes the certificate of occupancy because you failed to maintain the premises, you owe a tenant who is not in default the full deposit, prepaid rent, and actual damages including moving costs, utility connection fees, storage fees and lost wages, plus costs and attorney's fees (§ 92.023). A city may also order occupants of a substandard building relocated (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code § 214.001(d)). A separate rule requires owners of licensed migrant labor housing facilities to relocate occupants in some cases (Tex. Gov't Code § 2306.936(d)); it does not reach ordinary rentals.

title: No Right to Enter to Care for a Tenant's Animal
bodyText:
No Texas statute lets you enter a tenant's home to feed, water, care for or remove the tenant's animal when the tenant is away, in the hospital or otherwise unable to care for it. Texas also has no general entry-notice statute, so your right to enter comes from the lease. If you want to be able to act, get the tenant's consent in advance: the optional Animal Care clause has the tenant name a person who may be let in for that purpose only.

If an animal is being cruelly treated, which Texas defines to include being "unreasonably abandoned" or "unreasonably deprived of necessary food, care, or shelter", a peace officer or animal control officer may seek a court warrant to seize it (Tex. Health & Safety Code §§ 821.021, 821.022), so call animal control rather than acting yourself. If a tenant who lived alone dies, the deceased-tenant rules govern removal of the tenant's property, using the contact person the tenant named (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.014).

title: Asbestos in Rental Buildings
bodyText: No Texas statute requires you to inspect a rental for asbestos or to tell a tenant or applicant that a building contains it (all Texas codes searched). What Texas regulates is asbestos work in a "public building", a term that covers an apartment building with five or more units but not a private residence or "an apartment building that has not more than four dwelling units" (Tex. Occ. Code § 1954.002(11)). In a covered building, only a person licensed under the Texas Asbestos Health Protection Act may remove, encapsulate or enclose asbestos, do maintenance, repair or renovation that disturbs asbestos material, or perform an asbestos survey (§ 1954.101(a)); the person doing removal must notify the state health department in writing at least 10 days before starting (§ 1954.252). If a city requires a permit to renovate or demolish a public or commercial building, it may not issue the permit without a licensed asbestos survey of the affected parts or an engineer's or architect's certification that they contain no asbestos (§ 1954.259). If a state inspection finds an apparent danger to occupants, the department must require the owner to complete an immediate asbestos inspection (§ 1954.059(b)). Hire licensed contractors for work that may disturb old flooring, ceilings, insulation or pipe wrap. Asbestos that is damaged and releasing fibers may also be a condition that materially affects tenants' health or safety, which you must repair (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.052).

title: Renting a Home in an Owners' Association
bodyText: No Texas statute requires you to put an owners' association's obligations in the lease or to give the tenant the declaration, bylaws or rules (all Texas codes searched). Texas does set rules on what the association may do about your tenants. A subdivision property owners' association may not require your applicant or tenant to be approved by the association, and may not require you to hand over the applicant's credit report or rental application; it may still restrict occupancy or leasing, and it may ask for the name, mailing address, phone number and e-mail of each person who will live there and the lease start date and term (Tex. Prop. Code § 209.016). For a condominium whose declaration was recorded on or after January 1, 1994, or that has opted into the Uniform Condominium Act, the declaration may be amended to let the board evict your tenant for violating the declaration, bylaws or rules, evict a tenant who does not pay for substantial damage the tenant caused to common elements, or collect rent from your tenant when you are at least 60 days behind on amounts owed to the association (§ 82.067(h)). Because your tenant must follow rules the tenant may never have seen, give the tenant a copy of the association's current rules before signing, keep the lease's association compliance clause, and stay current on assessments.

title: Attorney's Fees in Texas Lease Disputes
bodyText: In an eviction, you can recover attorney's fees only if the written lease gives you a right to them, or you sent the tenant a written demand to vacate, by registered or certified mail at least 10 days before filing, warning that you may recover fees if the tenant does not leave before the 11th day after receiving it (Tex. Prop. Code § 24.006(a), (b)).
