Either route makes fees mutual: if the lease entitles you or the tenant to fees, or you sent that demand, a tenant who wins also recovers reasonable attorney's fees from you, without giving any notice (§ 24.006(c)). The winner recovers court costs in any event (§ 24.006(d)). In a suit under the general, repair, owner-disclosure or smoke-alarm subchapters of the residential tenancy chapter, the prevailing party recovers costs and reasonable attorney's fees, except fees for property damage, personal injury or criminal acts in disclosure and smoke-alarm suits (§ 92.005). For a claim on a written or oral contract, such as unpaid rent or damages, a represented party who presents the claim and is not paid the just amount within 30 days may recover fees from an individual or organization (Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code §§ 38.001(b)(8), 38.002). Many specific remedies add their own fee awards. The library's default clause carries a mutual prevailing-party fee sentence.

title: Automatic Renewal Clauses
bodyText: No Texas statute regulates automatic renewal clauses in residential leases: nothing requires special type, a reminder notice before the renewal date, or the tenant's separate consent, and nothing limits how early you may ask a tenant to commit to renewing (all Texas codes searched). A clause that renews the lease for a new fixed term unless someone gives notice is therefore a matter of contract, and this library does not offer one: the Texas lease ends at its end date, and if the tenant stays and you accept rent it continues month to month, which either of you may end on one month's notice unless you both signed an agreement setting a different period (Tex. Prop. Code § 91.001). If you want a fixed-term renewal by silence, have a lawyer draft it, make it prominent, and remind the tenant before the deadline, since case law on unexpected renewals was not reviewed. Two related rules: a guarantor is bound for a renewal only if the original lease meets the conditions in § 92.021 (see the guarantor row), and leases of manufactured-home lots have their own renewal-offer procedure (§ 94.055).

title: No Balcony Inspection Requirement
bodyText: No Texas statute requires periodic inspection of balconies, decks, walkways or other exterior elevated elements of a rental building, or a report to tenants or the city (all Texas codes searched). The closest state rule is the old fire escape law: the owner of an apartment house, rooming house or similar building of at least three stories must equip it with at least one fire escape, unless the city has a model building code with an equivalent fire-resistive escape requirement; the fire escape must be inspected before it is approved for use, and an iron or steel one must be repainted at least every two years (Tex. Health & Safety Code §§ 791.002, 791.004, 791.006, 791.016, 791.021). A loose railing or a rotting balcony is still a condition that may materially affect tenants' safety, which you must repair after notice (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.052), so inspect exterior elevated elements yourself on a regular schedule. City building and property-maintenance codes may impose their own inspections.

title: Pest Treatments and Tenant Cooperation
bodyText:
No Texas statute requires a tenant to report, prepare for or cooperate with bed bug or other insect treatment, so those terms come from the lease; the optional Pest Reporting and Treatment clause supplies them. The only statute on cost is narrow: under the county poison subchapter, a tenant must poison listed pests that infest the premises, such as rats, gophers and prairie dogs, and the tenant's expenses "shall be charged against the landowner" (Tex. Health & Safety Code §§ 825.021, 825.024(b)); it does not reach bed bugs or other insects.

Texas does regulate notice of indoor pesticide treatments. At a rental property with fewer than five units, the licensed applicator must make the state's pest control information sheet available to the tenant of each unit. At a property with five or more units, the applicator gives the sheet and sign to you, and you or your staff must notify residents in the treatment area or an adjacent area at least 48 hours before each planned treatment, either by posting the sign in a common area or by leaving the sheet on or inside each unit's door (Tex. Occ. Code § 1951.453).

Your repair duty covers an infestation that materially affects an ordinary tenant's health or safety, but not one caused by the tenant, a lawful occupant, family member or guest (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.052). Entry for treatment runs through the lease's entry clause.

title: Arbitration Clauses in a Lease
bodyText:
No Texas statute speaks to arbitration clauses in residential leases specifically, but the Texas Arbitration Act limits them. A written agreement to arbitrate future disputes is generally valid (Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 171.001). The Act does not apply, though, to an agreement by an individual to acquire property or services for total consideration of $50,000 or less unless both parties agree in writing and the agreement is "signed by each party and each party's attorney", and it does not reach a personal injury claim unless each party agrees on the advice of counsel and both parties and their attorneys sign (§ 171.002).

Most residential leases fall under the $50,000 limit. In addition, a tenant's right to a jury trial in an action under Chapter 92 of the Property Code cannot be waived in a lease (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.006(h)), and eviction suits belong in the justice court (§ 24.004). Federal law also matters here: the Federal Arbitration Act overrides state rules that block arbitration directly or indirectly (for example, a rule against giving up a jury), and the U.S. Supreme Court has held that renting out real estate is activity it reaches.

On that basis the library now offers an optional clause, `arbitration-agreement`: money claims only, with possession, small claims, security-deposit, injury, emergency and government-agency matters kept out, every remedy and the right to a lawyer kept, the arbitration fees above a court filing fee paid by you, a 30-day opt-out for the tenant, and separate initials from both of you.

Because state law points the other way, a court here could still refuse to enforce it; if one did, the dispute would simply go to court.

title: Marijuana and Low-THC Cannabis
bodyText:
Texas has no adult-use marijuana law: knowingly possessing a usable quantity of marihuana is a crime (Tex. Health & Safety Code § 481.121). The one exception for patients is low-THC cannabis, which may contain no more than 10 milligrams of THC per dosage unit, prescribed under the Compassionate Use Program (Tex. Occ. Code § 169.001(3)). The exemption covers only a patient who possesses low-THC cannabis "obtained under a valid prescription from a dispensing organization" (§ 481.111(e)(1)), so home growing is not protected.

Medical use excludes smoking, though vaporizing is allowed (Occ. Code § 169.001(4)-(5)). No Texas statute protects a patient or anyone else in housing, or stops you from banning marijuana, including prescribed low-THC cannabis, in a lease. The rule that cities and counties may not prohibit possession of low-THC cannabis binds local governments, not landlords (§ 487.201).

The Smoking Policy clause already bans smoking marijuana anywhere on the property; the optional Marijuana Restrictions clause can also ban vaping, growing, or possessing or using it in any form. If a tenant with a prescription asks for an exception because of a disability, get advice first: federal fair housing law may apply; not reviewed here.

title: Carpet Cleaning Charges at Move-Out
bodyText: No Texas statute deals with carpet cleaning at move-out: nothing lets you require professional cleaning, and nothing sets a carpet age or depreciation rule (all Texas codes searched). The deposit rules decide it. You may deduct "damages and charges for which the tenant is legally liable under the lease or as a result of breaching the lease", but you "may not retain any portion of a security deposit to cover normal wear and tear" (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.104(a)-(b)). Normal wear and tear is deterioration from the intended use of the dwelling; it does not include deterioration from negligence, carelessness, accident or abuse by the tenant, a household member or a guest (§ 92.001(4)). So you may charge the reasonable cost of cleaning or repairing stains, pet damage and other soiling beyond ordinary use, listed in the written itemization, but a routine cleaning charge for carpets that show only ordinary use risks being a deduction for normal wear and tear. A bad-faith deduction costs $100 plus three times the amount wrongfully withheld and attorney's fees, and you bear the burden of proving a deduction was reasonable (§ 92.109). For that reason this library does not offer a mandatory professional-cleaning clause for Texas. Photograph the carpets at move-in and move-out.

title: Which Casualty and Re-Letting Rules a Lease May Change
bodyText:
Texas lets a lease change one casualty rule and none of the others. If a casualty not caused by the tenant's household or guests leaves the unit partially unusable, the tenant's proportional rent reduction is available "only on judgment of a county or district court", but "A landlord and tenant may agree otherwise in a written lease" (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.054(c)); the Casualty Loss clause uses that permission to make the reduction automatic.

The rest of the casualty section sits in the repair subchapter, whose duties and tenant remedies "may not be waived" except through the specific tenant-repair agreements the statute lists (§ 92.006(c)). So a lease may not take away the right of either party to end the lease when a non-tenant-caused casualty makes the unit totally unusable, or change the tenant's pro rata rent and deposit refund (§ 92.054(b)), and knowingly contracting to waive the repair duty carries one month's rent plus $2,000, actual damages and attorney's fees (§ 92.0563(b)).

Mitigation cannot be waived at all: if a tenant abandons in violation of the lease you must mitigate your damages, and a lease term that "purports to waive a right or to exempt a landlord from a liability or duty under this section is void" (§ 91.006).

title: No Certificate of Occupancy Disclosure
bodyText: No Texas statute requires you to tell a tenant whether the unit has a certificate of occupancy, to give the tenant a copy, or to state its status in the lease, and no state statute bars collecting rent for a unit that lacks one (all Texas codes searched). Certificates of occupancy are issued by cities and counties under their own codes. Two state rules matter. If a city or county revokes the certificate of occupancy because you failed to maintain the premises, you owe a tenant who is not in default the full deposit, any rent paid in advance for the unused period, the tenant's actual damages including moving costs, utility connection fees, storage fees and lost wages, and court costs and attorney's fees (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.023). And on your request a city that has a record of the original certificate must give you a document verifying it, which the city must accept for display in place of the original (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code § 214.909). Before renting, especially a converted space or an added unit, confirm with the city that the unit may lawfully be occupied as a residence.

title: Children in the Household
bodyText:
Texas fair housing law protects families with children. You may not refuse to rent, set different terms, or otherwise deny a dwelling "because of ... familial status" (Tex. Prop. Code § 301.021), which covers a person who is pregnant, who lives with a child under 18 as parent or legal custodian or with the parent's written permission, or who is in the process of getting legal custody of a child (§ 301.004). That protection also covers a child born or adopted during the tenancy, so do not raise the rent, add fees or end a tenancy because a child joins the household.

The state occupancy cap counts only adults: you may not allow more than three adults (18 or older) per bedroom, unless a fair housing law requires a higher rate or the extra adult is seeking temporary sanctuary from family violence for no more than one month (§ 92.010), and children do not count toward it. The fair housing law does not affect a reasonable local or state limit on the number of occupants or a health or safety standard (§ 301.044(a)), so any occupancy limit of your own must be reasonable and applied the same way to every household.

Qualifying senior housing is exempt from the familial-status rules (§ 301.043). No Texas statute requires the lease to list or address children; name them as occupants in the Permitted Occupants clause. Federal fair housing law may also apply; not reviewed here.

title: No Cold-Weather Vacating Notice in Texas
bodyText: Texas has no rule requiring a tenant to warn you before leaving a unit empty in cold weather, and no statute on freezing pipes or a heating season for rentals (all Texas codes searched). If you want that notice, put it in the lease: the library's optional Notice of Extended Absence clause asks the tenant to tell you before a long absence, and the tenant's notice also helps you avoid treating an empty unit as abandoned when it is not (see the library's abandonment rows). Your repair duty does not change with the season: once the tenant gives notice of a condition that materially affects the physical health or safety of an ordinary tenant, such as a burst pipe, you must make a diligent effort to repair it, unless the tenant, an occupant, family member or guest caused it other than by normal wear and tear (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.052(a), (b)). The cold-weather rules Texas does have run against you, not the tenant: if you submeter or allocate electricity, you may not cut it off for nonpayment on a day after a high of 32 degrees Fahrenheit or lower when the temperature is predicted to stay there for 24 hours (§ 92.008(i)(3)(A)); after an extended freeze or other natural disaster, a repair-delay affidavit can delay the tenant's own repairs by 30 days for a general shortage of labor or materials, and later affidavits by no more than six months in all from the first (§ 92.0562(c)(2), (d)); if the freeze makes the unit totally unusable and you move the tenant to another of your units, you may not require a longer lease than the term left (§ 92.062); and an officer executing a writ may not put belongings outside while it is raining, sleeting or snowing (§ 24.0061(d)(2)(D)).

title: Collection Fees in Texas
bodyText: Texas's debt-collection law bars collecting, or trying to collect, any interest, charge, fee or expense incidental to a debt unless the agreement creating the debt expressly authorizes it or it is otherwise legally chargeable (Tex. Fin. Code § 392.303(a)(2)). It also bars representing that a debt may be increased by attorney's fees, service fees or other charges that no written contract or statute authorizes, or that it will definitely be increased by fees a court has discretion over (§ 392.304(a)(12), (13)). So if you intend to pass on a collection-agency fee or other collection cost, the lease must say so expressly, and you should collect only the amount it describes. Whether the act reaches a landlord collecting its own rent, rather than a third-party collector, is not settled by the statute and has not been reviewed here, so follow it either way. A violation can be enforced by injunction and actual damages and is also a deceptive trade practice (the library's consumer protection row). Attorney's fees in an eviction follow their own rule (the library's attorney's fees row).

title: Common-Area Lighting and Its Electricity
bodyText: No Texas statute sets a lighting standard for hallways, stairways, entrances or parking areas of a rental property, and none lists lighting among the security devices you must provide (all Texas codes searched). A broken or missing light in a common area may still be a condition that materially affects tenants' safety, which you must repair after notice (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.052), and city codes may set standards. Who pays for common-area electricity is regulated only where you submeter. In a submetered apartment house of more than five units, condominium or mobile home park, the lease must state that "electrical consumption charges for all common areas and common facilities will be the responsibility of the owner and not of the tenant", and each tenant's bill may reflect only that unit's submetered use (16 Tex. Admin. Code § 25.142(d)); the Submetered Electricity clause carries that statement. Outside submetering, no Texas statute addresses common-area lights that are wired to a tenant's own electric account. If that is the case in a small building, say so plainly in the lease's utilities terms before the tenant signs, or move the lights to your own meter.

title: No Government Approval Needed for a Lease
bodyText: Texas has no communal, tribal or native land-tenure system that makes an ordinary residential lease wait for a government officer's approval, and no statute that makes rent or possession depend on such an approval (all Texas codes searched). Your lease is valid when you and the tenant make it. The one state formality is length: a lease of real estate "for a term longer than one year" is not enforceable unless it, or a memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by the person to be charged (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 26.01(b)(5)). Leases of land held in trust for one of the federally recognized tribes in Texas are governed by federal law; if you are asked to lease on tribal land, get advice first.

title: Rent After a City Orders a Unit Vacated
bodyText: No Texas statute says in so many words that you may not collect rent for a unit that a city has condemned, ordered vacated or found unfit to live in (all Texas codes searched). The result usually follows from other rules. If a city or county revokes the certificate of occupancy because you failed to maintain the premises, you owe a tenant who is not in default the full deposit, the pro rata share of any rent paid in advance, actual damages including moving costs, utility connection fees, storage fees and lost wages, and court costs and attorney's fees (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.023). If a casualty not caused by the tenant's household or guests makes the unit totally unusable, either of you may end the lease by written notice given before repairs are completed, and the tenant then gets a pro rata rent refund from the date the tenant moves out (§ 92.054(b)). A city acting on a substandard building may order it vacated and the occupants relocated (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code § 214.001(d)). And a condition that materially affects health or safety, left unrepaired after proper notice, lets the tenant end the lease with a pro rata rent refund (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.056(e)-(f)). Do not demand rent for any period the tenant cannot lawfully live in the unit; get advice before doing so.

title: No Move-In Inventory or Inspection Requirement
bodyText:
No Texas statute requires a move-in inventory or condition checklist, a joint walk-through, a signed statement of condition, or a move-out inspection, and none makes deposit deductions depend on one. Two move-in checks are required for specific equipment: you must test each smoke alarm at the beginning of the tenant's possession (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.258(b)), and if you installed a residential fire extinguisher you must check at move-in that it is present and its gauge shows the correct pressure (§ 92.263).

A written record still matters, because in a deposit suit you have "the burden of proving that the retention of any portion of the security deposit was reasonable" (§ 92.109(c)), and you may not deduct for normal wear and tear (§ 92.104(b)). So complete a dated move-in condition report with photos, have the tenant sign it, attach it to the lease as the exceptions the Existing Condition clause refers to, and repeat it at move-out.

title: Confession of Judgment Is Barred in Texas
bodyText: A Texas lease cannot include a confession of judgment, a waiver of service or an agreement that the tenant will appear in court on your behalf. Texas law says that in an instrument signed before a suit is brought, a person "may not accept service and waive process, enter an appearance in open court, or confess a judgment" (Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 30.001). So a lease clause authorizing judgment against the tenant without a suit, or appointing someone to accept service for the tenant, has no effect. To recover possession or money you must file suit and have the tenant served in the ordinary way; an eviction citation may be served only by a sheriff or constable, or, if they have not served it within five business days, by another trained law enforcement officer on an alias citation the clerk issues at your request (Tex. R. Civ. P. 510.8(d); Tex. Prop. Code § 24.0051(f)). Agreements made after a suit is filed, such as an agreed judgment, are a different matter and are not covered by this row.

title: Habitability: What Texas Has and Lacks
bodyText: How Texas compares on habitability features found in other states. Present: a statutory duty to repair conditions that materially affect an ordinary tenant's health or safety, and hot water at 120 degrees, after the tenant's notice given while not delinquent in rent, with the tenant's remedies of termination, limited repair-and-deduct and court orders; this scheme replaces common-law habitability warranties (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.061); see the repair-duty row. Absent (all Texas codes searched): (1) an implied warranty of habitability for an ordinary dwelling lease (the only statutory lease warranty is that a manufactured home lot is suitable for installing a home, § 94.151); (2) any right to withhold rent for repairs: a tenant who does so in violation of the repair subchapter owes you actual damages, and after your written notice of the illegality and the penalties, a tenant who does so in bad faith owes one month's rent plus $500, which you must prove by clear and convincing evidence (§ 92.058); (3) rent escrow for repairs (rent is paid into a court registry only during an eviction appeal); (4) a minimum indoor temperature or heating standard; (5) any duty to supply air conditioning, which matters only if the lease furnishes cooling equipment (§ 92.0561(d)(3)(C)); (6) a statutory list of uninhabitable conditions. Covered in their own rows: no alternate-housing duty, no express rent bar for condemned units, no mold, bed bug, carbon monoxide alarm or balcony inspection statute. City housing codes may set heat, cooling or other standards.

title: Other Rules Texas Does Not Have
bodyText: Rules found in some other states for which no Texas statute was found (all Texas codes searched). (1) Rent reporting: no Texas statute requires, limits or sets notice for reporting a tenant's rent payments to a credit bureau. (2) Energy or utility-cost disclosure: beyond the submetering disclosures, nothing requires you to give an applicant the unit's past energy use or utility costs. (3) Blank spaces: the Texas rules against signing a contract with blank spaces apply to retail installment and consumer credit contracts (for example Tex. Fin. Code § 345.108), not leases; still fill in or strike every blank before anyone signs. (4) Government shutdown or late benefits: no Texas statute gives a tenant extra time or a defense when a government benefit payment is delayed. Each of these is also absent and covered in its own row: no accessory dwelling unit statute, no government approval needed for a lease, no automatic-renewal rule, no rent-increase notice statute, no algorithmic rent-setting rule, no EV-charging right, no tenant camera rule, no immigration-inquiry rule, no eviction-record sealing, no just-cause eviction, no landlord self-cure statute, no lease-completeness or quiet-possession statute, and no plain-language rule. Federal law and city ordinances were not reviewed, nor was case law.

title: Checked Across All of Texas Law
bodyText: These questions were checked across every Texas code, not only the Property Code. (1) Squatters: present. Since September 1, 2025 an owner may ask the sheriff or a constable to remove an unauthorized occupant without an eviction suit, on strict conditions (see the squatter removal row). (2) Rent receipts: present for cash. If you accept cash rent you must give a written receipt and record the date and amount in a record book; a tenant who wins a suit over it may recover court costs, reasonable attorney's fees and the greater of one month's rent or $500 per violation (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.011(c)). (3) Registration before eviction: absent for rentals, but two business-registration rules can stop a suit. Texas has no state rental registration or landlord licensing law, and nothing in the eviction statutes makes registration a condition of filing or winning an eviction. But an out-of-state LLC, corporation or limited partnership that is transacting business in Texas may not maintain a suit, including an eviction, on a claim arising from that business until it registers with the secretary of state (Tex. Bus. Orgs. Code §§ 9.001, 9.051(b)); owning Texas property, without more, is not transacting business (§ 9.251(15)), but whether renting it out is more is not settled by statute, so register before filing. And if you regularly rent under an assumed name (for an individual, a name without your surname; for an entity, a name other than the one in its formation papers), you may not maintain a suit arising from a lease made under that name until you file an assumed name certificate (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §§ 71.002(2), 71.051, 71.101, 71.201(a); the library's landlord registration row). Neither failure voids the lease or stops you from defending a suit (Tex. Bus. Orgs. Code § 9.051(c); Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 71.201(a)). Some cities have registration ordinances, which may be limited by state preemption (see the preemption row). (4) Lease print and plain language: no Texas statute sets a type size, plain-language or readability standard for a residential lease as a whole; specific print rules apply only to specific terms, which the library's clauses mark.

title: Contractor Liens for a Tenant's Work
bodyText:
Texas's mechanic's lien law gives a lien to a person who furnishes labor or materials for an improvement "under a contract with the owner or the owner's agent, trustee, receiver, contractor, or subcontractor" (Tex. Prop. Code § 53.021), and the lien reaches the improvements and the land they sit on (§ 53.022). An original contract is one to which the owner is a party "either directly or by implication of law" (§ 53.001(6)).

Chapter 53 never mentions tenants, leases or lessees, so whether a contractor your tenant hires can lien your ownership interest turns on whether the tenant acted as your agent or you became a party by implication of law. Only case law answers that, and it is not reviewed here. One rule is statutory: when a tenant uses the repair-and-deduct remedy, you are not liable to the repairers or suppliers, and they "shall not have a lien" for those repairs (§ 92.0561(i)).

No other Texas statute deals with liens for work a tenant orders. What to do: require your written consent before any alteration or improvement, and say in that consent that you are not agreeing to pay for the work. The optional "No Liens for Tenant Work" clause gives you a lease remedy and evidence that the tenant was not your agent, but it cannot bind a contractor who never signed it. If a lien is filed against your property for a tenant's work, get legal advice promptly.

title: Converting Rentals to Condominiums
bodyText: If you convert a rental building into condominiums, the Texas Uniform Condominium Act protects the residential tenants in it. A conversion building is one that was occupied, in whole or part, by people other than purchasers before the condominium was created (Tex. Prop. Code § 82.003(a)(9)). As declarant you must give each residential tenant or subtenant in possession notice of the conversion at least 60 days before the date you will require them to vacate. The notice must state generally the tenants' rights under the statute and be hand-delivered to the unit or sent by certified mail, return receipt requested (§ 82.160(a)). You may not require a tenant to vacate on less than 60 days' notice except for nonpayment of rent, waste, or conduct that violates the lease or is illegal, and you may not change the terms of the tenancy during that period. Failing to give the notice is a defense to your eviction suit. A conversion notice that names a vacate date and meets the eviction-notice rules also serves as the notice to vacate, but it does not let you end a lease early in breach of its terms (§ 82.160(b)). Unless the lease expressly allows it, you may not make substantial alterations inside a leased unit for the conversion (§ 82.160(c)). Your condominium information statement must also report the building's condition and uncured code violations (§ 82.154). Texas gives tenants no right to buy their unit on conversion and requires no conversion statement in the lease (all Texas codes searched). City ordinances may add rules; check locally.

title: Criminal Activity and Ending the Lease
bodyText:
Texas has no statute that gives you a fast-track eviction for drug or violent crime, no statute that implies a no-crime promise into a lease, and no statute requiring you to evict a tenant for crime. The Property Code's fast-track rule ending possession for prostitution, human trafficking or an unlicensed massage business applies only to commercial leases (Tex. Prop. Code §§ 93.001, 93.013). So your lease is what makes criminal conduct a ground for ending the tenancy.

Texas's retaliation law treats it that way: ending a lease because the tenant "materially breached the lease ... by an action such as violating written lease provisions prohibiting serious misconduct or criminal acts" is a valid ground in any event and is not retaliation (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.332(b)(3)). Intentional damage to property, or threats to the safety of you, your employees or another tenant, by the tenant, family or guests is a separate valid ground (§ 92.332(b)(2)).

Use the optional "Criminal Activity" clause to put that written prohibition in the lease, then give the written notice to vacate the lease and § 24.005 require before you file. A conviction under the Penal Code's public indecency chapter for use of the property is its own termination right (§ 91.003; see the public indecency row). Crime you tolerate can also expose the property to a common-nuisance suit (see the nuisance row). Never penalize a tenant for calling the police or for emergency help (§ 92.015).

title: Eviction Grounds and the Missing Cure Period in Texas
bodyText:
Texas sets no cure period for a lease violation. The eviction ground is a tenant who refuses to leave after "the termination of the tenant's right of possession" (Tex. Prop. Code § 24.002(a)(1)), so the question is what ended that right: the end of the term, a month-to-month termination notice (§ 91.001), or a default your lease makes a ground for ending the tenancy.

Before filing you must give at least three days' written notice to vacate, or the period your lease sets (§ 24.005(a)). The only statutory chance to pay is for rent: if you evict solely for nonpayment and the tenant was not late before the month of the notice, the notice must be a notice to pay rent or vacate (§ 24.005(a)). For any other breach, no Texas statute gives the tenant a right to cure; a cure opportunity exists only if your lease promises one, and then you must honor it.

No statute lists which breaches justify ending the lease; that turns on your lease and case law, so say plainly in the lease which failures are defaults. Two statutes help: some grounds are valid "in any event" against a retaliation defense, including rent delinquency, intentional damage or threats to safety, and a material breach such as violating written lease rules against serious misconduct or criminal acts (§ 92.332(b)); and if you never gave the tenant a copy of the lease and the tenant shows the court evidence of that, the court must pause an action to enforce the lease, other than one for nonpayment of rent, until you do (§ 92.024(d)).

A lease combined with an option to buy a home the tenant-buyer or a close relative lives in is different: the tenant-buyer gets 30 days after your default notice to cure before forfeiture (§§ 5.062(a)(2), 5.064, 5.065), unless the contract provides for delivering the deed within 180 days (§ 5.062(c)).

title: No Defective Drywall Disclosure Statute
bodyText: No Texas statute requires you to disclose defective (corrosive or imported) drywall to a tenant, or says anything about drywall in rentals. Two general rules still reach the problem. First, if drywall gives off fumes, corrodes wiring or causes another condition that materially affects the physical health or safety of an ordinary tenant, it falls under your repair duty once the tenant gives notice (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.052; see the repair duty row). Second, the Deceptive Trade Practices Act treats real property leased for use as goods (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 17.45(1)). It lists as deceptive "failing to disclose information concerning goods or services which was known at the time of the transaction" when the silence was meant to induce a deal the consumer would otherwise have refused (§ 17.46(b)(24)). What to do: if you know or suspect problem drywall (a sulfur smell, blackened copper wiring or pipes, failing air-conditioner coils), have it assessed and fixed before you rent, and tell a prospective tenant in writing about any known problem that is not fixed.

title: Pre-Set Cleaning and Repair Charges
bodyText:
Texas has no statute on pre-set cleaning, carpet or repair charges and no special notice for them. The deposit statute lets you deduct "damages and charges for which the tenant is legally liable under the lease or as a result of breaching the lease" (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.104(a)), so a charge your lease clearly makes the tenant liable for can come out of the deposit.

Three limits apply to any schedule. You may never keep any part of the deposit for normal wear and tear (§ 92.104(b)). You must still give a written, itemized list of every deduction within 30 days (§§ 92.103(a), 92.104(c)). And if the tenant sues, you bear the burden of proving that what you kept was reasonable (§ 92.109(c)), so a flat charge far above the real cost, or one charged when the work was not needed, is hard to defend; whether a court would treat it as an unenforceable penalty is case law, not reviewed here.

Some charges have their own statutory rules and override a general schedule: the turnover rekey is at your expense, and you may deduct a rekey cost only when a tenant leaves in breach and a bold or underlined lease term allows it (§ 92.156); a tenant pays for security-device repairs only for misuse and only under an underlined lease term, at cost (§ 92.162); and if a tenant who never moves in is replaced by a tenant who moves in by the lease start date, you keep nothing when the tenant found the replacement, and only the agreed cancellation fee or your actual re-letting costs when you did (§ 92.1031).

What to do: if you list charges, keep each close to your actual cost, apply it only when the work is done, and itemize it.

title: No Right to Pay the Deposit in Installments
bodyText: No Texas statute gives a tenant the right to pay a security deposit in installments, or requires you to offer that. Texas also sets no cap on the deposit amount (see the deposit cap row). You may agree to take the deposit in installments if you want to; if you do, write the schedule into the lease and treat every amount received as part of the deposit, because a security deposit is "any advance of money" meant mainly to secure performance under the lease (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.102), and all the refund and itemization rules apply to it. The one statutory alternative is a fee in lieu of a security deposit: you may offer it only alongside the option of paying a regular deposit, it must be a recurring fee paid with each rent payment, and it carries written-notice and insurance rules of its own (§ 92.111; see the fee in lieu row). Whatever you choose, offer the same terms to every applicant, so that the choice cannot be read as treating a protected group differently.

title: Who May Make a Tenant Repair
bodyText: Texas sets by statute who may make a repair the tenant has done under the repair-and-deduct remedy, and it gives you no right to choose that person. The repair "must be made by an independent company, contractor, or repairman", licensed where the city requires a license, and in compliance with building codes and permits (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.0561(f), (h)). Unless you and the tenant agree otherwise, it may not be made by the tenant, the tenant's immediate family, employer or employees, or a company the tenant owns part of, and no tenant repair may touch the foundation or load-bearing structure of a building with two or more units (§ 92.0561(f)). For a lease signed or renewed before September 1, 2025, the older rule applies: a repairer listed in the yellow or business pages or newspaper classifieds. No Texas statute lets you name the repairer a tenant must use. Because the repair remedies cannot be waived except in the narrow ways § 92.006 allows, do not put a clause in your lease that limits the tenant to your contractor; it risks being a void waiver, and a knowing waiver of the repair duty costs one month's rent plus $2,000, actual damages and fees (§ 92.0563(b)). What you may do: give tenants a repair contact, require repair requests in writing (§ 92.052(d)), agree with a tenant in a particular case that the tenant will repair a condition at your expense (§ 92.0561(g)), and, best of all, repair promptly so the remedy never opens.

title: Disability Modifications and Accommodations
bodyText:
Under the Texas Fair Housing Act, refusing a disabled tenant's request can itself be discrimination. The disability section does not apply to a single-family house you rent yourself if you own no more than three such houses and rent it without a broker, anyone in the rental business or a discriminatory advertisement. It also does not apply to a building of up to four units where you live in one (Tex. Prop. Code § 301.041(a)).

Federal law may still apply. You must permit a reasonable modification of the premises, at the tenant's expense, if it may be needed for the tenant's full enjoyment of the premises. You must also make a reasonable accommodation in your rules, policies, practices or services if it may be needed to give the tenant equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling (Tex. Prop. Code § 301.025(c)(1)-(2)).

You need not rent to someone whose tenancy would be a direct threat to others' health or safety or would cause substantial physical damage to others' property (§ 301.025(f)). The Texas text says nothing about making the tenant restore the unit at move-out or pay into an escrow account for restoration, and no Texas statute requires your lease to state such a condition.

Federal law (e.g. the Fair Housing Act) may allow a restoration condition and may also apply; it is not reviewed here, so get advice before you impose one. Separately, a tenant with a trained service dog is entitled to full and equal access to housing (any home or sleeping place, except a single-family residence whose occupants rent out only one room) and "may not be required to pay extra compensation or make a deposit for the animal", though the tenant is liable for damage the animal does beyond reasonable wear and tear (Tex. Hum. Res. Code §§ 121.002(1), 121.003(g)-(h)).

A violation is a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $300 and 30 hours of community service, and the tenant may sue with damages conclusively presumed to be at least $300 (§ 121.004). On request, a smoke alarm must be able to alert a hearing-impaired person in the bedrooms it serves (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.254(a-1)). Answer each request promptly and in writing, and discuss alternatives before saying no.

title: Housing Disaster Evacuees as Guests
bodyText: No Texas statute lets a tenant house people displaced by a hurricane, flood or other disaster in spite of the lease's guest or occupancy terms, or stops you from enforcing those terms after a disaster. Your lease's guest terms therefore still apply, and you may give written consent to longer stays if you want to help. One statutory ceiling does not bend for disasters: you may not allow more than three adults per bedroom to occupy a dwelling. The only exceptions are where fair housing law requires more, or for an adult seeking temporary sanctuary from family violence for up to one month (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.010(a)-(b)). Neighbors within 3,000 feet can sue to stop a violation and recover $500 per violation plus fees (§ 92.010(c)). Whether a short-term guest counts as an occupant under that section is not settled by its text, so count long-stay evacuees. In a declared disaster the governor may control "the movement of persons and the occupancy of premises" in the disaster area and may commandeer private property, with compensation (Tex. Gov't Code §§ 418.017(c), 418.018(c)); follow any such order. If your own tenant's unit is destroyed and you move the tenant to another of your units, see the disaster duties row.

title: Natural Disasters and Your Lease
bodyText: No Texas statute ends a tenancy, suspends rent or stops evictions just because a disaster is declared. The damage rules do the work instead. If the unit is, as a practical matter, totally unusable after a casualty the tenant did not cause, either of you may end the lease by written notice before repairs are finished; the tenant then gets only a pro rata rent refund from move-out and the deposit refund the law requires (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.054(b)). If it is partly unusable, the tenant's rent reduction comes only by court judgment unless the lease agrees otherwise (§ 92.054(c); the Casualty Loss clause does). For an insured loss, the repair period starts when you receive the insurance money (§ 92.054(a)). A post-disaster shortage of labor or materials lets you delay a tenant's own repair by a 30-day sworn affidavit (§ 92.0562(c)(2)). If you move a displaced tenant to another of your units, you may not require a lease term longer than what was left on the old lease (§ 92.062). Three disaster-only rules matter too. During a declared disaster period, leasing lodging or another necessity at an exorbitant or excessive price is a deceptive trade practice (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §§ 17.46(b)(27), 17.4625). A city may adopt rent control for a disaster housing emergency if the governor approves (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code § 214.902). And only the Legislature may change eviction procedure, except for a general Supreme Court disaster order that applies to all courts (Tex. Prop. Code § 24.0043). So hold rents steady during a declared disaster and check for local and court orders before you file.

title: Renting One Unit to Two Tenants
bodyText: No Texas statute deals with double letting, meaning renting the same unit or room to two tenants for the same period, or sets a special remedy for it. Texas also has no statute on a landlord's failure to deliver possession on the start date. If you promise one unit to two people, you are in breach of at least one lease, and ordinary contract remedies apply. The shared Possession Delay clause only covers a delay "through no fault of Landlord", so it will not protect you from your own double booking. Representing that a lease gives a tenant rights it does not have, or hiding known information to get a tenant to sign, can also be a deceptive trade practice (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 17.46(b)(12), (24)). Once a tenant is in possession, you may not lock that tenant out to make room for someone else except as the lockout statute allows; a wrongful lockout lets the tenant recover possession or end the lease, plus one month's rent plus $1,000, actual damages, court costs and attorney's fees, less any delinquent rent or other sums the tenant owes you (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.0081(b), (h)). What to do: keep one booking record per unit, do not take a second application or deposit for a unit you have already promised, and if you do double-book, tell the second tenant at once and refund everything that tenant paid.

title: No Drug-Free Lease Addendum Statute
bodyText: No Texas statute requires, authorizes, regulates or forbids a drug-free or crime-free lease addendum, and no state statute lets a city require one. Texas's "drug-free zones" raise criminal punishment for drug offenses near schools, playgrounds and similar places (Tex. Health & Safety Code § 481.134); they are not a housing rule. You do not need a separate addendum. A written lease term that prohibits illegal drug activity and other crime already does the job Texas law recognizes: ending a lease because the tenant violated "written lease provisions prohibiting serious misconduct or criminal acts" is a valid ground that is not retaliation (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.332(b)(3)). The library's optional Criminal Activity clause is that term (see the criminal activity row). If you use your own addendum, make sure it does not limit or penalize a tenant's call for police or emergency help, because a lease provision that does so is void and carries a penalty (§ 92.015). If your property is in a federally assisted program, the program's own lease rules may require specific language; they are not reviewed here.

title: Keeping Sexual-Offense and Stalking Information Confidential
bodyText: If a tenant gives you documents or a termination notice to end a lease after sexual assault, other listed sexual offenses or stalking, you may not disclose that information to anyone except for a legitimate or customary business purpose or as the law requires (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.0161(j)). The family-violence termination section has no matching sentence (§ 92.016), but treat family-violence documents the same way: share them only with staff who need them to process the termination, keep them out of tenant screening reports and references, and don't discuss them with other tenants. A victim of certain offenses may also choose a pseudonym for public files and records about the offense, and a stalking termination may come with the victim's pseudonym form; keep it with the termination file and do not use the victim's name where the form is used (Tex. Code Crim. Proc. art. 58.152(a); Tex. Prop. Code § 92.0161(c-1)(2)(B)).

title: Deposits After a Family-Violence Termination in Texas
bodyText: Texas has no special deposit rule for a lease ended after family violence, sexual assault or stalking (all Texas codes searched). The ordinary rules apply: refund the deposit, with an itemized list of any deductions, within 30 days after the tenant surrenders the premises, once the tenant has given a written forwarding address (Tex. Prop. Code §§ 92.103(a), 92.104, 92.107). The statute does not say whether the 30 days wait until every occupant or cotenant has left when only the victim terminates; that turns on the lease and on case law not reviewed here. The cautious course: when a victim leaves and a cotenant stays, say in writing to both how the deposit will be handled, and refund or account for the victim's share within 30 days of the victim's surrender unless the lease makes the deposit a single joint fund held until everyone leaves.

title: Evicting a Tenant Who Is a Family-Violence Victim in Texas
bodyText: Texas has no statute that bars evicting, refusing to rent to or ending the tenancy of a tenant because the tenant is a victim of family violence, sexual assault or stalking (all Texas codes searched). Related protections do apply. You may not limit a tenant's right to call the police or emergency help, or penalize a tenant for doing so, when the tenant reasonably believes someone needs help, and a lease term waiving that right is void (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.015). A violation costs a civil penalty of one month's rent, the tenant's actual damages, court costs and attorney's fees, and a court may order injunctive relief (§ 92.015(c)). A victim has the statutory right to end the lease early (§§ 92.016, 92.0161). A court's protective order may give one party exclusive possession of a jointly leased home and order another party to leave (Tex. Fam. Code § 85.021(2)); follow any such order you are shown. Fair-housing law may also apply, and federally assisted housing has its own protections; neither is reviewed here. The cautious course: don't treat a tenant's victimization, or a police call it prompts, as a lease violation, and base any eviction on the tenant's own conduct.

title: Ending a Lease After Family Violence, Sexual Assault or Stalking
bodyText: A Texas tenant may end the lease early and avoid future rent if the tenant or an occupant is protected by a family-violence order or has documentation of family violence, or if the tenant (or a child or ward the tenant lives with) was the victim of certain sexual offenses, or of stalking on the premises, in the previous six months (Tex. Prop. Code §§ 92.016, 92.0161). The tenant must give you a copy of the qualifying document, give written notice of termination, and move out; the tenant is free of future liability after the 30th day after the notice, and, where a cotenant or occupant committed the family violence, without the 30-day notice if the tenant relies on a protective order, injunction or emergency order or on provider documentation (§§ 92.016(c), (c-1), 92.0161(d)). Rent already owed before termination stays owed (§§ 92.016(d), 92.0161(e)), unless your lease lacks the required statements about these rights, in which case the tenant is released from all delinquent rent too (§§ 92.016(f), 92.0161(g)); the library's statement clause supplies them. The rights cannot be waived, and violating them costs actual damages, one month's rent plus $500 and attorney's fees (§§ 92.016(e), (g), 92.0161(f), (h)). The library's early termination rights row covers the military and death rights as well.

title: Lock Changes for Family-Violence Victims in Texas
bodyText: Texas has no lock-change right written for victims of family violence (all Texas codes searched), but every Texas tenant already has one: you must rekey or change a security device whenever the tenant asks, at the tenant's expense, and the tenant may ask as often as the tenant likes (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.156(b)); you must do it within a reasonable time, presumed to be seven days after the request or any advance payment you lawfully require, or 72 hours if the tenant reports a recent unauthorized entry or a crime of personal violence at the property (§ 92.161); if you fail to act in time, the tenant may rekey and deduct the cost from rent, end the lease, or sue, and a lease cannot waive these remedies (§§ 92.165, 92.006(a)). When the person to be kept out is a cotenant, don't lock out a tenant on the lease on your own: lockouts are tightly limited (§ 92.0081). Act on a court order instead. A protective order may give the victim exclusive possession of a jointly leased home and order the abuser to leave (Tex. Fam. Code § 85.021(2)); with such an order, change the locks and keep the abuser out as it directs. What you charge the tenant for rekeying may not exceed the total a third-party contractor charges for material, labor, taxes and extra keys (§ 92.162(d)).

title: Protective-Order Citations in the Texas Termination Statutes
bodyText: The Texas lease-termination statutes for victims point to protective orders in other codes, and some of those provisions have moved. The current homes are: Family Code chapter 6, subchapter F (temporary injunctions), chapter 83 (temporary ex parte orders) and chapter 85 (protective orders); Code of Criminal Procedure article 17.292 (magistrate's emergency protection); and Code of Criminal Procedure chapter 7B, subchapters A and B (protective orders for victims of sexual offenses, stalking and trafficking), in force since January 1, 2021 (Tex. Prop. Code §§ 92.016(b-1), 92.0161(c), (c-1)). Each of these is in force, so an order issued under any of them qualifies. One related cross-reference is out of date: the property-retrieval writ chapter still defines "peace officer" by Code of Criminal Procedure article 2.12, which no longer exists: the recodified list of peace officers, effective January 1, 2025, is article 2A.001 (Tex. Prop. Code § 24A.001(3)); read the reference as article 2A.001(1) and (2), sheriffs and constables. Accept an order that cites either the old or the new number.

title: Documents That Support a Texas Family-Violence or Sexual-Offense Termination
bodyText: For family violence, the tenant must give you a copy of one of these: a temporary injunction in a divorce or similar suit (Family Code ch. 6, subch. F); a temporary ex parte order (Family Code ch. 83); a protective order (Family Code ch. 85); or a magistrate's order for emergency protection (Code of Criminal Procedure art. 17.292). Instead of an order, the tenant may give documentation of the family violence from a licensed health care provider who examined the victim, a licensed mental health provider who examined or evaluated the victim, or a family-violence advocate who assisted the victim (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.016(b-1)). For sexual assault, aggravated sexual assault, indecency with a child, sexual performance by a child, continuous sexual abuse or an attempt, in the previous six months: documentation from a licensed health care or mental health provider, from a person authorized to provide sexual-assault services, or a protective order under Code of Criminal Procedure ch. 7B, subch. A (not a temporary ex parte order) (§ 92.0161(c)). For stalking on the premises in the previous six months: a ch. 7B protective order (not temporary ex parte), or provider documentation plus a police incident report (and the pseudonym form if the report uses a pseudonym) (§ 92.0161(c-1)). Accept any document on the list; you may not demand more.

title: When the Property Is Condemned
bodyText:
No Texas statute says what happens to a residential lease, or to the rent, when the government takes the property by eminent domain. Texas's condemnation statute measures the award as "the damage to the property owner" (Tex. Prop. Code § 21.042) and does not mention tenants or leases, so whether the tenancy ends and who shares the award is left to the lease and to case law.

The optional Condemnation clause settles it: the lease ends on a total or substantial taking, rent is prorated to the day the tenant must leave, rent drops in proportion on a partial taking, and the award goes to you except the tenant's own relocation or moving payments. Keep that exception. When the state or a political subdivision acquires property, it must pay moving expenses and rental supplements, make relocation payments and help with replacement housing for a displaced individual or family (§ 21.046(b)), and those payments belong to the tenant.

If the lease ends this way, refund the deposit, less lawful deductions, within 30 days after the tenant surrenders the unit, with an itemized list (§§ 92.103(a), 92.104(c)).

What to do: tell tenants promptly when you receive an offer or notice of condemnation, and give the acquiring agency the tenants' names so they can be offered relocation help.

title: Criminal Background Checks on Your Staff
bodyText: Texas lets, but does not require, the owner or managing company of a residential dwelling project to run a state criminal history check on a job applicant who may need access to tenants' homes (Tex. Health & Safety Code §§ 765.002(a), 765.003(f)). A residential dwelling project includes a house, condominium, apartment building or duplex used as a dwelling (§ 765.001(6)). You may ask an applicant about criminal history at any time. You may check the Department of Public Safety's records only after making a job offer, and only with the applicant's signed authorization, following the department's rules (§ 765.003(a)-(d); Tex. Gov't Code § 411.118). What you receive is privileged. Share it only with your own officers, employees or agents deciding whether the person is suitable for the job, and otherwise only by court order or with the person's written consent (§ 765.004). Knowingly breaking that rule, or giving the department false information, is a Class A misdemeanor (§ 765.005). You may fire an employee who gave you false criminal history information (§ 765.006). The chapter does not cover independent contractors or people employed by a tenant (§§ 765.001(4), 765.002(b)). Negligent-hiring suits based only on an employee's conviction are limited, but not where you knew or should have known of a conviction for an offense related to the job, one of the serious offenses listed in Code of Criminal Procedure article 42A.054 (such as murder, aggravated robbery, sexual assault or stalking) or a sexually violent offense (Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 142.002). What to do: screen anyone who will hold keys, and keep the results confidential.

title: Getting a Tenant's Energy Usage Data
bodyText:
No Texas statute requires building energy benchmarking or says a lease may authorize the release of a tenant's utility usage to you. Two statutes control who may release the data. In the competitive electric market, "All meter data ... shall belong to a customer", including historical load data, and the utility may share it with others only for electric service or "other customer-approved services" under commission rules (Tex. Util. Code § 39.107(b), (k)).

A city-owned or other government-operated water, gas, electric or similar utility may not disclose a customer's usage or billing amounts unless the customer asks it to in writing, and the customer may take that request back at any time (§ 182.052(a)-(d)). So when the account is in the tenant's name, the data is the tenant's, and the route is the tenant's own signed release to the utility.

The optional Energy Usage Data Authorization clause does that: the tenant promises to sign the utility's release on request, you limit how you use the data, and the tenant may withdraw without breaching the lease. Separately, a tenant of a separately metered unit in a competitive area may choose the retail electric provider, and you must give utilities and providers reasonable access for metering (§ 39.107(c)).

title: Who Can Appear for a Company Landlord in a Texas Eviction
bodyText: A company landlord does not need a lawyer to run a Texas eviction in justice court. In an eviction suit in justice court, the parties "may represent themselves or be represented by their authorized agents, who need not be attorneys" (Tex. Prop. Code § 24.011(a)), and the eviction rules let a corporation or other entity appear through a non-attorney employee, owner, officer or partner, through a property manager or other authorized agent, or through an attorney (Tex. R. Civ. P. 510.3(b)); a corporation "need not be represented by an attorney in justice court" (Tex. Gov't Code § 27.031(d)). The agent route is narrower in two places. On appeal to county court, a non-lawyer agent is allowed only for an owner of a multifamily residential property, and only in an appeal of an eviction for nonpayment of rent (§ 24.011(b); Rule 510.20(d)). For any other appeal, such as a single-family rental or a holdover or lease-violation case, plan on a lawyer: the general rule lets a party appear "in person or by an attorney of the court" (Rule 7), and whether an entity can appear in county court through its own officer is a case-law question this library has not reviewed. And if you sue for rent alone, without possession, as a small claims case in justice court, an entity may appear through its own non-attorney employee, owner, officer or partner or through an attorney, but that rule does not list a property manager or other outside agent (Rule 500.3(b)). Give any agent written authority to act for you.

title: No Environmental-Event Termination Right
bodyText: No Texas statute gives you, or the tenant, a right to end a residential lease because of an environmental or public-health event such as contamination, a chemical spill or mold, and none lets a lease add such a right. Two statutes cover most of the same ground. If a casualty not caused by the negligence or fault of the tenant, a family member or a guest leaves the unit, as a practical matter, totally unusable, either of you may end the lease by written notice before repairs are finished. The tenant then gets only a pro rata rent refund from move-out and the deposit as the law requires (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.054(b); the Casualty Loss clause). The statute does not define casualty, so whether contamination with no physical damage counts is unsettled. And you may close a unit at any time by certified-mail notice to the tenant and the local health officer and building inspector, stating that you are ending the tenancy as soon as legally possible and will demolish the unit or stop using it as a residence (§ 92.055(a)). After the tenant moves out, the unit may not be occupied until the local health officer or building inspector certifies it, and you may not allow reoccupancy for six months. If you close it before the tenant has given a repair notice, the repair remedies do not apply; if you close it after a repair notice, the tenant is entitled only to the civil penalty (one month's rent plus $500), actual damages and court costs and attorney's fees under § 92.0563(a)(3)-(5) and, if the tenant moves out on or before the end of the rental term, to your payment of the tenant's actual and reasonable moving expenses, a pro rata rent refund from the move-out date and the deposit as the law requires; breaking the reoccupancy bar or that payment duty costs one month's rent plus $100 and attorney's fees (§ 92.055(b)-(e)). The library does not offer a separate environmental-event termination clause for Texas. A broader landlord exit could be read as getting around the repair remedies, which the lease cannot waive (§ 92.006(c)). If you want one anyway, get legal advice first. If a city or county revokes the certificate of occupancy because you failed to maintain the unit, you owe a tenant who is not in default under the lease the full deposit, the pro rata share of any rent paid in advance, the tenant's actual damages, including moving costs, and court costs and attorney's fees (§ 92.023).

title: A Tenant's EV Charger at Move-Out
bodyText: No Texas statute says who owns, or who may remove, an electric vehicle charger a tenant installed when the tenancy ends. Texas also gives tenants no right to install one, so the answer comes from your lease and your written consent. Two library clauses already settle it for a Texas lease, and they should be read together. The No Alterations clause makes any approved alteration stay with the property at the end of the term unless you require its removal. The optional Tenant EV Charger Installation clause makes you choose at signing between the tenant removing the system and repairing any damage, and the system staying in place and becoming yours. Pick one and fill it in. The library does not offer Texas the separate end-of-tenancy charger clause used in some other states. That clause makes a tenant-paid charger the tenant's property, and it would contradict whichever choice you made. If a tenant leaves a removable charger behind after moving out, treat it like other property left in the unit and follow your lease's abandonment terms and the statute on property left after an eviction (see the abandoned property rows).

title: Rules for EV Chargers at Your Rental
bodyText:
Texas gives tenants no statutory right to install or use an electric vehicle charger (see the EV charging row), so any charger at your rental is there by your choice or your agreement with the tenant. Three statutes then matter.

First, the state's charging-equipment law covers an owner or operator of chargers "available and accessible to the public" that sells charging through an app, website or other digital network: registration with the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation, inspection, measurement standards, fee and surcharge disclosures, receipts on request, and taking unsafe units out of service (Tex. Occ. Code §§ 2311.0101, 2311.0301-.0306). Equipment is exempt, under the department's rules, if it is at a private residence for noncommercial use, is provided for the exclusive use of tenants or residents of a multiunit development, or is free (§ 2311.0206(b)). Those rules are not reviewed here, so check them before you charge for public use.

Second, charging electric vehicles does not make you an electric utility or a retail electric provider (Tex. Util. Code § 31.002(6)(J)(iv), (17)).

Third, a charger used by your tenants and not run commercially is not a public charging station under the utility-planning rules (§ 42.0102(7)(B)). If you let a tenant install one, use the optional Tenant EV Charger Installation clause: your written consent, a licensed contractor, codes and permits, association rules, insurance, and payment for the electricity it uses. Any money you hold as security for the charger is part of the security deposit.

title: No Hardship Stay of a Texas Eviction
bodyText: No Texas statute or court rule lets a court delay an eviction or the writ of possession because of the tenant's hardship, such as illness, age, children in school, weather or trouble finding housing (all Texas codes and the eviction rules searched). The law runs the other way. Only the Legislature may modify or suspend eviction procedure; the Supreme Court may do so only in a declared disaster, on terms that apply to all affected courts and on a written public request (Tex. Prop. Code § 24.0043). A justice court "must not modify or suspend any part of Rule 510" (Tex. R. Civ. P. 510.1(b)). Trial is held 10 to 21 days after filing and cannot be postponed more than seven days without the parties' written agreement (§ 24.0051(g); Rule 510.13(b)). Issuing the writ is "a ministerial act not subject to review or delay" (§ 24.0061(b-1)). Cities and counties cannot add delays (§ 1.004(b)). What does affect timing: the writ cannot issue before the sixth day after judgment or the day after the appeal deadline, whichever is later, unless a possession bond is approved (§ 24.0061(b); Rule 510.18(g)(1)); a tenant who perfects an appeal and pays rent into the court registry stays in possession (Rule 510.19(d)(2)); a county court judgment is stayed only by a supersedeas bond filed within 10 days (§ 24.007); a federal notice period delays service of the writ, not filing (§ 24.005(c-1)); and the officer may not put belongings outside while it is raining, sleeting or snowing (§ 24.0061(d)(2)(D)). Ask for the writ in time: it cannot issue after 60 days (90 for good cause) or be executed after 90 days (Rule 510.18(g)). Federal law (for example the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act) may give some tenants a stay; not reviewed here.

title: No Texas Ban on Eviction Charges
bodyText: No Texas statute bans, or authorizes, a lease clause that charges the tenant a fixed amount for being evicted (all Texas codes searched). The money you can recover in an eviction is set by statute and rule: possession, court costs, delinquent rent up to judgment and attorney's fees if recoverable by law (Tex. Prop. Code § 24.006; Tex. R. Civ. P. 510.18(d)), with a separate suit for other damages. Texas has no general statute voiding contract penalties; whether a fixed eviction charge is an unenforceable penalty, rather than an agreed estimate of damages that are hard to measure, is a question of case law. Charging a fee the lease does not expressly authorize can also violate Texas's debt-collection law (Tex. Fin. Code § 392.303(a)(2)). The cautious course: leave out any flat eviction charge, recover costs and fees through the court, and claim your actual, documented losses.

title: No Lease Agent for Eviction Papers in Texas
bodyText: A Texas lease cannot name someone to accept the eviction citation for the tenant: in an instrument signed before suit, a person "may not accept service and waive process" (Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 30.001), and no statute or rule lets a lease designate a service agent (all Texas codes and the eviction rules searched). Service is fixed by rule. Only a sheriff or constable may serve the citation (or, after five business days without service, another trained officer on an alias citation), by delivering it with the petition to the tenant or leaving it with a person over 16, other than you, at the tenant's usual residence, at least 4 days before trial (Tex. R. Civ. P. 510.8(d)). If that fails, the judge may authorize delivery to the premises plus first-class mail, but only if your petition lists every home and work address of the tenant you know and the officer swears to diligent efforts on at least two occasions at all the tenant's addresses in the county (Rule 510.8(e)). So the lease's job is information: collect the tenant's work address and e-mail; if you obtain a default judgment you must serve it by e-mail when you know an address (Rule 510.16(b)). Pre-suit notices to vacate differ: a written agreement may allow e-mail delivery (Tex. Prop. Code § 24.005(f-3)(4)). A tenant in the attorney general's address confidentiality program (for victims of family violence, sexual assault or abuse, stalking, child abduction or trafficking) designates the attorney general as agent, and process "may be served on the attorney general on behalf of the participant" by delivering two copies (Tex. Code Crim. Proc. art. 58.052(c)). How that fits eviction service is not settled; if a tenant says they participate, get advice, serve under Rule 510.8 and consider also delivering two copies to the attorney general.

title: "Landlord Is Not Liable" Clauses
bodyText: Texas has no general statute that voids every lease clause saying you are not liable for injury or damage, unlike states that adopted the uniform landlord-tenant act (all Texas codes searched). But many specific terms of that kind are void. A lease term that would waive a right or "exempt a party from a liability or duty" is void as to utility interruptions (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.008(g)), lockouts and removal of doors, locks or appliances (§ 92.0081(j)), the tenant's right to call police or emergency help (§ 92.015(b)), late fees (§ 92.019(d)) and rental applications (§ 92.355). Your duties on security deposits, security devices, disclosure of ownership and management, utility cutoffs and smoke-alarm installation cannot be waived at all, and the repair duty can be shifted only in the narrow bold or underlined ways § 92.006 allows (§ 92.006(a), (c)-(f)). Some liability is fixed by statute whatever the lease says: for example, you are liable for damage to a tenant's vehicle caused by the negligence of an uninsured towing company you contract with (§ 92.0131(g)). Outside those rules, whether a clause releasing you from your own negligence is enforceable is a common-law question, and it is not reviewed here. So the library's Texas clauses avoid blanket "Landlord is not liable" wording. Using a void term can also be a deceptive trade practice, because it represents that the lease gives you rights it does not (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 17.46(b)(12)). Instead of disclaiming liability, require renter's insurance, limit any disclaimer to causes beyond your reasonable control, and carry your own liability insurance.

title: No Fast-Track Eviction for Crime in Texas
bodyText: Texas has no separate or faster eviction track for drug, violent or other criminal activity (all Texas codes searched). Every eviction of a tenant uses the same justice court procedure, which is already quick: trial 10 to 21 days after filing (Tex. Prop. Code § 24.0051(g)). The summary disposition shortcut is only for a forcible entry and detainer, someone who entered by force, not a tenant (§ 24.005106). Against a tenant, either side may still move for ordinary summary disposition, which the court cannot consider until it has been on file 14 days (Tex. R. Civ. P. 510.10(b), 503.2(c)). Your tools: (1) Make criminal activity a lease default and, if you want speed, shorten the notice to vacate in the lease (§ 24.005(a)). An eviction for intentional damage or threats to safety, or for a material breach "such as violating written lease provisions prohibiting serious misconduct or criminal acts", is valid in any event against a retaliation claim (§ 92.332(b)(2), (3)). (2) If a tenant or occupant is finally convicted under Penal Code chapter 43 (prostitution and related offenses) for an activity on the property, you may end the lease by written notice given within six months, and possession reverts to you on the 10th day, whatever the lease says (§ 91.003). (3) A court in a common-nuisance suit may order a landlord to terminate a tenant's lease if both are parties and the tenant violated the injunction (Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 125.045(b)(6)). Do not wait: an owner of multiunit residential property where people habitually go to commit listed crimes, who knowingly tolerates them and fails to make reasonable attempts to abate them, maintains a common nuisance and can be enjoined, and the property closed for a year (§§ 125.0015(b), 125.002(e)); calling the police is not evidence of tolerating the activity (§ 125.004(d)). For an intruder who was never your tenant, see the library's squatter-removal row. Federal housing program rules are not reviewed here.

title: No Expedited Deposit Procedure
bodyText: Texas has no fast-track or early-disposition procedure for security deposits, and no statute on returning a deposit early at the tenant's request (all Texas codes searched). The ordinary rule governs: refund the deposit, with a written itemized list of any deductions, on or before the 30th day after the tenant surrenders the unit (Tex. Prop. Code §§ 92.103(a), 92.104(c)). Your duty waits until the tenant gives you a written forwarding address, but the tenant never forfeits the deposit by not giving one (§ 92.107). Nothing stops you from refunding sooner, and a refund or accounting mailed and postmarked by the deadline is presumed on time (§ 92.1041). No Texas statute authorizes a fee for early or expedited processing either. Because you may deduct only damages and charges the tenant is legally liable for under the lease or because of a breach (§ 92.104(a)), and you bear the burden of proving that what you kept was reasonable (§ 92.109(c)), the library does not offer a processing-fee clause for Texas. If you and a tenant cannot agree, either of you may bring a small claims case in justice court for up to $20,000, excluding statutory interest and court costs but including attorney fees (Tex. R. Civ. P. 500.1(a)).

title: Tenants Running Home Child Care
bodyText: No Texas statute requires you to let a tenant run a child care business in the unit, or limits a lease term that forbids one. Texas defines a family home as regular care in the caretaker's own residence for not more than six unrelated children under 14, plus up to six after-school children, with no more than 12 in total (Tex. Hum. Res. Code § 42.002(9)); a larger operation is a group day-care home (§ 42.002(8)). Two recent laws limit cities, not landlords. A city may not hold a licensed, registered or listed family home or group day-care home to health and safety standards stricter than state law (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code § 250.014). A city also may not ban a no-impact home-based business run by an owner or tenant, but that law "does not prohibit ... a person from enforcing a rule or deed restriction imposed by a homeowners' association or by other private agreement" (§ 229.902(b), (d)(1)), and a lease is such an agreement. So the Residential Use Only clause still controls. If you choose to allow child care, give written consent, require the tenant to keep any state listing, registration or license current, require liability insurance that covers the business, and check your own insurer and any association rules first.

title: Hunting and Fishing on Rented Land
bodyText:
Texas does not say whether a tenant of farm or ranch land gets the hunting or fishing rights; that is left to the lease. What Texas does say points to you. No one may hunt or catch a wildlife resource on land "unless the owner of the land ... or the owner's agent, consents". Violations are a Class A Parks and Wildlife Code misdemeanor, and a felony for killing certain deer, pronghorn or bighorn sheep (Tex. Parks & Wild. Code § 61.022).

The statute does not name a tenant, so whether a tenant alone can give that consent is unsettled. In a county of 3.3 million or more people, a hunter needs written consent signed by the owner or the owner's agent, lessee or legal representative (§ 62.012). If you or a tenant take paying hunters, the owner or the landowner's agent must hold a hunting lease license (§§ 43.041-43.042).

To avoid disputes, use the optional Hunting, Fishing and Trapping Reserved clause. It keeps the sporting rights with you, bars the tenant from giving others permission without your written agreement, and lets you and your guests use the open land without entering the dwelling. Tell the tenant before a hunting party arrives. If you want the tenant to have hunting rights, say so in writing and name the tenant as your agent for giving consent.

title: No All-In Rent Pricing Law in Texas
bodyText: Texas has no rental fee-transparency or all-in pricing law: no statute requires advertised or leased rent to include every mandatory fee, puts fees on the lease's first page, or bans "junk fees" for rentals (all Texas codes searched; agency rules mostly not held). One narrow exception: for a multifamily development that claims the housing-finance-corporation property-tax exemption, "rent" for the development's income-restricted units includes every recurring fee a tenant must pay as a condition of occupancy, but not optional charges such as pet, storage or covered-parking fees (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code § 394.9026(a)(8)). For everyone else, two general laws matter. The Deceptive Trade Practices Act reaches residential leasing and makes it unlawful to represent that an agreement gives rights or obligations it doesn't (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 17.46(b)(12)), and the debt-collection law bars collecting a fee the lease does not expressly authorize (Tex. Fin. Code § 392.303(a)(2)). The cautious course: state every mandatory fee, with its amount, in the lease and in what you advertise.

title: Charging for Services You Do Not Provide in Texas
bodyText: No Texas statute specifically bars a landlord from charging a fee for a service or amenity it does not provide (all Texas codes searched). General laws point the same way. Texas's debt-collection law bars collecting a fee or charge incidental to the rent unless the lease expressly authorizes it or it is otherwise legally chargeable (Tex. Fin. Code § 392.303(a)(2)), and the Deceptive Trade Practices Act, which reaches residential leasing, makes it unlawful to represent that an agreement confers rights, remedies or obligations it does not have (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 17.46(b)(12)). In submetered or allocated water billing you may not charge more than the rules allow (the library's water submetering rows).
