The cautious course: charge a service fee only for a service you actually provide, at the amount the lease states, and stop charging it when the service stops.

title: Which Fire and Building Code Applies
bodyText: Texas has no single statewide fire code for private rental housing (all Texas codes searched). Fire and building standards come from where the property is. Inside a city, the International Residential Code "as it existed on May 1, 2012" is the municipal code for one- and two-family homes and small multiple single-family buildings, and the International Building Code of the same date is the code for larger apartment buildings. Each city may adopt local amendments and later editions by ordinance (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code §§ 214.211, 214.212, 214.216). These codes govern construction, alteration and repair, not every existing building. In an unincorporated area, a county with more than 250,000 people, or a county next to one, may adopt a fire code based on the International Fire Code or the Uniform Fire Code. It reaches only buildings built there that are commercial, public, or multifamily with four or more units (§§ 233.061, 233.062). No city, county or emergency services district may require fire sprinklers in a new or existing one- or two-family dwelling, apart from narrow older exceptions (§ 250.012). The state fire marshal may enter a building on a complaint and order dangerous fire conditions corrected, and the owner or occupant must comply at once (Tex. Gov't Code § 417.008). Fire inspections follow the most recent local fire code or the state fire marshal's code (§ 419.909(b)). A city of 1.7 million or more must have minimum habitability standards and inspections for rental buildings of three or more units (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code § 214.219). Smoke alarms have their own statewide rules (see the smoke alarm row). What to do: ask your city or county which fire code edition and amendments apply to your building.

title: Fire Sprinklers in Texas Rentals
bodyText: Texas has one statute that makes owners put fire sprinklers in existing residential buildings, and it is narrow. A residential high-rise (a building used mainly for residences that is 75 feet or more tall) must have a complete fire protection sprinkler system in good working order if it is in a county of more than 1.5 million people where more than 70 percent of the population lives in one city, at least half its residents are elderly or have a disability or mobility impairment, and it is not a designated historic site (Tex. Health & Safety Code §§ 766.051-766.053). Owners of such buildings built before September 1, 2015 must have sprinklers on all floors by September 1, 2027 (§ 766.054). The owner, or the agent of an out-of-state owner, of a building that does not comply commits an offense with a fine of up to $10,000, and the state may seek an injunction (§§ 766.055, 766.056). Apart from that, no Texas statute requires sprinklers in rental housing or makes a landlord retrofit them (all Texas codes searched). Whether a new or renovated apartment building needs them depends on the building and fire codes your city or county has adopted (see the fire code row). No city, county or emergency services district may require sprinklers in a new or existing one- or two-family home, apart from narrow exceptions for rules adopted before 2009 or 2013 (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code § 250.012). If you have a system, use a registered sprinkler contractor to install, maintain or service it (Tex. Ins. Code § 6003.151).

title: No Duty to Disclose a Pending Foreclosure
bodyText: No Texas statute requires you to tell a prospective or current tenant that your loan is in default, that a notice of sale has been posted, or that the property faces foreclosure (all Texas codes searched). The only foreclosure notice to tenants the statutes mention is one the foreclosing lender may choose to give before the sale, and the 30-day notice to vacate a buyer at a foreclosure sale under a superior lien must give, if it chooses not to continue the lease, a tenant who timely pays rent and is not otherwise in default (Tex. Prop. Code § 24.005(b)); see the row on notice of foreclosure and other proceedings, and the foreclosure row for what happens to the lease. The Deceptive Trade Practices Act, which reaches leases, lists as deceptive failing to disclose information known at the time of a transaction when the failure was intended to induce the consumer into a transaction the consumer would not have entered had it been disclosed (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §§ 17.45(1), 17.46(b)(24)). Cautious course: if a notice of default or sale has been given on the property, tell an applicant in writing before signing, and tell current tenants whom to pay if a sale happens.

title: When Your Rental Is Foreclosed
bodyText: If the lender forecloses on your rental, a tenant whose lease is subordinate to the foreclosed lien becomes a tenant at sufferance whom the buyer can evict (Tex. Prop. Code § 24.002(a)(2)); which liens are superior turns on recording and priority rules not reviewed here. After a tax or trustee's foreclosure sale, a buyer who chooses not to continue the lease must still give a residential tenant who pays rent on time and is not otherwise in default at least 30 days' written notice to vacate. Rent for the month of the sale counts as timely if the tenant paid you before learning a sale was scheduled, or paid the lender or buyer within five days after a written request naming the buyer (§ 24.005(b)). A buyer takes subject to some of a tenant's pending repair remedies (§ 92.0562(g)). A mortgage lender that takes title by foreclosure is not liable for the security deposits, and you remain liable for deposits you received until a new owner receives or assumes them (§ 92.105). If your loan includes an assignment of rents, after a default the lender may notify your tenants, in a statutory form, to pay rent to it; a tenant living there as a primary residence is still credited for rent paid to you (§§ 64.055, 64.056). Selling your own homestead below market value and leasing it back at more than fair rent is treated as a loan, and the deed is void, unless the sale is to a close relative the statute lists (§ 41.006). No Texas statute addresses equity or rent skimming by a buyer of a defaulted home (all Texas codes searched). For what you must tell tenants, see the notice of proceedings row. Federal law (e.g. the Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act) may also apply; not reviewed here.

title: No Relief From Forfeiture for a Texas Tenant
bodyText: No Texas statute lets a residential tenant undo the loss of the tenancy by paying the arrears and costs after the notice period has run, whether before trial, after judgment or before the writ is executed, and none lets a court relieve a tenant from forfeiture of the lease (all Texas codes and the eviction rules searched). The tenant's one statutory chance is the notice: for nonpayment by a tenant who was not late before the month of the notice, the notice must be a notice to pay rent or vacate (Tex. Prop. Code § 24.005(a)); for other breaches, Texas gives no cure right unless your lease does. The justice court decides only who has the right to actual possession (§ 24.004(c)); whether a court could relieve against forfeiture as a matter of fairness is case law. One real exception: a residential lease combined with an option to buy is treated as an executory contract for conveyance (§ 5.062(a)(2)). Before you enforce rescission or forfeiture against that tenant-buyer for a default, you must send a notice by registered or certified mail, in 14-point bold type, stating the default, the amount or the action needed to cure, and the remedy you intend, and the tenant-buyer avoids the remedy by curing within 30 days "Notwithstanding an agreement to the contrary" (§§ 5.063-5.065). Get advice before signing a lease with an option to purchase.

title: Which Code Edition Applies in Texas
bodyText: Texas statutes adopt most model building codes as a fixed edition and then let local governments move forward. Inside a city, the International Residential Code as it existed on May 1, 2012 governs construction, alteration and repair of one- and two-family homes and multiple single-family dwellings of up to three stories, and the International Building Code of the same date governs commercial buildings, which include larger multifamily buildings. A city may adopt local amendments by ordinance after a public hearing and may consider later editions (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code §§ 214.211, 214.212, 214.216). The National Electrical Code is fixed at its May 1, 2001 edition (§ 214.214) and the pool and spa code at its May 1, 2019 edition, which a city may replace with a newer one (§ 214.103). A county fire code, which applies only to commercial and public buildings and multifamily dwellings of four or more units in unincorporated areas, must conform to the 2005 International or Uniform Fire Code or exceed it, and the county may adopt later editions (§ 233.062). Energy codes move by agency rule (Tex. Health & Safety Code § 388.003). Fire safety inspections, by contrast, follow the most recent local fire code or the state fire marshal's most recent code (Tex. Gov't Code § 419.909(b)), so that standard changes without new legislation. No Texas statute adopts a property maintenance code for existing rentals (all Texas codes searched). In practice the edition that governs your building is the one your city or county adopted by ordinance, with its local amendments. Ask your building official which edition applies and keep a note of it.

title: Good-Cause Lease Terms in Texas Affordable Housing
bodyText:
Texas has no general good-cause eviction law. For an ordinary private rental there is no notice telling the tenant whether the unit is covered, and you need not give a reason for not renewing a lease or for ending a month-to-month tenancy; cities and counties cannot add a cause rule unless another statute expressly authorizes it (Tex. Prop. Code § 1.004). Three kinds of tax-advantaged affordable housing are different, and their leases must carry good-cause terms.
- (1) A multifamily development owned by a public facility corporation that claims the property-tax exemption (this rule does not cover a development with at least 20 percent of its units reserved as public housing, one in HUD's Rental Assistance Demonstration program, or one receiving tax-exempt bond or housing tax credit financing): each lease must provide that you will not retaliate against tenant-organization activity, that you may decline to renew only for material noncompliance (including nonpayment of rent), substantial violations, failure to give required household information, or repeated minor violations of the kinds listed, and that you will serve written notice of proposed nonrenewal at least 30 days before nonrenewal; the tenant cannot waive these protections (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code §§ 303.0421, 303.0425(i), (j)).
- (2) A development owned by a housing finance corporation that claims its exemption: the same terms in the lease of each income-restricted unit, but without the material-noncompliance ground; this rule does not cover a development that receives housing tax credits (§ 394.9026(b), (c)(9), (f)).
- (3) A housing tax credit, TCAP or Exchange development monitored by the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs: the lease or an addendum must state that evictions or terminations of tenancy for other than good cause are prohibited, a termination notice must specify the grounds, and nonpayment requires 30 days' written notice (10 Tex. Admin. Code § 10.613(a); Tex. Gov't Code § 2306.6735); HOME and similar developments have parallel rules (§ 10.613(b)).

The library's conditional good-cause clause supplies the lease wording for these properties. Federal program rules are not reviewed here.

The library's clause does not supply the different lease statement 10 Tex. Admin. Code § 10.613(b) requires for HOME, ERA, TCAP RF, NHTF, NSP and HOME-ARP developments, and each program has other lease requirements of its own to check.

title: No Statutory Guest Rights in Texas
bodyText:
No Texas statute gives a residential tenant a right to receive guests, visitors or suppliers, bars a guest fee, or limits a lease's guest rules, in any size of building. Guests are a matter for the lease; the library's guest policy clauses apply in Texas. A few statutes touch guests. Unless state or federal law prohibits firearms on the property, you may not prohibit a tenant's guest from lawfully possessing, carrying or storing a firearm in the unit, in a vehicle in tenant or guest parking, or on the way in and out (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.026).

The occupancy limit of three adults per bedroom applies to every adult you allow to occupy the unit, with exceptions where fair housing law requires more or for up to a month of sanctuary from family violence (§ 92.010), which is why long-staying guests should be added as occupants. Damage caused by a tenant's guest is not normal wear and tear (§ 92.001(4)), and an eviction because a guest intentionally damaged property or threatened someone's safety is not retaliation (§ 92.332(b)(2)).

Under the Texas Fair Housing Act, refusing a reasonable accommodation in your rules that a tenant with a disability needs, such as letting a caregiver stay or visit, is discrimination (§ 301.025(c)(2)). Write guest rules that apply evenly to every tenant.

title: Which Defects Count Under the Texas Repair Law
bodyText: Texas uses one test for repair problems: whether the condition materially affects the physical health or safety of an ordinary tenant. Your statutory repair duty reaches only such a condition, plus a failure to keep a hot water device working at 120 degrees Fahrenheit (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.052(a)(3)), and the tenant's remedies (ending the lease, repair and deduct, and court orders) depend on a condition that materially affects the physical health or safety of an ordinary tenant (§ 92.056(b)(2)). The test is objective: an ordinary tenant, not the particular tenant's preferences. A condition caused by the tenant, a lawful occupant, a family member or a guest does not count unless it comes from normal wear and tear (§§ 92.052(b), 92.056(a)). No Texas statute lists which defects qualify (all Texas codes searched). Seriousness does change the timetable. Once you are liable under § 92.056(b) and the tenant has given the required repair notices, one of them stating an intent to repair, the tenant may repair and deduct up to one month's rent or $500, whichever is greater: immediately after the notice of intent for raw sewage backing up or flooding inside the unit; if you have not repaired within three days after it, for a total loss of water you agreed to furnish, or for inadequate heat or cooling from equipment you agreed to furnish once a local official has notified you in writing that it materially affects health or safety; and if you have not repaired within seven days after it, for any other condition a local official has so notified you of (§ 92.0561(a)-(e)). The seven-day presumption of a reasonable repair time may be rebutted by the severity and nature of the condition (§ 92.056(d)). A court may reduce rent in proportion to the reduced rental value (§ 92.0563(a)(2)). Cosmetic and convenience items fall outside the statute and are left to your lease. What to do: treat anything that could injure or sicken an ordinary tenant as covered and repair it promptly after notice.

title: What a Texas Lease May Change About Repairs
bodyText: Your Texas repair duty for conditions that materially affect an ordinary tenant's health or safety, including the 120-degree hot water duty, may be changed only in the ways Tex. Prop. Code § 92.006(c)-(f) allows: the tenant may repair at your expense; a landlord who owns only one rental dwelling, free of health or safety defects at the start and with no reason to expect one, may shift repairs to the tenant at the tenant's expense in a specific, clear, underlined or bold written term made knowingly, voluntarily and for consideration; and, with the same formalities, the tenant may pay for stoppages from foreign or improper objects in lines serving only the tenant's unit, damage to doors, windows and screens, and damage from windows or doors left open, except where you were negligent. The library's row on shifting the repair duty explains each route, and the tenant repair agreement clause carries the lawful version. Some limits come from the statute itself rather than the lease. You need not furnish utilities from a utility company if, as a practical matter, its lines are not reasonably available, and you need not furnish security guards (§ 92.052(c)). The tenant's fast-track repair rights for a total loss of water or for inadequate heat or cooling apply only if the lease expressly or impliedly provides the water or the heating or cooling equipment (§ 92.0561(d)(3)(B)-(C)), so describe what you supply accurately in the lease. Outside these routes, a term waiving the repair duty is void, and knowingly contracting for one costs one month's rent plus $2,000, actual damages and attorney's fees (§ 92.0563(b)). The parties may also agree that the tenant will fix any condition at your expense, whether or not it affects health or safety (§ 92.0561(g)).

title: Presumptions in Texas Repair Disputes
bodyText: Texas repair law uses several rebuttable presumptions, mostly in your favour. Seven days after you receive the tenant's notice is presumed a reasonable time to repair; it can be rebutted by the date you received notice, the severity and nature of the condition, and the availability of materials, labor and utilities (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.056(d)). Your first sworn affidavit delaying the tenant's own repairs is presumed made in good faith; for later ones you must prove good faith (§ 92.0562(f)). You are presumed not to have knowingly waived the repair duty, and the tenant must prove otherwise, by clear and convincing evidence if the written lease complies with the law (§ 92.0563(b)). If a tenant sues for retaliation over a code complaint and the inspector finds in writing that no violation exists, the tenant is presumed to have acted in bad faith (§ 92.334(a)). Security-device requests are presumed reasonably handled within seven days, or 72 hours if the tenant told you of an actual or attempted break-in at the unit, or one elsewhere in the complex or a crime of personal violence there in the past two months (§ 92.161), and a smoke alarm working at move-in is presumed to keep working until the tenant asks for repair (§ 92.258(g)). No Texas statute presumes a unit uninhabitable because of a code violation, or presumes retaliation from timing alone (all Texas codes searched); retaliation is barred within six months after a protected act, but the tenant must still show it. Keep dated records of every notice, repair and affidavit. Deposit presumptions are in the security deposit row.

title: No Fitness Statement Required in a Texas Lease
bodyText: No Texas statute requires your lease to state that you will deliver or keep the unit fit to live in, or prescribes habitability wording (all Texas codes searched). What Texas requires instead is notice of the tenant's repair remedies: a lease must contain language in underlined or bold print telling the tenant of the remedies under the repair statutes (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.056(g)). The library's required clause on repairs and the tenant's statutory remedies carries that language; keep it in bold or underlined type. Texas also has no implied warranty of habitability in an ordinary dwelling lease, because the repair subchapter replaces the common-law warranties and duties for maintenance, repair, security, habitability and nonretaliation (§ 92.061). A manufactured home lot lease is the exception: signing it warrants that the lot is suitable for installing a manufactured home during the term (§ 94.151). Do not describe the unit as code-compliant or defect-free unless it is, and do not tell the tenant it has no repair rights, because a term waiving the repair duty is void outside the narrow routes the statute allows (§ 92.006(c)).

title: Shifting the Repair Duty in Texas
bodyText:
Texas's repair statute is its habitability law: your duty to repair conditions that materially affect the physical health or safety of an ordinary tenant replaces the common-law warranties (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.061). A lease cannot remove that duty (§ 92.006(c)). It can do only three things.

(1) Let the tenant make repairs at your expense (§ 92.006(d)). (2) Make the tenant repair at the tenant's own expense, but only if, at the start of the lease, you own just one rental dwelling, the dwelling has no health or safety defect and you have no reason to expect one, and the lease is written, the agreement is underlined or in bold (in the lease or a separate written addendum), specific and clear, and made knowingly, voluntarily and for consideration (§ 92.006(e)).

(3) Make the tenant pay, with the same formalities, for damage from wastewater stoppages caused by foreign or improper objects in lines serving only the tenant's unit, damage to doors, windows or screens, and damage from windows or doors left open, except where you were negligent; you still repair stoppages from deterioration, roots, ground conditions, faulty construction or broken equipment (§ 92.006(f)). Texas has no rule letting a tenant accept named defects for a rent reduction, and no separate-document rule for heat. Knowingly contracting around the repair duty costs one month's rent plus $2,000, actual damages and attorney's fees (§ 92.0563(b)). The library's tenant repair agreement clause carries the lawful version.

title: Contaminated Land and Closed Landfills
bodyText: Texas has one contamination disclosure that reaches leases: land over a closed municipal solid waste landfill. You may not lease or offer to lease such land unless the existing development complies with the state's landfill-development rules, or you tell the prospective tenant what is needed to bring the land and development into compliance and what limits apply to future development (Tex. Health & Safety Code § 361.537). The owner must also record a notice of the land's former use as a landfill, and must notify each lessee and each occupant of a structure over the site of that former use and of the structural controls in place to reduce future danger (§ 361.539). A structure over a closed landfill must have approved methane sensors with an audible alarm (§ 361.536(a)). Apart from that, no Texas statute requires a residential lease or landlord to disclose that the property is contaminated, has been through a cleanup, or is subject to recorded environmental restrictions (all Texas codes searched); the property disclosure statutes cover sales, not leases. The Deceptive Trade Practices Act, which reaches leases, lists as deceptive failing to disclose known information to induce a consumer into a transaction the consumer would otherwise have refused (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 17.46(b)(24)). Cautious course: tell an applicant in writing, before signing, about any contamination, landfill history or recorded environmental restriction you know of. Lead paint has its own row.

title: Local Health Officials and Texas Rentals
bodyText: No Texas statute requires you to give a tenant a copy of local health rules on request, or to refer tenants to a health department (all Texas codes searched). Local health officials matter in other ways. If the appropriate local housing, building or health official notifies you in writing that a condition, including inadequate heat or cooling from equipment you agreed to furnish, materially affects the health or safety of an ordinary tenant, that notice is one of the events that lets a tenant who has given the required repair notices, one of them stating an intent to repair, use the repair and deduct remedy if you do not repair within the statutory time (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.0561(d)(3)(C)-(D), (e)). If you close a unit instead of repairing it, you must send notice by certified mail, return receipt requested, to the tenant and to the local health officer and building inspector, if any, stating that you are ending the tenancy as soon as legally possible and will demolish the unit or stop using it as a residence; after the tenant moves out, the unit may not be occupied until the officer certifies it, and you may not allow reoccupancy for six months. If you close before any repair notice, the repair remedies do not apply; if you close it after a repair notice, the tenant is entitled only to the civil penalty (one month's rent plus $500), actual damages and court costs and attorney's fees under § 92.0563(a)(3)-(5) and, if the tenant moves out on or before the end of the rental term, to your payment of the tenant's actual and reasonable moving expenses, a pro rata rent refund from the move-out date and the deposit as the law requires; breaking the reoccupancy bar or that payment duty costs one month's rent plus $100 and attorney's fees (§ 92.055). A city of 1.7 million or more must adopt minimum habitability standards for buildings with three or more rental units and run an inspection program that includes the city's health authority; an owner who violates the ordinance commits a Class C misdemeanor for each day (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code § 214.219). A rooming house operator must keep the premises sanitary, clean each unit and supply clean linens before a new occupant, or the rooming house is a public health nuisance (Tex. Health & Safety Code § 341.066). In a county's unincorporated area, a county that has adopted nuisance-abatement procedures must give written notice to the owner, lessee, occupant, agent or person in charge of the premises (Tex. Health & Safety Code §§ 343.011(a), 343.021(a), 343.022(b)). A tenant who complains in good faith to a code-enforcement agency is protected from retaliation (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.331(a)(3)).

title: Heating and Cooling in Texas Rentals
bodyText: No Texas statute requires you to supply heat or air conditioning, sets a minimum indoor temperature, or limits shifting heating costs to the tenant (all Texas codes searched). Heat enters Texas law through the repair statute. If the lease expressly or impliedly provides heating or cooling equipment (listing it among the included appliances does that), and it produces inadequate heat or cooled air that a local housing, building or health official certifies in writing materially affects the health or safety of an ordinary tenant, the tenant may repair and deduct if you have not fixed it within three days after the tenant's notice of intent to repair, provided the other repair-and-deduct conditions are met, including the § 92.056(b) notices and your liability under that section (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.0561(a), (d)(3)(C), (e)(3)). Any heating condition that materially affects health or safety also triggers your ordinary repair duty after the tenant's notice, if the tenant is not delinquent in rent when giving it (§ 92.052(a)). The same duty covers a failure to provide and maintain a hot water device supplying water of at least 120 degrees Fahrenheit (§ 92.052(a)(3)(B)). If you submeter electricity and interrupt it for nonpayment, you may not do so on a day after a high of 32 degrees Fahrenheit or below with freezing weather forecast for the next 24 hours, or during or just after a heat advisory for the county (§ 92.008(i)(3)). A city of 1.7 million or more must adopt minimum habitability standards for buildings of three or more rental units (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code § 214.219), and local codes elsewhere may set heating rules. Say in the lease which heating and cooling equipment you provide and who pays for the energy it uses.

title: Renting in a Texas HOA or Condominium
bodyText:
If your rental is in a subdivision with a property owners' association, the association may not require your applicant or tenant to be approved by it, and may not demand the applicant's credit report or rental application. It may ask for the name, mailing address, phone number and e-mail of each person who will live there and the lease's start date and term (Tex. Prop. Code § 209.016(b), (e)). It may still enforce leasing or occupancy restrictions in its dedicatory instruments (§ 209.016(d)), but it may not stop you from renting to someone because the rent is paid with a housing voucher or other housing assistance (§ 202.024).

The § 209.016 rules do not apply to condominiums (§ 209.003(d)), but the voucher rule does, because chapter 202's association includes a condominium regime (§ 202.001(2)). A condominium association may adopt rules on leasing to the extent leasing affects the common elements or other units (§ 82.102(a)(7)). It may also amend its declaration to let its board evict your tenant for violating the declaration, bylaws or rules, or for not paying for common-element damage the tenant substantially caused, and to collect rent directly from your tenant if you are at least 60 days behind on amounts owed to the association (§ 82.067(h)).

Condominium fines are levied against you as owner, after notice to you; the association may send your tenant a copy (§ 82.102(d)-(e)). The eviction, rent-collection and fine-notice rules apply only to a condominium whose declaration was recorded on or after January 1, 1994, or that has opted into the act; the leasing-rule power applies to older condominiums too (§ 82.002(a), (c)). No Texas statute caps an association's leasing fees, or says whether rent your tenant pays to a condominium association counts against rent owed to you.

Give the tenant the association's rules before signing and use the library's association compliance clause.

title: Holding Deposits and Application Deposits
bodyText:
Texas regulates money taken before the lease through its rental application law. An application deposit is money given with a rental application that is refundable if the applicant is rejected; an application fee is a nonrefundable payment to cover screening (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.351). If you do not give notice of acceptance by the seventh day after the applicant submits a completed application on your form, or after you accept an application deposit without giving a form, the applicant is deemed rejected, and rejecting one co-applicant rejects all (§ 92.352).

A rejected applicant gets the application deposit back. If you reject an applicant without having made your printed tenant selection criteria available, you must also return the application fee (§ 92.3515(e)). Notice is presumed given by phone or by mail postmarked by the deadline, and a refund must be mailed to the address the applicant gives if asked (§ 92.353). A bad-faith failure to refund costs $100 plus three times the amount kept, plus attorney's fees (§ 92.354), and an application term waiving these rules is void (§ 92.355).

The statute does not say whether you may keep an application deposit when an accepted applicant backs out before signing. Cautious course: say in writing on the application how much, if any, you will keep in that case, and credit the deposit to the security deposit or first rent once the lease is signed. After signing, money that secures the lease is a security deposit (§ 92.102), and if the tenant never moves in you may keep it only as § 92.1031 allows.

title: No Statutory Holdover Rate in Texas
bodyText:
No Texas statute sets a holdover rent, such as double rent, or caps a holdover charge written into a lease, for ordinary or subsidized housing. A tenant who stays after the right of possession ends commits a forcible detainer, and you recover the unit through an eviction suit after a written notice to vacate of at least three days, unless the lease sets a different period (Tex. Prop. Code §§ 24.002(a)(1), 24.005(a)).

If the tenancy is month to month, you must first end it with the notice § 91.001 requires (§ 24.005(a)). The eviction suit does not bar a separate suit for damages, rent or mesne profits for the time the tenant held over (§ 24.008). The library's holdover clause measures your recovery as actual damages, including the reasonable rental value, and lets you accept rent and continue month to month instead.

No statute forbids an agreed daily holdover charge (for example 150 percent of the daily rent), but whether a Texas court would enforce one or treat it as a penalty is a question of case law, so the library does not offer one. If you add your own after taking advice, state the amount in the lease, keep it a reasonable estimate of your loss, and do not also claim the regular rent for the same days. Federal rules for subsidized housing may also apply; not reviewed here.

title: Tenants Running a Home Business
bodyText: No Texas statute requires you to allow a tenant's home business or limits a lease term that forbids one (all Texas codes searched). The statewide rules bind cities, not landlords. Since June 12, 2025, a city may not ban a no-impact home-based business, or require a license or permit for one. That is a business whose employees and clients on the property never exceed the city occupancy limit, that creates no on-street parking or substantial traffic, is not visible from the street, and does not substantially increase noise. A city also may not make any home business rezone the property or, in a single-family home or a building of no more than two units, install fire sprinklers (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code § 229.902(a)-(b)). Cities may still require compliance with fire, building, health and other codes, and may limit or bar businesses that sell alcohol or illegal drugs, sober living homes and sexually oriented businesses (§ 229.902(c)). The statute does not prohibit a person from enforcing a rule or deed restriction imposed by a homeowners' association or other private agreement (§ 229.902(d)(1)), and a lease is a private agreement. Likewise, a city zoning ordinance may not prohibit cottage food production in a home (§ 211.032), which again limits only the city. So the library's Residential Use Only clause controls. If you allow a business, give written consent saying what is allowed, require the tenant to follow all laws and carry liability insurance that covers it, and check your own insurer and any association rules. Home child care has its own row.

title: Exemption and Homestead Waivers in a Texas Lease
bodyText: Do not put an exemption or homestead waiver in a Texas lease. Your residential landlord's lien for unpaid rent reaches only the tenant's nonexempt property in the unit or a storage room, and never listed items such as clothing, tools of a trade, schoolbooks, family portraits, one couch, two living room chairs and a dining set, beds and bedding, kitchen furniture and utensils, food, medicine, one car and one truck, and children's toys. A lease term that waives or diminishes those protections is void, and a contractual lien is enforceable only if it is underlined or in conspicuous bold print (Tex. Prop. Code §§ 54.041-54.043). If you get a money judgment, the tenant's personal property up to $100,000 for a family or $50,000 for a single adult (home furnishings, clothing, vehicles, tools and more), current wages and qualified retirement and savings accounts are exempt from execution (§§ 42.001, 42.002, 42.0021). Those limits do not stop a creditor with a contractual landlord's lien (§ 42.001(c)), but the lien exemptions above still apply. The Texas Constitution protects a homestead from forced sale for all debts except a short list, such as purchase money, taxes and certain improvement and home-equity loans, and no lien on a homestead is valid unless it secures one of those debts (Tex. Const. art. XVI, § 50(a), (c)). Rent is not on the list, so a lease term giving you a lien on a tenant's homestead would be invalid. Whether a tenant's leasehold can itself be a homestead is case law, not reviewed. If you rent out your own home temporarily, it keeps its homestead character as long as you have not acquired another homestead (art. XVI, § 51; Tex. Prop. Code § 41.003). No Texas statute lets a residential lease waive these protections (all Texas codes searched).

title: No Early Termination for Age or Illness in Texas
bodyText: No Texas statute lets a residential tenant end a lease early because of age, illness or disability, or because the tenant must move into a nursing home, assisted living or other care facility (all Texas codes searched). Texas's statutory early-termination rights are limited to family violence, certain sexual offenses or stalking, military service or orders, and the death of a tenant who was the sole occupant, which the estate's representative may use (Tex. Prop. Code §§ 92.016, 92.0161, 92.017, 92.0162); see the row on statutory early termination rights. So unless the lease gives such a right, a tenant who leaves early for health reasons is treated like any other tenant who leaves before the term ends: the tenant remains liable under the lease, but you have a duty to mitigate your damages, which a lease cannot waive (§ 91.006; see the row on the duty to re-let). A month-to-month tenant may end the tenancy on the usual notice (§ 91.001). One caution: under the Texas Fair Housing Act, refusing a reasonable accommodation in your rules, policies or practices that a tenant with a disability needs is discrimination (§ 301.025(c)(2)), and a request to be released early or on shorter notice may be such a request; consider it in good faith. Federal law may also apply; not reviewed here. If you want to offer a medical or care-facility release, put it in the lease or an addendum with the notice and proof you will accept.

title: Disclosing Code and Vacate Orders in Texas
bodyText: No Texas statute requires you to tell a prospective or current tenant about an outstanding code violation, inspection order, substandard-building order or order to vacate (all Texas codes searched). The orders run to you. A city's substandard-building ordinance must give notice to the owner; after a hearing the city may order the building vacated, secured, repaired or demolished and the occupants relocated, and the order goes to the owner and any lienholder or mortgagee (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code § 214.001(b), (d), (g)). The city may also record notice of the hearing, which binds later buyers (§ 214.001(e)). The state fire marshal may order a dangerous building or fire condition corrected, and the owner or occupant must comply immediately (Tex. Gov't Code § 417.008(c)-(d)). If a city or county revokes the certificate of occupancy because you failed to maintain the premises, you owe a tenant who is not in default the full deposit, any prepaid rent, actual damages including moving costs and lost wages, and attorney's fees (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.023). The Deceptive Trade Practices Act, which reaches leases, lists as deceptive failing to disclose known information to induce a consumer into a transaction the consumer would otherwise have refused (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 17.46(b)(24)). Cautious course: clear outstanding orders before renting, disclose any pending order in writing before the lease is signed, and never rent a unit under an order to vacate. See the rows on notice of proceedings and on rent after a vacate order.

title: No Inspection-Notice Penalty in Texas
bodyText: No Texas statute requires you to tell a tenant about a right to a move-in or move-out inspection, so there is no penalty for leaving such a notice out, and no Texas rule makes you forfeit the deposit, or pay a multiple of it, for skipping an inspection (all Texas codes searched). Texas's deposit penalties turn on refunding and itemizing instead. You must refund the deposit within 30 days after the tenant surrenders the premises (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.103(a)). You need not refund or itemize until the tenant gives a written forwarding address, though the tenant does not lose the deposit by not giving one (§ 92.107). Keeping a deposit in bad faith costs $100 plus three times the amount wrongfully withheld plus attorney's fees. Failing in bad faith to give the written description and itemized list of deductions forfeits your right to keep any of the deposit or to sue the tenant for damage to the premises. You are presumed to have acted in bad faith if you neither refund nor itemize by the 30th day, and in a suit you must prove that keeping any part was reasonable (§ 92.109). That burden is why a dated, signed move-in and move-out condition record with photos is your best protection; see the condition inspection row.

title: Jury Waivers in a Texas Lease
bodyText: A Texas lease cannot waive the tenant's right to a jury trial "in an action brought under" the residential tenancy chapter, which covers suits over repairs, deposits, lockouts, utility cutoffs, security devices, smoke alarms and retaliation (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.006(h)). The Texas Constitution also keeps the right of trial by jury "inviolate" (Tex. Const. art. I, § 15). In an eviction, no jury sits unless a party demands one: either side may file a written jury demand at least three days before trial (or three days after service, if later) and pay the jury fee or file a statement of inability to pay; with no timely demand, the judge decides (Tex. R. Civ. P. 510.15(c)). Section 92.006(h) does not expressly reach an eviction or a suit for unpaid rent, but whether a pre-printed residential lease waiver would be enforced there is a question for case law. The cautious course is to leave jury waivers out of your lease altogether; the library's lease has none.

title: Key Control and Staff Screening in Texas
bodyText: No Texas statute requires a landlord, at any size of complex, to adopt a key-control policy, to secure master keys, or to run background checks on employees or contractors who have access to units (all Texas codes searched). Texas handles keys through its security device rules instead. You must rekey every lock operated by a key, card or combination within seven days after each tenant turnover, at your expense; you pay to rekey when your master key is used or changed; and you must rekey or change a device at the tenant's request, at the tenant's expense (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.156(a)-(c)). You may charge a tenant no more than a third-party contractor's cost for that work (§ 92.162(d)). These duties cannot be waived in the lease (§ 92.006(a)); the library's keys clause and security device rows carry them. For screening, Texas requires an in-home service company, meaning one that sends employees into homes to repair appliances, heating and cooling, plumbing or electrical systems for a fee, to get criminal history records (or confirm a license that required a background check) before hiring anyone whose duties include entering a residence, and gives it a presumption against negligent hiring if those records showed no listed recent convictions (Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code §§ 145.001-145.003). Whether that chapter reaches your own maintenance staff is unsettled. Cautious course: keep master keys and key codes locked and logged, limit who can use them, rekey when staff with access leave, use repair companies that run those checks, and take advice before using criminal records in your own hiring.

title: Penalties for Using Void Lease Terms in Texas
bodyText: Texas has no general penalty for knowingly putting a prohibited term in a residential lease; most of its anti-waiver rules simply make the term void (for example Tex. Prop. Code §§ 54.043(b), 92.0081(j), 92.019(d), 92.355). One section does penalize the knowing use itself: a landlord who knowingly contracts with a tenant, orally or in writing, to waive the repair duty owes the tenant actual damages, a civil penalty of one month's rent plus $2,000, and reasonable attorney's fees. You are presumed not to have known, the tenant must plead and prove a knowing violation, and if your written lease complies with § 92.006 the proof must be clear and convincing (§ 92.0563(b)). Manufactured home community landlords face the same rule (§ 94.159(b)). Other penalties attach to what you do under a term, whether or not you knew it was unlawful: collecting a late fee the statute does not allow costs $100 plus three times the fee plus attorney's fees (§ 92.019(c)), and keeping a deposit in bad faith costs $100 plus three times the amount wrongfully withheld plus fees (§ 92.109(a)). The Deceptive Trade Practices Act, which reaches leases, lists representing that an agreement confers rights, remedies or obligations it does not have, or that the law prohibits, as deceptive, and a consumer who relied on it to the consumer's detriment can recover up to three times economic damages if you acted knowingly (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §§ 17.46(b)(12), 17.50(b)(1)). The library's row on lease terms Texas voids lists them; leave them out.

title: No Landlord Insurance Mandate in Texas
bodyText: No Texas statute requires a residential landlord to carry liability or property insurance, to file proof of insurance with a state or local office, or to tell tenants whether you are insured or what your policy covers. A city ordinance, your lender, a property owners' association or an affordable-housing program agreement may still require coverage, so check those. Insurance does appear in Texas tenancy law in four other ways. If a condition results from an insured casualty loss such as fire, smoke, hail or explosion, your repair period does not begin until you receive the insurance proceeds (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.054(a)). The floodplain notice you must give tells the tenant that most tenant insurance policies do not cover flood loss (§ 92.0135(b)). If you offer a fee in lieu of a security deposit, the fee may buy insurance for the tenant's lease liabilities, at no more than its reasonable cost, with the written terms the statute lists (§ 92.111(e), (f)). And a condominium association must, to the extent reasonably available, carry property insurance on the common elements and commercial general liability insurance (§ 82.111(a)); that does not replace your own policy. The cautious course: carry landlord liability coverage, and tell tenants in the lease that your policy does not cover their belongings (the library's renter's insurance clause).

title: No State Landlord Registration in Texas
bodyText: No Texas statute makes a residential landlord, as a landlord, register with a state or county office, hold a rental licence or a general business licence, or (if you live out of state) hire an in-state broker or manager before renting (all Texas codes searched). Your city may have its own rental registration, inspection or certificate-of-occupancy program; city ordinances were not reviewed, so check yours. Three state laws can still reach you. First, real estate licensing: a person who, for compensation and for another person, leases or offers to lease real estate, or controls the acceptance or deposit of rent from a resident of a single-family home, is a broker and must hold a Texas Real Estate Commission licence (Tex. Occ. Code §§ 1101.002(1), 1101.351). That licence is not needed by you as owner, or your employee, leasing your own property, by an on-site manager of an apartment complex, or by the manager or an employee of your LLC or the general partner of your limited partnership (§ 1101.005(7), (8), (10), (11)). So a third-party property manager you hire must be licensed. Second, if you own through an out-of-state LLC, corporation or limited partnership, the entity must register to transact business in Texas (Tex. Bus. Orgs. Code § 9.001); owning Texas property, without more, is not transacting business (§ 9.251(15)), but whether renting it out is more is not settled by statute, so the cautious course is to register. The registration must name a Texas registered agent and registered office (§§ 5.201(a), 9.004(b)(9)), and until the entity registers it may not maintain a suit in a Texas court, including an eviction, on a claim arising from business it transacts here (§ 9.051(b)). Third, assumed names: if you regularly rent under an assumed name (for an individual, a name without your surname; for an entity, a name other than the one in its formation papers), you must file an assumed name certificate, with the county clerk if you are an individual or with the secretary of state if you are an entity; until you do, you may not maintain a suit arising from a lease made under that name, and an intentional violation is a Class A misdemeanor (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §§ 71.002(2), 71.051, 71.054, 71.101, 71.103(a), 71.201(a), 71.202). Separately, you must disclose the owner's and any off-site management company's name and address on request (the library's ownership and management rows).

title: Possession, Rent and Damages After a Texas Tenant Defaults
bodyText:
When a Texas tenant defaults, you can recover possession and rent in one eviction suit and keep your other money claims for a separate suit. In the justice court eviction you may join a claim for unpaid rent if the rent due and unpaid is not more than $20,000, excluding statutory interest and court costs but including attorney fees (Tex. R. Civ. P. 510.1(a), 510.6(e)). A judgment for you awards possession, costs, delinquent rent as of the date of judgment, and attorney fees if recoverable by law (Rule 510.18(d)), and you may recover the unpaid rent even if the tenant moves out after you file (Tex. Prop. Code § 24.0051(b)).

Nothing else rides along: counterclaims and claims against third parties are not allowed in an eviction (§ 24.004(c)), and an eviction "does not bar a suit for trespass, damages, waste, rent, or mesne profits" (§ 24.008). So sue separately for damage to the unit, for charges that are not rent, or for rent above the cap; a money-only claim of up to $20,000 can be a small claims case in justice court (Tex. Gov't Code § 27.031(a)(1); Rule 500.1(a)).

If the tenant abandons in breach of the lease, you must mitigate your damages, and a lease term waiving that duty is void (§ 91.006). Attorney's fees depend on a lease fee clause or the statutory demand letter (§ 24.006). No Texas statute addresses accelerating rent for the rest of the term on default; whether future rent is recoverable, and how much, turns on the lease and case law. Get advice before claiming it.

title: Texas Late-Fee Limits, Including Manufactured Home Lots
bodyText: For an ordinary residential lease, Texas limits late fees: notice of the fee must be in a written lease, the fee must be reasonable, and you may charge it only once rent has remained unpaid two full days after it was due (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.019(a)). A fee is reasonable if it is not more than 12 percent of the rent for the rental period in a structure with four or fewer units, or 10 percent in a larger one, or is not more than your uncertain damages from the late payment; an initial fee plus daily fees count as one fee (§ 92.019(a-1), (b)). Breaking the rule costs $100 plus three times the fee collected plus the tenant's attorney's fees, and a lease waiver is void (§ 92.019(c), (d)); the library's late-fee rules row has the details. Texas works the other way round from some states for manufactured home communities: a lease of a lot for the tenant's own manufactured home falls under its own chapter, which sets no late-fee cap, but the lease must state any late charge, an increase in fees during the term is void unless the tenant initials it, and any unconscionable provision is void (§§ 94.002, 94.053(c)(5), (d), (e)). Texas has no separate cap on utility charges in those communities in that chapter; water submetering rules apply where used.

title: Police Cooperation and Crime-Free Terms in Texas
bodyText: No Texas statute requires or regulates a crime-free lease addendum, requires you or your tenants to cooperate with police investigations, or requires you, as a landlord, to give police information about tenants or access to a unit (all Texas codes searched; case law and city ordinances not reviewed, and some cities run crime-free or nuisance-property programs by ordinance, so check yours). Three statutes still shape how you deal with police. First, you may not prohibit or limit a tenant's right to summon police or emergency assistance based on a reasonable belief that someone needs help, or penalize the tenant for doing so, and a lease waiver is void (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.015; the library's summon-police row). Second, under the common-nuisance law, anyone deciding whether to sue over crime at a property must consider whether the owner promptly notifies law enforcement of criminal acts there and cooperates with the investigation (Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 125.002(h)); your request for police or emergency help cannot be used to show you tolerated the activity, but evidence that you refused to cooperate with law enforcement is admissible against you (§ 125.004(d)). Third, a written lease provision prohibiting criminal acts lets you end the tenancy for a material breach without a retaliation claim (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.332(b)(3); the library's criminal-activity rows). Separately, reporting duties that bind every person bind you and your staff. Anyone with reasonable cause to believe a child's physical or mental health or welfare has been adversely affected by abuse or neglect must report it immediately to a law enforcement agency or the Department of Family and Protective Services, and a knowing failure is a Class A misdemeanor (Tex. Fam. Code §§ 261.101(a), 261.103(a), 261.109(a), (b)). Anyone with cause to believe an elderly person or a person with a disability is being abused, neglected or exploited must report it immediately to the department, and a knowing failure is a Class A misdemeanor (Tex. Hum. Res. Code §§ 48.051(a), 48.052(a)). A person who sees a felony in which serious bodily injury or death may have resulted must report it immediately to the police if a reasonable person would believe it has not been reported and reporting is safe (Class A misdemeanor; Tex. Penal Code § 38.171), and a person who sees a sexual or assaultive offense against a child and could safely help the child or report it must do one or the other (third-degree felony; § 38.17). In a county with a medical examiner, a private citizen who becomes aware of a violent, unnatural, suspicious or unwitnessed death or a suicide, as when a tenant is found dead in a unit, must report it immediately to the medical examiner or the police, and a knowing violation is a Class B misdemeanor (Tex. Code Crim. Proc. art. 49.25, §§ 6(a), 7(a), 14); that article is repealed effective April 1, 2027 by the Code of Criminal Procedure recodification, so recheck it then. The cautious course: report crime at the property, cooperate with investigations, and keep a record of both.

title: No Lead-Safe Rental Certificate in Texas
bodyText: Texas does not require a lead-safe or lead-free certificate for a rental, an inspection certificate attached to the lease, or registration of a rental as lead-safe. Texas lead certification is for people, not properties. The Department of State Health Services certifies persons who do lead-based paint activities (inspection, testing, risk assessment, abatement and similar work) in target housing, meaning housing built before 1978 other than most housing for the elderly or persons with disabilities and dwellings without bedrooms, and in child-occupied facilities, and its rules require certified and accredited personnel for that work (Tex. Occ. Code §§ 1955.001, 1955.051). So if you have lead-based paint inspected, assessed or abated, hire a department-certified inspector, risk assessor or abatement firm; the firm must give its reports to you as the building owner who contracted for the work (25 Tex. Admin. Code § 295.212(h)). Keep them: they are records you must list in the federal lead disclosure for pre-1978 housing, which the library's lead-based paint clause carries. Federal renovation and disclosure rules are not reviewed here.

title: No Texas Lead Notice Beyond Federal Law
bodyText: Beyond the federal lead-based paint disclosure for housing built before 1978 (the library's lead-based paint clause), Texas requires no state lead notice, certificate, pamphlet or information packet at lease signing or renewal. The state lead rules point back to the federal disclosure: they say building owners are subject to the federal requirements for disclosure of known lead-based paint and hazards upon sale or lease (25 Tex. Admin. Code § 295.212(h)). Two related state rules are not lease notices. The seller's disclosure notice asks a seller of a single-dwelling home whether it has lead-based paint, but it applies to sales, not leases (Tex. Prop. Code § 5.008(a), (b)). And if a child living in your rental is reported with a blood lead level warranting an environmental lead investigation, the Department of State Health Services or its agent may investigate the home with an adult occupant's written consent (Tex. Health & Safety Code § 88.008(a)(1)); if you receive the results, keep them, because they may be records you must list in your federal disclosure.

title: What a Texas Lease Must Contain
bodyText: Texas has no single statute listing what a residential lease must contain, and no rule that the start and end dates, or anything else, appear on the first page (all Texas codes searched). Instead, particular statutes require particular items. Every lease must carry, in underlined or bold print, language telling the tenant about the statutory repair remedies (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.056(g); the library's repair remedies clause). Every lease should carry the two statements that tenants may have special statutory rights to end the lease early (family violence or a military deployment or transfer; certain sexual offenses or stalking): without them, a tenant who ends the lease under those rights is released from any delinquent rent owed at termination (§§ 92.016(f), 92.017(g), 92.0161(g); the early termination rights clause). For leases of 30 days or more, the floodplain and flood-history notices go in the lease, an addendum or a separate signed document (§ 92.0135; the flood disclosure clause). Many of your rights also exist only if the written lease states them, several in underlined or bold print: a late fee (§ 92.019(a)(1)), changing the locks for unpaid rent (§ 92.0081(d)(1)), a contractual landlord's lien (§ 54.043(a)), advance notice of surrender as a condition of the deposit refund (§ 92.103(b)), deducting rekeying costs after a breach (§ 92.156(e)) and charging for a security device the tenant damages (§ 92.162(b)). The library's clauses carry each with the required print. A manufactured home community lot lease must list sixteen items, including the lot, term, rent, fees, deposit and your maintenance duties (§ 94.053(c)).

title: No Lease-Initialing Rule in Texas
bodyText: No Texas statute requires a tenant to initial particular provisions of an ordinary residential lease (all Texas codes searched). Texas uses print and placement instead: several terms work only if they are underlined or in bold print in the lease (the library's row on what a Texas lease must contain lists them), and a servicemember tenant's waiver of the military early-termination right is valid only if it is signed and in writing in a document separate from the lease, and only for a move into base housing or other housing within 30 miles; the waiver does not apply to a move into housing owned or occupied by the tenant's family or relatives, or a move caused by a significant military-service loss of income (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.017(j)-(k)). The one initialing rule is for manufactured home community lot leases: a provision requiring an increase in rent or in fees or charges during the lease term must be initialed by the tenant or the provision is void (§ 94.053(d)). Having the tenant initial key terms, such as the late fee, the lockout right, the landlord's lien and the deposit-surrender notice, is still a sensible way to show the tenant saw them; it does not replace the required print.

title: No Lease Recording Duty in Texas
bodyText: Texas does not require a residential lease to be recorded or registered with any office, has no land registry for leases, and recording changes none of your or the tenant's rights under the residential tenancy chapter (all Texas codes searched). You may record a lease, or a short memorandum of it, in the county real property records if it has been acknowledged, sworn to with a proper jurat, or proved (Tex. Prop. Code § 12.001(a)); a properly recorded instrument is notice to everyone of its existence (§ 13.002). The reason to consider it is priority: a conveyance of real property or an interest in it is void as to a creditor or a later purchaser for value without notice unless it has been acknowledged and recorded, though it still binds the parties, their heirs and anyone with notice (§ 13.001). Whether a lease is such a conveyance, and whether a tenant's possession gives a later buyer or lender notice of an unrecorded lease, are questions for case law, not read here; Texas has no special rule for leases to relatives. For an ordinary one-year lease, recording is rare; consider it for a long lease, a lease with a purchase option, or a rental you may sell or refinance. If a lien superior to the lease is foreclosed, a residential tenant who is paying rent is entitled to at least 30 days' written notice to vacate if the buyer chooses not to continue the lease (§ 24.005(b)).

title: Lease Length Rules in Texas
bodyText: Texas sets no maximum or minimum term for a private residential lease (all Texas codes and the Constitution searched). What the law requires turns on length. A lease of real estate for a term longer than one year is not enforceable unless the lease, or a memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by the person to be charged or someone lawfully authorized to sign for that person (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 26.01(a), (b)(5)), so put any lease over a year in writing, signed by you and every tenant; an agent who signs a lease of more than one year for you must be "authorized in writing" (Tex. Prop. Code § 5.021), but Texas adds no seal or acknowledgment requirement. If the rental is your homestead and you are married, neither spouse may sell, convey or encumber the homestead without the other's joinder (Tex. Fam. Code § 5.001); no statute says whether a lease encumbers a homestead, so have both spouses sign. A manufactured home community must offer an initial lot lease of at least six months, though the parties may agree to a different term if the tenant asks (Tex. Prop. Code § 94.052(a)). Statutes that cap lease terms bind only the government bodies they name, not private landlords; for example, a civic center authority may not lease its facilities for longer than 40 years (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code § 281.045). A lease of one year or more can also matter under Texas's foreign-acquisition law (the library's row on that law).

title: No Lease-Type Parity Rule in Texas
bodyText: No Texas statute requires the same terms for month-to-month and fixed-term tenants, bars charging more rent for a month-to-month tenancy, or caps the difference between lease types (all Texas codes searched). The statutes on tenancy length only set defaults: either side may end a month-to-month tenancy by notice, effective on the later of the day the notice gives or one month after it is given, unless you and the tenant agreed in an instrument signed by both on a different notice period or on no notice (Tex. Prop. Code § 91.001(a), (b), (e)). So you may offer different rents or terms for different lease lengths, for example a lower rent for a twelve-month lease. Offer each option on the same terms to every applicant; Texas and federal fair-housing law may also apply and are not reviewed here. In a manufactured home community, the 60-day notice before you end or decline to renew applies to fixed-term and month-to-month lot leases alike (§ 94.055(a)).

title: No Lease Type-Size Rule in Texas
bodyText: No Texas statute sets a minimum type size for a whole residential lease, or keeps a small-print lease out of evidence (all Texas codes searched). Texas sets print rules for particular terms instead: the repair-remedies statement and several of your rights must be underlined or in bold (see the library's row on what a Texas lease must contain). Two rules use a type size. A manufactured home community must give a prospective tenant a separate disclosure statement, about the right to a six-month initial lease and the nonrenewal notice periods, printed in at least 10-point type, and its lot lease must be typed or printed in legible handwriting (Tex. Prop. Code §§ 94.051(3), 94.053(a)(1)). At a multiunit rental complex with a pool, a lease term requiring the tenant to make repair requests for door and window latches, locks and similar devices in writing is effective only if it is in capital letters and underlined, or in 10-point boldfaced print (Tex. Health & Safety Code §§ 757.009(b), 757.013). The cautious course: print the whole lease in a readable size, no smaller than 10-point, with the required terms in bold.

title: Deadlines to Sue in Texas Lease Disputes
bodyText: Texas has no limitations period written specifically for rent or other lease claims (all Texas codes searched), so the general periods apply. A suit on a debt, and any action with no express limitations period other than one to recover real property, must be brought within four years after the claim accrues (Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code §§ 16.004(a)(3), 16.051), so a suit for unpaid rent or other money owed under the lease has four years. Suits for injury to property, conversion of personal property, personal injury, and forcible entry and detainer or forcible detainer (the eviction suit) must be brought within two years (§ 16.003(a)). A lease clause that shortens the time to sue on the lease to less than two years is void (§ 16.070(a)), so do not use one, in either direction. No statute says a partial payment restarts the period. A written acknowledgment matters: an acknowledgment of a claim that appears barred by limitations is admissible to defeat limitations only if it is in writing and signed by the party to be charged (§ 16.065). Whether a payment by itself extends the period is a question for case law, not read here, so do not rely on it: sue within four years of the earliest unpaid amount, and get any promise to pay an old balance in a signed writing.

title: Liquidated Damages in a Texas Lease
bodyText:
Texas has no general statute on liquidated damages or penalties in a residential lease. The Uniform Commercial Code's liquidated-damages rule applies to leases of goods, not of real property (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 2A.504). Two residential statutes do speak to agreed amounts. A late fee is lawful only if the written lease gives notice of it, rent has stayed unpaid two full days after its due date, and the fee is reasonable, which it is if it stays within 12 percent of the rent for the rental period (four or fewer units) or 10 percent (more than four), or, if higher, is not more than your uncertain damages from the late payment (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.019(a-1)). And if a tenant never moves in and a replacement tenant you find occupies by the start date, you may keep only a lease cancellation fee agreed in the lease or your actual re-letting expenses (§ 92.1031).

Otherwise, whether an agreed amount, such as an early termination fee, is enforceable or a penalty is a question of case law.

The cautious course: set agreed amounts as a reasonable estimate of losses that are hard to measure at signing, say so in the lease, and never pair one with a waiver of your duty to mitigate, which is void (§ 91.006(b)).

title: When a Texas Lease May Shift Repairs to the Tenant
bodyText:
A Texas lease may shift repair duties to the tenant only in the ways Tex. Prop. Code § 92.006(c)-(f) allows; the library's row on shifting the repair duty walks through each. On the points other states' laws turn on: the restriction covers your duty to repair conditions that materially affect the physical health or safety of an ordinary tenant, and the 120-degree hot water duty (§§ 92.006(c), 92.052(a)); ordinary chores outside that duty, such as yard care or changing light bulbs, are left to the lease (the library's tenant maintenance clause).

An agreement that the tenant will make covered repairs at your expense needs no special form (§ 92.006(d)). Shifting the cost of covered repairs to the tenant needs a written lease, with the agreement underlined or in bold in the lease or a separate written addendum, specific and clear, and made knowingly, voluntarily and for consideration (§ 92.006(e)(4), (f)). The statute does not name the consideration or say whether the rent itself is enough, so state the consideration in the agreement, such as a stated rent reduction.

A whole-duty shift is open only to a landlord who owns just one rental dwelling that is free of health or safety defects at the start, with no reason to believe one will occur or recur during the term (§ 92.006(e)(1)-(3)); otherwise only three kinds of damage may be shifted (§ 92.006(f); the library's tenant repair payment clause). You have no duty to repair conditions caused by the tenant, an occupant, a family member or a guest, unless caused by normal wear and tear (§ 92.052(b)).

title: No Meter Conservation Charge in Texas
bodyText: Texas has no meter conservation charge, on-bill energy-efficiency charge or similar utility-bill charge that you must disclose to a new tenant, and no statute giving a tenant notice of one or a rent deduction for one (all Texas codes searched; Public Utility Commission rules mostly not held). Texas's energy-efficiency financing reaches the owner, not the tenant's bill. A city or county property-assessed clean energy program covers commercial or industrial property and residential property with five or more dwelling units, and an assessment may be imposed only under a written contract with the record owner (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code §§ 399.002(5), 399.005); cities may also make contractual assessments to finance energy-efficiency improvements permanently fixed to real property (§ 376.001). If you take on such an assessment and plan to recover any of it from tenants, say so in the lease as rent or a stated fee: Texas's debt-collection law bars collecting a fee the lease does not expressly authorize unless it is otherwise legally chargeable (the library's row on fees your lease must state). On submetered or allocated water, the Kansas-style question, Texas regulates closely what you may bill beyond the utility's charges, with lease disclosures; see the library's water billing rows.

title: No Military Zone Lease Disclosure in Texas
bodyText: Texas requires no lease disclosure that a rental is near a military installation, in a noise or accident-potential zone, or within a set distance of a base, and gives tenants no termination right tied to one (all Texas codes searched, including the defense-community chapter, Tex. Loc. Gov't Code ch. 397). The military notice Texas has is for sales: a seller of a home of not more than one dwelling unit must give the buyer a disclosure notice stating that the property may be located near a military installation and may be affected by high noise or air installation compatible use zones or other operations, with information in the installation's Air Installation Compatible Use Zone Study or Joint Land Use Study (Tex. Prop. Code § 5.008(a), (b)). Counties and cities with an installation must work with it to make the most recent study, or a link to it, available on their websites (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code § 397.007). If your rental is near a base, the cautious course is to tell prospective tenants and point them to that study, since noise and overflights can matter to them.

title: Minors as Tenants and Eviction Defendants in Texas
bodyText: The age of majority in Texas is 18 (Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 129.001). A person under 18 who is or has been married, or whose disabilities of minority have been removed for general purposes by a court, is not a minor and has an adult's capacity to contract (Tex. Fam. Code §§ 101.003(a), 1.104, 31.006). No Texas statute lets an unmarried minor sign a binding residential lease (all Texas codes searched); the only housing-consent rules cover transitional living programs and emergency shelters (Tex. Fam. Code §§ 32.202, 32.203), and whether a minor can later avoid a lease is case law. So have an adult sign as tenant or guarantor and list the minor as an occupant. In the eviction, name as defendants all tenants obligated under a written residential lease who live in the unit and whom you seek to evict; no writ may issue or be executed against such a tenant who was not named and served (Tex. R. Civ. P. 510.6(d)). Minor occupants need not be named: the writ orders the officer to remove the tenant "and all persons claiming under the tenant" (Tex. Prop. Code § 24.0061(d)(2)(B)). No statute or eviction rule bars naming a minor, and the eviction rules have no procedure for a minor party; the general next-friend and guardian ad litem rules do not apply unless the law or the rules provide (Rule 510.1(b)). If a minor did sign as a tenant, get advice before suing. Two 16-year lines matter: a notice to vacate may be handed to a tenant 16 or older (§ 24.005(f-3)(3)), and the officer may leave the citation with a person over 16 at the residence (Rule 510.8(d)(4)).

title: City Utility Liens for Tenant Bills
bodyText: A Texas city may, by ordinance, put a lien on an owner's property for delinquent bills for city utility service to it, but not on a homestead (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code § 552.0025(d)). You can keep a tenant's unpaid city utility bills off your property: the lien does not apply to bills for service connected in a tenant's name after you, as owner, notify the city that the property is rental property (§ 552.0025(e)), nor, under a lien ordinance adopted on or after August 28, 1989, to service connected in a tenant's name before the ordinance took effect (§ 552.0025(f)). So require the tenant to put city utilities in its own name, and give the city written notice that the property is a rental before the tenant's service starts; keep a copy. A lien that does attach is perfected by recording a notice in the county real property records, may include penalties, interest and collection costs, and ranks below only a bona fide mortgage recorded earlier (§ 552.0025(g), (h)). The city also may not make a new customer pay a previous customer's bill at the same connection as a condition of service, or require a third party to guarantee a customer's bill (§ 552.0025(a), (b)). This section governs city-owned utilities, and your city's ordinance sets the details; water districts, other utilities and county solid-waste programs have their own rules, not covered here.

title: No Separate Notice for Nonrefundable Fees in Texas
bodyText:
No Texas statute requires a nonrefundable fee to be disclosed in a separate notice or document, or to be separately signed or initialed. Listing each fee by name and amount in the lease, and saying it is not refundable, is enough; the library's optional nonrefundable fees clause does that. Two related writings are required by statute.

If you offer a fee in lieu of a security deposit, you must tell the tenant in writing, when you offer it, that the tenant may pay a deposit instead and may later switch to one, with the charges for each, and the agreement to pay the fee must be in writing signed by you and the tenant; if the fee buys insurance, that agreement must state, among other things, that the fee, unless otherwise specified, is not refundable (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.111(b), (c), (f); the library's fee-in-lieu row). And the acknowledgment an applicant signs for your tenant selection criteria must warn that the application fee will not be refunded if the application is rejected for not meeting the criteria or for inaccurate or incomplete information (§ 92.3515(c); the rental application row). Whatever the paperwork says, money held primarily to secure performance of the lease is a security deposit (§ 92.102).

title: Out-of-State Owners Renting in Texas
bodyText: Texas does not require an owner who lives out of state to appoint an in-state agent, name an agent in the lease, or file an agent designation before suing a tenant (all Texas codes searched), and there is no state withholding on rent paid to a nonresident owner, because Texas may not impose a tax on individuals' net incomes (Tex. Const. art. 8, § 24-a). Three rules still matter if you live elsewhere. First, service of process in a tenant's suit: if you gave the tenant written notice of your management company's name and business street address, that company is your sole agent for service; otherwise your management company, on-premise manager or rent collector is your agent, unless you gave the tenant your own name and business street address in writing (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.003). Second, a nonresident who engages in business in Texas without a designated or maintained resident agent can be served through the Texas secretary of state, and a nonresident does business in Texas by contracting with a Texas resident where either party is to perform the contract in whole or in part in Texas (Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code §§ 17.042(1), 17.044(a)(1), (b)); a lease of Texas property to a Texas tenant appears to qualify. The secretary of state is also your agent for service if you move out of Texas after a tenant's claim arises but before the tenant sues (§ 17.044(a)(3)). Third, anyone you pay to lease your property or collect rent on a single-family home needs a Texas real estate licence, and an out-of-state LLC or other entity that transacts business in Texas must register (the library's landlord registration row); its registration names a Texas registered agent for service, and until it registers it may not maintain a suit, including an eviction, on a claim arising from that business (Tex. Bus. Orgs. Code §§ 5.201(a), 9.004(b)(9), 9.051(b)). If you rent under an assumed name, the same bar on suing applies until you file an assumed name certificate (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 71.201(a)). Give tenants a local emergency phone number and the ownership and management disclosure (the library's rows).

title: No Texas Rule on Notice or Filing Fees
bodyText: No Texas statute authorizes, caps or bans a lease charge for preparing or serving a notice to vacate or for filing an eviction (all Texas codes searched). What the law does say: the winner of an eviction recovers all court costs, and attorney's fees follow their own rule (Tex. Prop. Code § 24.006(b)-(d)); and anyone collecting a consumer debt, including a landlord collecting its own rent from an individual tenant, may collect a fee incidental to the debt only if the lease expressly authorizes it or it is otherwise legally chargeable (Tex. Fin. Code §§ 392.001(2), (5)-(6), 392.303(a)(2)). Texas has no general statute on penalties in contracts, so whether a fixed notice or filing fee is an unenforceable penalty is decided by case law. The cautious course: don't charge a flat "notice fee" or "eviction fee"; recover court costs through the judgment, and, if you want other costs repaid, have the lease authorize your actual, documented costs and charge only those.

title: Shortening the Notice to Vacate in Texas
bodyText:
Texas lets the lease change the notice to vacate.
