Before filing an eviction you must give at least three days' written notice to vacate, "unless the parties have contracted for a shorter or longer notice period in a written lease or agreement" (Tex. Prop. Code § 24.005(a), (b)). So a written lease may set a shorter or longer period; the library's optional notice-to-vacate clause does this.

The statute speaks of a shorter period, not of no notice, so never set the period at zero; the cautious course is at least one day. Some parts of the notice cannot be contracted away: for nonpayment by a tenant who was not late before the month you give notice, it must be a notice to pay rent or vacate (§ 24.005(a)); it must be delivered by one of the statute's methods unless the tenant actually receives it (§ 24.005(f-3), (f-4)); and a federal notice period, where one applies, delays service of the writ (§ 24.005(c-1)).

Ending a month-to-month tenancy is separate: it takes one month's notice for a monthly rent period unless you and the tenant signed an instrument agreeing a different period or no notice (§ 91.001(b), (e)(1)), and a holdover eviction must satisfy that rule as well as the notice to vacate (§ 24.005(a)).

title: What Goes in a Texas Notice to Vacate, and What Stays the Same While It Runs
bodyText: Texas says little about what a notice to vacate must contain, and nothing freezes the unit while one is pending (all Texas codes searched). The notice must be written, give at least three days or the period your lease sets, take the form of a notice to pay rent or vacate where the statute requires it, and be delivered by an approved method (Tex. Prop. Code § 24.005(a), (f-3)). You may add to it: if your lease or a law requires a chance to respond to a notice of proposed eviction before filing, the notice may include that opportunity and the periods may run together (§ 24.005(e)). A statutory attorney's-fee demand must say you may recover fees if the tenant does not leave before the 11th day after receiving it, and go by registered or certified mail at least 10 days before filing (§ 24.006(a)). No statute requires a statement of tenant rights, legal-aid information, a reason or a state form, or bars an offer of a new lease; keep the notice plain, because your sworn petition must say when and how you gave it and which form it took (Tex. R. Civ. P. 510.6(a)(9)). While the notice runs, your duties continue: no utility interruption except for bona fide repairs, construction or an emergency (§ 92.008(a), (b)); no removing doors, windows, locks or furnished appliances except for prompt repair, and no lockout except as the statute allows (§ 92.0081(a), (b)); and no retaliation (§ 92.331). Housing tax credit, TCAP and Exchange developments must state the grounds in a termination notice, and they and NHTF developments must give 30 days' written notice for nonpayment of rent (10 Tex. Admin. Code § 10.613(a); HOME and some other programs have their own notice rules, § 10.613(b)). A development subject to the 2025 HOME Final Rule must send every notice to vacate to the state housing agency within 14 days after issuing a 30-day notice, or on issuance for a shorter notice given for imminent threats (§ 10.613(o)(4)).

title: Lease Choices Texas Law Leaves to You
bodyText: Many Texas defaults give way to what your lease says, so these are real choices for your lease; a silent lease takes the statutory default. (1) Notice to end a month-to-month tenancy: one month by default, but an instrument signed by both of you may set a different period or none (Tex. Prop. Code § 91.001(e)). (2) Notice to vacate before an eviction suit: at least three days, unless the written lease sets a shorter or longer period (§ 24.005(a); the library's notice-to-vacate clause). (3) Delivery of that notice by e-mail or other electronic means, if the parties agreed in writing (§ 24.005(f-3)(4); the electronic notice clause). (4) Written repair requests: required only if the lease is written and requires written notice (§ 92.052(d)). (5) Rent reduction after a casualty leaves the unit partly unusable: only on a court judgment, unless a written lease provides otherwise (§ 92.054(c)). (6) A lease cancellation fee you may keep if a tenant never moves in and you find a replacement who occupies on time (§ 92.1031(b)). (7) Tenant repairs at your expense, and, with strict formalities, at the tenant's expense (§ 92.006(d)-(f); the row on shifting the repair duty). (8) A fee in lieu of a security deposit, but only if you also offer a deposit (§ 92.111(a)). (9) Rights that exist only if the lease states them, several in underlined or bold print: a late fee, changing locks for unpaid rent, a landlord's lien, advance notice of surrender for the deposit refund, rekeying deductions and security-device charges (the row on what a Texas lease must contain). The library offers each as an optional clause.

title: No Ordnance, Demolition or Shared-Meter Disclosure in Texas
bodyText: Texas requires no lease disclosure that a rental is near a former military ordnance or munitions site, that a demolition permit or plan is pending, or that a utility meter serves more than one unit or the common areas (all Texas codes searched). Related rules: you may close a rental unit by written notice sent by certified mail, return receipt requested, to the tenant and to the local health officer and building inspector, stating that you are ending the tenancy as soon as legally possible and that after the tenant moves out you will immediately demolish the unit or stop using it for residential purposes (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.055(a)). After the tenant leaves, you may not allow reoccupancy or reconnection of utilities by separate meter for six months, and the local health officer or building inspector may not allow occupancy until certifying that no condition materially affects an ordinary tenant's health or safety; if you close the unit before the tenant has given you a repair notice, the repair remedies do not apply; if you close it after a repair notice, the tenant is entitled only to the civil penalty (one month's rent plus $500), actual damages and court costs and attorney's fees under § 92.0563(a)(3)-(5) and, if the tenant moves out on or before the end of the rental term, to your payment of the tenant's actual and reasonable moving expenses, a pro rata rent refund from the move-out date and the deposit as the law requires; breaking the reoccupancy bar or that payment duty costs one month's rent plus $100 and attorney's fees (§ 92.055(b)-(e)). If you pay the utility bill for tenants and fall behind, the tenant-notice rules in the library's landlord-paid utility cutoff row apply, and submetered or allocated water and submetered electricity need the lease disclosures in the library's submetering clauses. A city order to repair or demolish a substandard building follows city procedures not reviewed here.

title: Facilities and Equipment Duties in Texas
bodyText: No Texas statute lists the facilities a landlord must supply in a rental, such as particular appliances, laundry, mailboxes or a garage door opener, and no consumer-protection or product-safety law puts a duty on landlords for a garage door opener or similar building equipment; no state statute requires a carbon monoxide alarm in a rental. The lease sets what you provide, so list every appliance and amenity (the library's appliances and services clauses). Texas does attach duties to particular facilities. Your repair duty covers conditions that materially affect an ordinary tenant's health or safety, and a device supplying hot water of at least 120 degrees Fahrenheit (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.052(a)); security devices and smoke alarms have their own rules (the library's rows). A pool at a multiunit rental complex, or at a rental in a condominium, cooperative or town home project, must meet the pool yard enclosure rules, and you must inspect enclosures, gates and self-closing devices at least every 31 days (Tex. Health & Safety Code §§ 757.002, 757.009(c); the library's pool row). If your building has an elevator, escalator, chairlift or platform lift, you as owner must have it inspected annually by a registered inspector, file the report, display the certificate of compliance, maintain it to the adopted codes and report any accident within 24 hours (§ 754.019); an elevator in a single-family dwelling is largely exempt (§ 754.0111(b)). Each one-family or two-family dwelling built in Texas must have working smoke detectors meeting the local building code (§ 766.002(a)).

title: What a Texas Lease Cannot Waive
bodyText: Texas has no single rule that every tenant right is non-waivable. The residential tenancy chapter instead says, duty by duty, what a lease may and may not change (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.006). These may not be waived at all: your duties and the tenant's remedies on security deposits, security devices, disclosure of ownership and management, and utility cutoffs; your duty to install smoke alarms and the tenant's remedies if you don't (your duty to inspect and repair them may be waived only by written agreement); the tenant's right to end the lease and avoid liability after family violence or a military deployment; and the tenant's right to a jury trial in a suit under the residential tenancy chapter (§ 92.006(a), (g), (h)). Your repair duty for conditions affecting health or safety may be shifted only in the three narrow ways the statute allows, each with specific written, bold or underlined terms (§ 92.006(c)-(f)), and knowingly contracting around it costs one month's rent plus $2,000, actual damages and attorney's fees (§ 92.0563(b)). Your security-device, disclosure and smoke-alarm duties may be enlarged only by specific written agreement (§ 92.006(b)). Other sections void lease waivers of their own rules, including lockouts, utility interruption, late fees, summoning police and the sexual-assault and stalking termination right. Treat a lease term that tries to waive any of these as unenforceable, and see the library's row on terms a Texas lease cannot waive for the full list.

title: Notice Before Indoor Pest Treatments
bodyText: Texas regulates notice of indoor pest treatments through the pest control licensing law, and the duty depends on the size of your property (Tex. Occ. Code § 1951.453). Fewer than five rental units: the licensed applicator or technician must make the state's pest control information sheet available to the tenant of each unit; you have no separate notice duty. Five or more units: the applicator gives the information sheet and the state's pest control sign to you or your manager, and you or your employee or agent (not the applicator) must notify residents in the treatment area or an adjacent area at least 48 hours before each planned treatment, either by posting the sign in a common area or by leaving the information sheet on the front door of, or in a conspicuous place inside, each unit. The 48-hour notice may be waived for emergency treatments under the licensing agency's rules, the sign, notice and sheet rules do not apply to vacant, unoccupied space, and you are not in violation if a properly posted sign is removed by an unauthorized person (§ 1951.456(b), (c), (e)). For an outdoor treatment at a property with fewer than five units, the applicator makes the sheet available at each unit at the time of treatment (§ 1951.457(b)). Entry for treatment runs through the lease's entry clause, and the library's pest treatment row covers tenant reporting and cooperation.

title: No Pet and Eviction Fact Sheet
bodyText: Texas does not require you to give a tenant a state fact sheet or any other notice about pets and eviction, at signing or later (all Texas codes searched). No Texas statute addresses a tenant's pets in an eviction notice, the eviction suit or the execution of a writ of possession, and none sets a procedure for an animal left behind after a tenant moves out or is evicted. The only Texas statute on tenant pets is narrow: a public housing authority whose policy allows tenants to keep pets must follow local dangerous-dog restrictions (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code § 392.0555). For everyone else, pets are a matter for your lease. Say in it which animals are allowed, what deposit or fee applies, and what happens to a pet if the tenant leaves or is removed; the library's pet clause and pet fee row cover this. Assistance animals for a person with a disability are not pets and follow the fair housing rules. City and county animal-control ordinances, which often govern stray or abandoned animals, were not reviewed, and neither was case law. If an animal is left behind, contact local animal control rather than disposing of it yourself.

title: Pet Deposits and Pet Fees in Texas
bodyText:
Texas defines a security deposit as any advance of money, other than a rental application deposit or advance rent, that is intended primarily to secure performance under the lease (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.102). A refundable pet deposit fits that definition, so it follows every deposit rule: refund within 30 days after surrender, no deduction for normal wear and tear, an itemized list of deductions, and the bad-faith penalties (§§ 92.103, 92.104, 92.109).

Texas sets no cap on a pet deposit, and no statute addresses monthly pet rent or a one-time pet fee; whether a charge labelled a nonrefundable pet fee is really a deposit depends on whether it secures performance, a question for case law not reviewed here, so describe each charge accurately in the lease. Assistance animals are not pets: you may not charge a person with a disability extra compensation or a deposit for a service animal, though the person remains liable for damage the animal does (Tex. Hum. Res. Code § 121.003(h)), and fair-housing law covers other assistance animals.

title: No Plain-Language Statement or Lease Preapproval
bodyText: Texas has no plain-language law for residential leases of the kind some states have: no readability test, no required statement listing every consumer restriction or waiver in the lease, no Attorney General preapproval of lease forms, and no dollar exclusion (all Texas codes searched). The library's row on plain-language lease rules makes the general point. Two Texas rules come close and are worth knowing. First, a consumer's waiver of the Deceptive Trade Practices Act is void unless it is in writing and signed, the consumer is not in a significantly disparate bargaining position, and the consumer has a lawyer the consumer chose; the waiver must also be conspicuous, in bold type of at least 10 points, headed Waiver of Consumer Rights, and in substantially the statute's own words (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 17.42). An ordinary residential tenant will rarely meet that test, so do not put a waiver of that Act in your lease. Second, the plain-English rule for rental-purchase agreements covers rent-to-own contracts for goods, not leases of housing (Bus. & Com. Code § 92.051). What Texas does require for leases is specific print for specific terms, such as bold or underlined text for the repair-remedies statement, which the library's clauses mark where they apply.

title: Political Signs, Canvassers and Candidate Visits
bodyText: No Texas statute requires you to let candidates, campaign workers or voter-registration canvassers into your rental property, to let tenants put up political signs, or to open common areas for political meetings (all Texas codes searched). The Texas rules on these subjects bind property owners' associations and cities, not landlords. A property owners' association may not ban an owner's signs for a candidate or ballot measure from the 90th day before an election until the 10th day after it, though it may limit size, number and placement (Tex. Elec. Code § 259.002). A city may not ban, require a permit for, or limit the size of a sign carrying mainly a political message on private property placed with the property owner's consent, with exceptions for large, tall, lit or moving signs (§ 259.003). Since September 1, 2025, a property owners' association, other than one tax-exempt under Internal Revenue Code § 501(c)(3), may not stop an owner or resident from inviting qualified candidates and public officials to meet residents in common areas it makes available for meetings, subject to the association's ordinary room rules (Tex. Prop. Code § 202.013). If your rental is in an association, the candidate-meeting rule (§ 202.013) protects your tenant as a resident against the association, but the sign rule (Elec. Code § 259.002) protects only the property owner; none of these rules binds you. Your lease may regulate signs, solicitation and common-area use, but apply the rules evenly, and remember that you may not retaliate against a tenant for organizing or joining a tenant organization (§ 92.331(a)(4)). Federal law and city ordinances may also apply.

title: Window and Portable Air Conditioners
bodyText: No Texas statute gives a tenant the right to install a window or portable air-conditioning unit, requires you to allow one, or requires a lease that limits window units to say so (all Texas codes searched). Texas also has no statute requiring you to provide air conditioning at all. Cooling enters Texas law only through the repair statute: if the lease expressly or impliedly provides cooling equipment and it produces inadequate cooled air, and a local housing, building or health official has notified you in writing that the lack of cooling materially affects the health or safety of an ordinary tenant, the tenant may repair and deduct if you have not fixed it within three days after the tenant's notice of intent to repair (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.0561(d)(3)(C), (e)(3)). The library's heating and cooling row covers that rule and the heat-advisory limit on cutting off submetered electricity. So whether tenants may bring their own window or portable units is your choice, and your lease should say it: allow them, allow them with conditions (approved models, secure installation, no blocked exits, your electrical capacity), or ban them. A tenant with a disability who needs a cooling device may ask for it as a reasonable accommodation, and you must consider the request (§ 301.025(c)(2)), unless the Texas Fair Housing Act's small-landlord exemptions apply (§ 301.041); federal law may still apply. City housing codes may set cooling or window rules.

title: Tenant Solar Devices
bodyText: No Texas statute gives a tenant the right to install a plug-in, balcony or other solar device, and none limits what your lease may say about solar (all Texas codes searched). Texas's solar-access rule binds property owners' associations, not landlords: an association may not prohibit or restrict a property owner from installing a solar energy device, and a provision that does is void, subject to listed exceptions such as roof placement and prior approval (Tex. Prop. Code § 202.010(b)-(d)); a related rule covers solar-generating roof shingles (§ 202.011). Those sections protect the owner, so if your rental is in an association they help you, not your tenant. The Utilities Code requires an electric utility to interconnect distributed renewable generation installed on a retail electric customer's side of the meter if it meets the warranty and capacity conditions (Tex. Util. Code § 39.916(b)). That rule regulates utilities; it gives a tenant no right to attach equipment to your building. So solar is a lease decision. Your lease may ban tenant solar devices or allow them on conditions, for example your written approval, no wiring into the building's electrical system or roof penetrations, safe placement that blocks no exit, compliance with the utility's interconnection rules, and removal and repair at move-out. Treat any installation as an alteration under your lease.

title: Texas Rules That Depend on How Many Units You Have
bodyText: Texas has no general small-landlord exemption: the residential tenancy chapter applies whether you rent one unit or thousands. Only two Texas rules count how much you own (all Texas codes searched). First, if at the start of the lease you own only one rental dwelling and it meets the other conditions, the tenant may agree in bold or underlined lease terms to make repairs at the tenant's expense (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.006(e)). Second, the state fair housing rules on refusing to rent, inspection, blockbusting and disability do not reach an owner of no more than three single-family houses who rents one without a broker, without the services of anyone in the business of renting dwellings (someone who was the landlord in three or more rentals in the past year or owns a dwelling for five or more families) and without discriminatory advertising, or an owner-occupant renting rooms or units in a building for four or fewer families; the advertising ban applies to everyone (§§ 301.022, 301.024, 301.041). Federal fair housing law may differ. Other thresholds count units in a building or complex: the late-fee safe harbor is 12 percent of rent for a structure of four or fewer units and 10 percent above that (§ 92.019(a-1)); the parking and towing notice rules apply in a multiunit complex of two or more dwellings under common ownership and management (§§ 92.0131(a), 92.151(8)); the pool-yard rules apply at a multiunit rental complex of two or more units (Tex. Health & Safety Code § 757.001(7)); a tenant's repair may not touch the foundation of a building with two or more units (§ 92.0561(f)); new buildings of four or more units must meet accessible-design rules (§ 301.025(c)(3), (g)); at a property with five or more rental units, you must post notice or leave an information sheet 48 hours before an indoor pest treatment (Tex. Occ. Code § 1951.453(c)); and a city of 1.7 million or more must inspect buildings of three or more rental units (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code § 214.219).

title: The Landlord's Possession Bond in a Texas Eviction
bodyText: Texas has a possession bond, but it is your bond, not the tenant's, and it buys speed. When you file the eviction, or any time before final judgment, you may file a possession bond, approved by the judge, in the probable amount of the costs of suit and the damages the tenant may suffer if the suit was improperly brought, conditioned on your paying any such costs and damages adjudged against you (Tex. R. Civ. P. 510.9(a)). The court must notify the tenant, served the same way as the citation (Rule 510.9(b)). Normally no writ of possession may issue before the sixth day after judgment, or the day after the tenant's appeal deadline if that is later (Tex. Prop. Code § 24.0061(b); Rule 510.18(g)(1)). With an approved bond, the writ must issue immediately on demand and payment of fees and may be executed immediately if notice of the bond was served at least 7 days before, a judgment for possession has been rendered, and, if the tenant did not appear, you served the judgment as the default-judgment rule requires (Rule 510.9(c)). The bond does not defeat an appeal: if the tenant has perfected an appeal and paid rent into the court registry, no writ may issue (Rule 510.9(d)). No Texas statute provides a bond that a tenant must post to keep or give up possession, at the end of the term or otherwise (all Texas codes searched), and a lease cannot contain a confession of judgment (Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 30.001). The bonds a tenant posts are appeal bonds (§§ 24.005107, 24.00512).

title: No Private Well Testing or Disclosure Rule
bodyText: No Texas statute requires you to test a private well that serves a rental, to give tenants well test results, or to tell tenants that their water comes from a private well (all Texas codes searched). The Texas well statutes found regulate drilling, placement and water-treatment work, not landlord disclosure. Two general rules still reach a rental on well water. If the water makes the unit unsafe, that is a condition materially affecting the physical health or safety of an ordinary tenant, and you must make a diligent effort to repair it after the tenant's notice, if the tenant is not delinquent in rent when giving it (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.052(a)). If the lease says or implies that you furnish potable water and service totally stops, the tenant may repair and deduct if you have not fixed it within three days after the tenant's notice of intent to repair, provided the other repair-and-deduct conditions are met, including the § 92.056(b) notices and your liability under that section (§ 92.0561(a), (d)(3)(B), (e)(2)). And the Deceptive Trade Practices Act makes it unlawful to fail to disclose information known at the time of the transaction to induce a consumer into a transaction the consumer would not otherwise have entered (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 17.46(b)(24)), so do not hide a known water-quality problem. The prudent course is to test the well periodically, keep the results, tell an applicant before signing if you know of a problem, and say in the lease who maintains the well and pump. Local health or groundwater district rules may apply.

title: Promises to Repair or Improve Before Move-In
bodyText: No Texas statute requires a landlord's promise to clean, repair or improve a unit to be in writing, to carry a completion date, or to be made before the lease is signed (all Texas codes searched). But a promise you make is still a promise you can be held to. The repair statute keeps contract rights that are consistent with it, so a repair or improvement you agree to in the lease is enforceable as part of the lease on top of your statutory repair duty (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.061). And the Deceptive Trade Practices Act makes it unlawful to represent that a rental has characteristics or benefits it does not have, or that an agreement gives rights or obligations it does not (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 17.46(b)(5), (12)), so a promise made to win a tenant and not kept can create liability. You and a tenant may also agree that the tenant will make a repair at your expense (§ 92.0561(g)). The safe course is to write every promised item and its completion date into the lease or a signed addendum before the tenant signs, and to keep the library's entire-agreement clause, so the written list is the whole of what was promised and an oral side promise does not become a later dispute. If something delays the work, tell the tenant in writing why and when it will be done.

title: No Chemical Exposure Warning Rule
bodyText: Texas has no chemical-exposure warning law of the kind some other states have: no statute requires a landlord to warn tenants or applicants about chemicals, carcinogens or reproductive toxicants in or around a rental (all Texas codes searched). The Texas statutes that use those terms define toxic substances for a state coordinating committee and health agencies, or deal with workplace chemicals, birth-defect registries and firefighter cancer benefits; none reaches leasing. What Texas has instead are a few hazard-specific rules covered elsewhere in the library: the lead-based paint disclosure, the asbestos rules, the flood disclosure notice, and confirmed absences for radon, mold and methamphetamine. Two general rules still apply to any known hazard. A condition that materially affects the physical health or safety of an ordinary tenant triggers your repair duty after notice to the place rent is normally paid, if the tenant is not behind on rent when giving it and the tenant's household or guests did not cause it (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.052(a)-(b)), and the Deceptive Trade Practices Act makes it unlawful to fail to disclose known information in order to induce a consumer into a transaction the consumer would otherwise have refused (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 17.46(b)(24)). If you know of a hazard, disclose it in writing before signing.

title: No Property Tax Statement for Tenants
bodyText: No Texas statute requires you to tell tenants how much of their rent goes to property taxes, to give an annual rent or tax statement, or to issue a certificate of rent paid, and Texas has no renter's property-tax credit or rebate program that would need one (all Texas codes searched). Property taxes on a rental are your cost, and you may build them into the rent however you choose. If you want to pass later tax increases through to a tenant during the lease, do it by a written escalation clause: Texas does not treat a rent increase under an escalation clause in a written lease for utilities, taxes or insurance as retaliation, even within six months after a tenant's complaint, unless it violates a prior court order (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.332(a)(1)). The library's optional escalation clauses cover how to word one.

title: Questions About Protected Characteristics
bodyText: The Texas Fair Housing Act bans discrimination and discriminatory statements, but no Texas statute separately forbids asking an applicant or tenant about race, color, religion, sex, familial status, national origin or disability, or keeping records of those traits (all Texas codes searched). What it does forbid comes close. You may not make, print or publish a notice, statement or advertisement about renting a dwelling that indicates a preference, limitation or discrimination based on any of those classes, and that rule applies even to an owner otherwise exempt from the Act (Tex. Prop. Code §§ 301.022, 301.041(a)). You may not refuse to rent, or set different terms, because of a protected class (§§ 301.021, 301.025). A question on an application or in an interview can itself be a statement indicating a preference, and it is evidence of intent if you later deny the applicant, so the cautious course is not to ask. Exceptions: you may ask about age where your housing qualifies as housing for older persons (§ 301.043), and you may ask for reliable information supporting a disability-related accommodation or modification request when the need is not obvious. Keep your written selection criteria to the grounds Texas expects you to state, such as criminal, rental and credit history, current income and inaccurate or incomplete applications (§ 92.3515(a)). Federal fair housing law and HUD rules also govern inquiries.

title: Unlawful Use Does Not Void a Texas Lease
bodyText:
No Texas statute makes a residential lease void, or ends it automatically, because the tenant uses the premises for an unlawful purpose. The automatic rule Texas does have is for commercial property only: a commercial tenant's right of possession ends, whatever the lease says, if the premises are used for prostitution, human trafficking or an unlicensed massage establishment (Tex. Prop. Code §§ 93.001, 93.013).

For a residential lease you have three routes instead. First, if the tenant or an occupant uses the property for an activity for which the tenant, occupant or their agent or employee is convicted under the Penal Code's public indecency chapter, and appeals are exhausted or abandoned, you may end the lease by written notice within six months, and possession reverts to you on the 10th day after notice, regardless of the lease (§ 91.003).

Second, in a common-nuisance suit, a court may order you to terminate a tenant's lease if you and the tenant are parties and the tenant violated the court's injunction (Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 125.045(b)(6)).

Third, and most useful, your own lease: a material breach such as violating written lease provisions prohibiting serious misconduct or criminal acts is a valid ground for eviction that is not retaliation (§ 92.332(b)(3)). So put a clear criminal-activity and lawful-use clause in the lease and enforce it through an ordinary eviction.

title: No Recycling Notice Requirement
bodyText: No Texas statute requires you to provide recycling at a rental property or to tell tenants where and how to recycle (all Texas codes searched). The state's recycling laws are aimed at government programs, manufacturers and waste facilities, not at landlords or tenants. A city ordinance may require recycling service or tenant notices at apartment properties; city ordinances were not reviewed, so check your city's solid waste rules. If you offer recycling, it is good practice to say in the lease or your community rules where the containers are, what goes in them and the pickup schedule, and the library's tenant maintenance clause already requires tenants to dispose of garbage and waste in a clean and safe manner.

title: No Right to Pay and Stop a Texas Eviction
bodyText: Texas gives a tenant no right to stop an eviction by paying after the notice period or after judgment (all Texas codes and the eviction rules searched). The only statutory payment window is the notice itself: when you evict solely for nonpayment and the tenant was not late before the month of the notice, the notice must be a notice to pay rent or vacate, so a tenant who pays within the notice period has met it (Tex. Prop. Code § 24.005(a)). After that, Texas law sets no deadline before the writ by which the tenant may pay and stay, no rule that paying a money judgment bars the writ, no required wording for accepting a partial payment, and no rule making you accept a payment from a charity or government program or limiting the payment methods you accept for it. Issuing the writ after judgment is "a ministerial act not subject to review or delay" (§ 24.0061(b-1)). The one payment that keeps a tenant in possession is rent paid into the court registry on time during an appeal (§ 24.0053(a-2); Tex. R. Civ. P. 510.19(d)(2)). The only redemption in the eviction chapter is the tenant's right to redeem belongings an officer had a warehouseman store after the writ (§ 24.0062). Whether accepting money after a notice or judgment waives your rights is case law; see the library's row on accepting rent after a notice. If you decide to take the money and let the tenant stay, put the terms in writing and dismiss or settle the suit.

title: Religious and Cultural Displays
bodyText: No Texas statute gives a tenant a right to display religious or cultural items at a rental, or limits a landlord's neutral rules on decorations, doors or exteriors (all Texas codes searched). Texas's religious-display rule binds property owners' associations, not landlords: an association may not adopt or enforce a provision that prohibits a property owner or resident from displaying or affixing religious items on the property or dwelling when the display is motivated by sincere religious belief, though it may bar items that threaten public health or safety, violate another law, are patently offensive for reasons other than religious content, sit on association or common property, violate setbacks or easements, or are attached to traffic devices, street lamps, hydrants or utility fixtures (Tex. Prop. Code § 202.018). Because the rule protects a resident as well as an owner, a tenant in an association community has it against the association. It does not bind you as landlord. Your own rules are limited by fair housing law, which bars discrimination in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental because of religion or national origin (§ 301.021(b)), unless one of that Act's exemptions applies, such as for some owners renting up to three single-family houses without an agent, or an owner-occupied building of up to four units (§ 301.041). So any rule on door decorations, window displays or exterior items should be neutral, written and enforced the same way for everyone, and should not single out religious or cultural items.

title: No Bar on Collecting Rent for an Unrepaired Unit in Texas
bodyText: No Texas statute bars you from demanding, collecting or suing for rent because the unit has code violations or unrepaired conditions, because an inspector has cited it, or because the property is unregistered (all Texas codes searched). Texas instead gives the tenant remedies the tenant must start, each after notice to you and only if the tenant was current on rent when the notice was given. If you fail to make a diligent effort to repair a condition that materially affects the physical health or safety of an ordinary tenant within a reasonable time after the required notices, the tenant may end the lease, repair and deduct in the limited cases the statute allows, or sue; a court may order the rent reduced "in proportion to the reduced rental value resulting from the condition" from the first repair notice until it is fixed, plus a civil penalty of one month's rent plus $500, damages, costs and fees (Tex. Prop. Code §§ 92.056, 92.0561, 92.0563). A rent deduction the tenant lawfully made is a defense to an eviction for nonpayment to the extent the chapter allows (§ 92.335). A tenant who withholds rent or deducts for repairs outside these rules is liable for your actual damages, and, if you warned the tenant in writing of the illegality and penalties and the tenant acted in bad faith, a civil penalty of one month's rent plus $500 (§ 92.058). Failing to give the tenant a copy of the lease does not stop a suit for nonpayment of rent (§ 92.024(c), (d)). For a unit a city has ordered vacated, see the library's row on rent after a city order.

title: Counterclaims and Rent Paid Into Court in a Texas Eviction
bodyText: In a Texas eviction the tenant does not pay rent into court to defend, and cannot counterclaim. Counterclaims and the joinder of suits against third parties are not permitted in eviction suits; a claim left out may be brought in a separate suit (Tex. Prop. Code § 24.004(c); Tex. R. Civ. P. 510.6(f)). A tenant's repair claims under the residential tenancy chapter may not be joined with an eviction or asserted as a defense or crossclaim, but retaliation is a defense, and a rent deduction the tenant lawfully made under that chapter is a defense to nonpayment to the extent the chapter allows (§ 92.335). No Texas statute or rule requires a tenant to pay rent into court to answer, raise a defense, get a jury or get a postponement in justice court (all Texas codes and the eviction rules searched); a jury takes only a jury fee or a statement of inability to afford it (Rule 510.15(c)). Rent into the court registry comes in only on appeal of a residential eviction. The judgment states the rent to be paid each rental pay period during the appeal; the tenant must pay one period into the justice court registry within five days after appealing, then each period on or before it begins; and if the tenant does not, the court on request must issue a writ of possession without a hearing, if the justice court gave the tenant the required written notice of the amounts and dates (§§ 24.0053(a), (a-1), (a-2), 24.0054(a); Rule 510.19(d)). The court releases registry rent to you on request, and each payment counts as rent only for the period it covers (§ 24.0053(a-3), (a-5)). Where a government agency pays part of the rent, the tenant pays only the tenant's portion (§ 24.0053(b)).

title: Who Keeps the Repair Duty in Texas
bodyText: Some states say that whoever receives the rent keeps the repair duty, whatever a lease, assignment, deed or mortgage says. Texas has no statute in those words (all Texas codes searched). Texas reaches a similar result another way. The repair duty is the landlord's, and "landlord" means the owner, lessor or sublessor, not a manager or agent unless the manager or agent claims in the lease to be the owner, lessor or sublessor (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.001(2)); the duty cannot be waived except as the statute allows (§ 92.006(c)), so no lease term shifts it to someone else. The tenant's repair notice goes to the person to whom, or the place where, rent is normally paid (§ 92.052(a)(1)), and if the tenant was given written notice of the management company's name and business street address, that company is the owner's sole agent for service of process; otherwise a management company, on-site manager or rent collector serving the dwelling is, unless the owner's name and business street address were given in writing (§ 92.003(b)-(c)). Texas also requires cash rent to be receipted and recorded (§ 92.011(b)). Keep whoever collects the rent able to receive repair requests and pass them to you.

title: Reporting Tenants to Credit Bureaus
bodyText: Texas has no rent-reporting law: no statute requires you to offer positive rent reporting to a credit bureau, bars you from requiring a tenant to enroll in a reporting service, or requires a general notice before you report late rent (all Texas codes searched). One Texas rule does govern reporting a former tenant's debt. If your lease required no security deposit and the tenant owes damages and charges on surrender, you must notify the tenant in writing of your claim on or before the date you report it to a consumer reporting agency or a third-party debt collector (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.110(a)). You need not send that notice if the tenant never gave you a forwarding address (§ 92.110(b)). If you skip it, you lose the right to collect those damages and charges (§ 92.110(c)). For a lease with a deposit, the deposit-accounting rules apply instead. Credit history is a lawful screening criterion that your written selection criteria may list (§ 92.3515(a)). If your rental is in a property owners' association, the association may not require you to submit a tenant's or applicant's consumer or credit report (§ 209.016(b)(2)). If you offer a reporting program, describe it in the lease, including any fee, and report accurately. Federal credit-reporting law also applies.

title: Taxes on Rent in Texas
bodyText: Texas does not tax the rent on an ordinary residential lease. The state sales tax applies to sales of taxable items, meaning tangible personal property and the services the Tax Code lists, and renting a dwelling is not one of the listed services (Tex. Tax Code §§ 151.009, 151.010, 151.0101, 151.051). Short stays are different. The state hotel occupancy tax of 6 percent applies to a person who pays for the use of a room in a hotel costing $15 or more a day (§§ 156.051, 156.052), and a hotel includes a short-term rental, meaning the rental of all or part of a residential property to someone who is not a permanent resident (§ 156.001(b)). A permanent resident is a person with the right to use or possess the room for at least 30 consecutive days, so long as payment is not interrupted, and owes no hotel tax (§ 156.101). The owner or operator must collect the tax (§ 156.053). Cities, and the counties the statute lists, may add their own hotel taxes, which also exempt permanent residents (§§ 351.002, 352.002). So a lease of 30 days or more with uninterrupted payment carries no hotel tax; for a stay under 30 days, collect and remit state and local hotel tax. One caution: motor vehicle parking and storage services are taxable services (§ 151.0101(a)(4)); whether a separately stated parking or storage charge to a tenant is taxable depends on Comptroller rules.

title: Government Inspections of Rentals
bodyText:
Texas has no statewide rental registration or inspection program, and no statute lets a lease authorize a government inspector to enter a tenant's home or says whether the tenant must let one in. Two state rules matter. A city of 1.7 million or more must adopt minimum habitability standards for buildings with three or more rental units and run an inspection program for them, and an owner who violates the ordinance commits a Class C misdemeanor for each day (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code § 214.219). And a fire marshal, health officer or code enforcement official may get a search warrant to inspect specified premises for fire or health hazards, unsafe building conditions or code violations, but only on probable cause, and in a county of 3.3 million or more a county code enforcement official cannot get one for unsafe building conditions or building-code violations (Tex. Code Crim. Proc. art. 18.05(b), (e)).

Other cities may have their own registration or inspection ordinances. Inspections also feed the repair statute: a written notice from a local housing, building or health official that a condition materially affects health or safety is one of the events that opens the tenant's repair-and-deduct remedy, if the other conditions are met, including the § 92.056(b) notices (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.0561(a), (d)(3)(D)), and you may not retaliate against a tenant who complains in good faith to a code agency (§ 92.331(a)(3)).

A lease clause can ask the tenant to cooperate with inspections and to tell you when an inspector asks to enter, and the library's inspection cooperation clause does that, but it cannot waive the tenant's own constitutional rights.

title: Renter's Insurance Requirements in Texas
bodyText:
No Texas statute regulates a landlord's renter's-insurance requirement. Texas does not bar you from requiring renter's or liability insurance, does not require you to let the tenant choose the insurer, sets no rules or caps for coverage you buy and charge back if the tenant fails to show proof, and requires no written advisory that your insurance does not cover the tenant's belongings.

The library's tenant insurance clause, which states that your insurance does not cover the tenant's property and requires the tenant to carry coverage at a minimum you set, is lawful in Texas. The only statutory mention of tenant insurance is in the flood disclosure notice every covered lease must include, which warns that most tenant insurance policies do not cover flood losses and that the tenant should seek coverage that does (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.0135(b)).

If you plan to buy coverage for a tenant who does not and charge the tenant for it, put that term and the charge in the lease: Texas's debt-collection law bars collecting a fee or charge incidental to an obligation unless the agreement creating it expressly authorizes it or it is otherwise legally chargeable (Tex. Fin. Code § 392.303(a)(2)), and whether that law reaches a landlord's own collection is unsettled.

title: No Right to End the Lease Because a Repair Costs Too Much
bodyText: No Texas statute lets you refuse a repair because it would cost too much and end the lease instead, and no cost threshold excuses the repair duty (all Texas codes searched). Once a tenant who is current on rent gives notice of a condition that materially affects health or safety, you must make a diligent effort to repair it; the only statutory limits are conditions the tenant's household or guests caused (other than normal wear and tear), utility lines not reasonably available, and security guards (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.052), plus the written tenant-repair agreements § 92.006(e)-(f) allow, and for an insured casualty the repair period starts only when you receive the insurance proceeds (§ 92.054(a)). A sworn affidavit can delay a tenant's own repair only for parts delays or a post-disaster shortage of labor or materials (§ 92.0562). Texas does give you two exits that are not cost-based. After a casualty not caused by the tenant's side, if the unit is as a practical matter totally unusable, either of you may end the lease by written notice before repairs are completed (§ 92.054(b)). And you may close a unit at any time by certified-mail notice, return receipt requested, to the tenant, the local health officer and the building inspector, stating that you are ending the tenancy as soon as legally possible and will demolish the unit or stop using it as a residence (§ 92.055(a)). After any closing, you may not allow reoccupancy or reconnection of utilities by separate meter for six months after the tenant moves out, and the local health officer or building inspector may not allow occupancy until certifying the unit. If you close before the tenant has given a repair notice, the repair remedies do not apply; if you close it after a repair notice, the tenant is entitled only to the civil penalty (one month's rent plus $500), actual damages and court costs and attorney's fees under § 92.0563(a)(3)-(5) and, if the tenant moves out on or before the end of the rental term, to your payment of the tenant's actual and reasonable moving expenses, a pro rata rent refund from the move-out date and the deposit as the law requires; breaking the reoccupancy bar or that payment duty costs one month's rent plus $100 and attorney's fees (§ 92.055(b)-(e)). The statute lets you end the tenancy only "as soon as legally possible" and does not say closing cuts a fixed term short, so the cautious course is to plan around the lease end.

title: No Rent Escrow, So No Small-Landlord Exemption Notice
bodyText: Texas has no rent-escrow repair remedy, so it has no small-landlord exemption from one and no exemption notice to give (all Texas codes searched). A Texas tenant's repair remedies are ending the lease, repair and deduct, and a court order with a rent reduction, penalty, damages and fees (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.056(e)); none of them has the tenant pay rent to a court or escrow. Rent goes into a court registry only when a tenant appeals an eviction judgment, which is not a repair remedy (§ 24.0053). Do not copy another state's notice that tells the tenant its remedies do not apply because you own few units: Texas has no such rule, and the repair duty and remedies may not be waived except in the ways § 92.006 allows (§ 92.006(c)); knowingly contracting around them costs one month's rent plus $2,000, actual damages and attorney's fees (§ 92.0563(b)). The nearest Texas rule turns on the size of your holdings. If, at the start of the lease, you own only one rental dwelling, it is free of health or safety defects and you have no reason to expect one, you and the tenant may agree that the tenant makes repairs at the tenant's own expense, but only in a written lease, in underlined or bold type, specific and clear, and made knowingly, voluntarily and for consideration (§ 92.006(e)). The library's row on shifting the repair duty explains that route.

title: How Tenants Give Repair Notice
bodyText:
How a Texas tenant must give repair notice depends on what needs repair, and your lease decides the form. For a condition that materially affects health or safety, the notice goes to the person to whom, or the place where, rent is normally paid, and it must be in writing only if the lease is written and requires written notice (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.052(a)(1), (d)).

The library's maintenance clause asks for written notice, which meets that rule. Before the tenant's statutory remedies open, the tenant must also give a second written notice after a reasonable time to repair, unless the first notice went by certified, registered or other tracked mail, and the tenant must not have been behind on rent when any notice was given (§ 92.056(b)(3), (6)).

In measuring your reasonable time to repair and your diligence, a notice counts as received when you, your agent or employee actually gets it, or when the Postal Service tries to deliver it (§ 92.056(c)). Other repairs follow other rules: security-device requests may be oral unless the lease requires writing in underlined or bold print (§ 92.159); a written lease may require the first smoke-alarm request in writing (§ 92.259(b)); and at a complex with a pool, latch repair requests may be oral unless the lease requires writing in capital letters and underlined, or in 10-point bold (Tex. Health & Safety Code § 757.013).

No Texas statute makes your own knowledge of a defect a substitute for the tenant's notice. A written-notice clause does not narrow the retaliation rule, which protects a tenant who gives a notice to repair (§ 92.331(a)(2)), so treat an oral request as protected and act on it.

title: Required Disclosures in Texas
bodyText: Texas has no single list of required disclosures, no state form that must be the first page of a lease, and no notice telling the tenant whether a rent or eviction law covers the unit (all Texas codes searched). Disclosures come from separate statutes. For a lease of 30 days or more, give the floodplain and flood-history notices at or before signing (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.0135). When you give out an application, make your printed tenant selection criteria available and get a signed acknowledgment (§ 92.3515). In a multiunit complex, give towing and parking rules before signing (§ 92.0131). Give a complete copy of the signed lease within three business days (§ 92.024), an emergency phone number (§ 92.020), and owner and off-site manager details on request or in the lease (§ 92.201). Other rows cover the required lease statements, submetering and fees in lieu of a deposit. A lease combined with an option to buy is an executory contract for conveyance unless a deed is due within 180 days (§ 5.062(a)(2), (c)). You may not sign one while your title is subject to a lien, apart from a purchase-money loan disclosed in a separate notice three days ahead and meeting other conditions (§ 5.085), and it may not penalize the tenant for requesting repairs (§ 5.073(a)(5)). If the term is over three years, the survey, encumbrance documents, property-condition notice, tax certificate, insurance copy and a 14-point merger statement are due before signing (§§ 5.062(f), 5.069, 5.070, 5.072). Whether the seller disclosure notice (§ 5.008) is due at signing or only at exercise is unsettled; give it at signing.

title: Fees Your Texas Lease Must State
bodyText: Texas has no general rule that a residential lease list every fee with its purpose, and no notice period for adding a fee later. But several charges are lawful only if the written lease states them: a late fee (notice of it must be in a written lease, Tex. Prop. Code § 92.019(a)(1)); a reconnection fee after a submetered electricity interruption (the lease must state the exact dollar amount, at most $10, § 92.008(r)); a charge for repairing a security device the tenant misused or damaged (an underlined lease provision, § 92.162(b)); deducting rekeying costs from the deposit when a tenant leaves in breach (an underlined or bold lease provision, § 92.156(e)); and charges for packing, removing and storing property seized under a landlord's lien (§ 54.044(c)). Texas's debt-collection law also bars collecting any fee incidental to the rent that the lease does not expressly authorize, unless it is otherwise legally chargeable (Tex. Fin. Code § 392.303(a)(2)). Manufactured home communities have stricter rules: the lot lease must state any late charge or fee for any service or facility, and a provision raising rent or fees during the term is void unless the tenant initials it (§ 94.053(c)(5), (d)). The safe course for any rental: list every fee, charge and deposit in the lease, with when it applies and how much it is.

title: Tenant Rights Guides
bodyText: Texas does not require an ordinary private landlord to give tenants a state-published guide to tenant rights and responsibilities, at signing or renewal, or to collect a signed acknowledgment of one (all Texas codes searched; of the Administrative Code only the few chapters held were checked). The Attorney General publishes a renter's rights page you may point tenants to, but no statute makes you hand it out. Three narrower duties exist. If your development is monitored by the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (for example a housing tax credit or HOME property), post the Department's brochure, A Tenant Rights and Resources Guide, in the leasing office, give it to each household during the application process and after a change to the amenities or services it lists, and have a household representative sign a certification of receipt no more than 120 days before the first lease is signed; the guide must also say if the site is in the 100-year floodplain (10 Tex. Admin. Code § 10.613(l)). For Section 811 project rental assistance units, keep the tenant's signed acknowledgment of the Resident Rights and Responsibilities brochure in the file (10 Tex. Admin. Code § 10.624(c)(3)). In a manufactured home community, give an applicant a separate printed statement of the six-month initial lease and nonrenewal notice rights (Tex. Prop. Code § 94.051(3)), and the lot lease must prominently say that chapter 94 governs certain tenant rights (§ 94.053(c)(14)).

title: Rules and Rule Changes in Texas
bodyText:
Texas has no general statute on house rules: none lists which rules are enforceable, requires rules to be reasonable, or bars a mid-lease rule change that substantially alters the bargain. A lease includes any agreement that establishes or modifies the terms, conditions or rules for using the dwelling (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.001(3)), so written rules bind as part of the lease; whether a rule you adopt later binds a tenant who never agreed to it is case law, not reviewed here, so reserve the right in the lease and keep changes reasonable.

Three statutes apply. Before a rule or policy change not in the lease that will affect a tenant's personal property outside the dwelling, give prior written notice in person (to the tenant or a resident 16 or older, or attached inside the main entry door) or by mail; otherwise you owe the tenant any expense your failure causes (§ 92.013).

Towing and parking rule changes in a multiunit complex need written notice, a necessity, safety, construction or parking-rights reason or the tenant's written consent, and 14 days before they take effect unless a construction or utility emergency requires the change; a violation costs $100 plus the tenant's towing or storage costs (§ 92.0131(d)-(f)).

In a manufactured home community, rules may not be arbitrary or capricious, are part of the lease, take effect 30 days after each tenant gets a written copy, and a tenant gets 90 days to comply with a new rule costing more than $25 (§ 94.008). A rule change made in bad faith within six months after a tenant's repair request or complaint can be retaliation (§ 92.331). Use the library's rules clause.

title: Selling the Property or Changing Managers
bodyText: When you sell a rental or change managers, Texas imposes these duties. Deposits: the buyer is liable for refunding security deposits from the date it takes title and must give each tenant a signed statement that it has acquired the property and is responsible for the tenant's deposit, with the exact dollar amount; you stay liable for deposits you received until the buyer receives or assumes them, unless you and the buyer agree otherwise in a written contract (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.105; see the deposit-on-sale row). Owner and manager information: if information you gave in the lease, written rules or a posting becomes wrong because a name or address changes, correct it; after a tenant's written notice warning of the statute's remedies you have seven days (you have a defense if the tenant owed rent when giving it), and willfully giving or keeping incorrect information is bad faith regardless of unpaid rent (§§ 92.201(e), 92.203, 92.204, 92.206). Service of process: once a tenant has written notice of a management company's name and business street address, that company is the owner's sole agent for service in tenant suits, so give tenants the new company's details when you change (§ 92.003). In a manufactured home community, correct the information within 15 days after it becomes incorrect (§ 94.010(g)), and a seller stays liable for deposits until the buyer delivers the signed statement (§ 94.106(b)). No Texas statute requires you to notify tenants of the sale itself, lets you end leases because of a sale, or releases you from the lease on notice (all Texas codes searched). Foreclosure has its own row.

title: No Code Variance Notice in Texas
bodyText: Texas has no state sanitary code for rental housing and no rule that a health, housing or building code variance for your property be given to tenants or attached to the lease (all Texas codes searched; of the Administrative Code only the few chapters held were checked). Minimum housing standards in Texas come from your statutory repair duty for conditions that materially affect an ordinary tenant's health or safety (see the repair-duty row) and from city codes: a city may by ordinance set minimum standards for the use and occupancy of buildings whatever their age (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code § 214.0011(a)), and city codes may have their own variance procedures. If a city grants your property a variance or exception that affects what tenants receive, telling applicants in writing before they sign is the cautious course.

title: Which Texas Lease Laws Apply
bodyText: Texas divides lease law by type of tenancy. Chapter 92 of the Property Code governs residential tenancies and applies only between landlords and tenants of residential rental property (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.002). It covers a dwelling, meaning one or more rooms rented for use as a permanent residence under a single lease, whether written or oral (§ 92.001(1), (3)). Its subchapters set their own limits. The security deposit rules apply to all residential leases (§ 92.101). The security device rules exclude hotel and similar transient rooms, accredited college and preparatory school housing, and a buyer's or seller's occupancy of 90 days or less around a closing, but include dormitory and rooming-house rooms, mobile homes, houses, duplexes, triplexes and units in apartment, condominium, cooperative and townhome projects (§ 92.152). The smoke alarm rules exclude a unit occupied by its owner with no part leased, some high-rises regulated by local ordinance and licensed nursing homes (§ 92.253). Chapter 94 governs leases of lots in a manufactured home community of four or more lots, but not the rental of a manufactured home you own (§§ 94.001(4), 94.002). Commercial leases fall under chapter 93 (§ 93.001), and chapter 91 has general rules for all leases, such as month-to-month notice (§ 91.001). Chapter 92 is not limited by county or population or by local adoption, and has no exclusion for long-term or farm leases (all Texas codes searched); a farm landlord also has a lien for rent and crop advances (§ 54.001).

title: No Seasonal Tenancy Rules in Texas
bodyText: Texas has no special rules for seasonal leases: no defined seasonal tenancy, no rule that one ends without a right to renew, and no seasonal notice period (all Texas codes searched). A fixed-term lease ends on its stated date unless it says otherwise, and a month-to-month tenancy ends on notice under the general rule (Tex. Prop. Code § 91.001; see the termination notice row). Three points matter for seasonal or vacation rentals. The residential tenancy chapter covers a dwelling rented for use as a permanent residence (§ 92.001(1)), so whether it reaches a short vacation stay is unsettled; the security device rules exclude hotel, motel and similar transient housing (§ 92.152(a)(1)), and the flood notices are not required for a lease of less than 30 days (§ 92.0135(a-1)). Renting residential property to someone without the right to use it for at least 30 consecutive days, with no interruption of payment for the period, is a short-term rental subject to hotel occupancy tax (Tex. Tax Code §§ 156.001(b), 156.101). Housing used for more than three days as living quarters for two or more seasonal, temporary or migrant families, or three or more such workers, is a migrant labor housing facility that needs a state license, applied for at least 45 days before opening (Tex. Gov't Code §§ 2306.921(3), 2306.922, 2306.923(b)). Cities may regulate short-term rental units (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code § 229.902(d)(2)).

title: Where You Keep the Deposit
bodyText: No Texas statute requires you to keep a tenant's security deposit in a separate, trust, escrow or interest-bearing account, to tell the tenant where it is held, or to post a bond in its place (all Texas codes searched; of the Administrative Code only the few chapters held were checked), so you may hold it with your own funds. What the law does require: keep accurate records of all security deposits (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.106), and know that the tenant's claim to the deposit comes ahead of any of your creditors, including a bankruptcy trustee (§ 92.103(c)). Two holders have stricter rules. A licensed real estate broker, such as a property manager, who accepts a deposit holds it as a fiduciary and must put it in a designated trust account, or with an authorized escrow agent, by the close of business on the second working day unless the parties agree otherwise in writing, may not commingle it with the broker's own money or keep it in a business account, and must keep trust account records for four years (22 Tex. Admin. Code § 535.146). If your property has Section 811 project rental assistance units, the deposit for those units goes in a segregated, interest-bearing account (10 Tex. Admin. Code § 10.624(f)(2)(A)). Manufactured home community deposits follow the same records and priority rules (§§ 94.102(b), 94.103(c)).

title: No Interest on Security Deposits
bodyText: No Texas statute requires a landlord to pay interest on a residential security deposit, sets an interest rate, or requires an interest-bearing account. The residential deposit subchapter and the manufactured home community deposit subchapter say nothing about interest (Tex. Prop. Code §§ 92.101-92.113, 94.101-94.111), so interest your own account earns is yours and the lease need not mention it. Two narrow rules exist. If a licensed real estate broker holding your tenants' deposits keeps them in an interest-bearing account, the money must be available when due and the interest goes to the parties the money is paid out to, unless the person who deposited the money agreed otherwise in a signed agreement (22 Tex. Admin. Code § 535.146(c)(3)). For Section 811 project rental assistance units, the deposit must be kept in a segregated, interest-bearing account whose balance always equals the amount collected plus accrued interest (10 Tex. Admin. Code § 10.624(f)(2)(A)). The interest Texas does require is on deposits a utility takes for water, electric, gas or telephone service, which does not apply to a rental deposit (Tex. Util. Code §§ 183.001, 183.002).

title: Deposit Rights a Texas Lease Cannot Waive
bodyText: A Texas lease cannot waive your security-deposit duties or the tenant's deposit remedies (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.006(a)). That reaches the whole deposit subchapter: refunding the deposit within 30 days after the tenant surrenders the premises; deducting nothing for normal wear and tear; giving a written description and itemized list of deductions; the bad-faith penalty of $100 plus three times the amount wrongfully withheld and attorney's fees; losing your right to keep any of the deposit, or to sue for damage, if you fail in bad faith to itemize; and the presumption of bad faith after 30 days (§§ 92.103(a), 92.104, 92.109). A lease term setting a flat deduction whatever the actual damage, forfeiting the deposit for leaving early, or excusing the itemized list does not bind the tenant. What the lease may do: make advance notice of move-out a condition of the refund, but only if that requirement is underlined or in conspicuous bold print (§ 92.103(b); the library's deposit surrender-notice clause), and agree a cancellation fee you may keep if the tenant never moves in and a replacement tenant you find occupies on time (§ 92.1031). Your refund duty waits until the tenant gives a written forwarding address, but the tenant loses nothing by not giving one (§ 92.107). Whether a payment labelled "nonrefundable" is a deposit at all turns on whether it is intended primarily to secure performance (§ 92.102); if it is, the label does not take it outside these rules.

title: Security Deposits When the Property Is Sold
bodyText: When your ownership ends by sale, assignment, death, receivership, bankruptcy or otherwise, the new owner is liable for refunding the tenants' security deposits under the deposit rules from the date it acquires title, and must give each tenant a signed statement acknowledging that it has acquired the property and is responsible for the tenant's deposit, specifying the exact dollar amount (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.105(a)-(b)). You stay liable for each deposit you received until the new owner has received the deposit or assumed liability for it, unless you and the buyer agree otherwise in a written contract (§ 92.105(b-1)). The new-owner rule does not apply to a mortgage lender that acquires title by foreclosure (§ 92.105(c)), so after a foreclosure the tenant's deposit claim generally stays with the former owner. In a manufactured home community the buyer is liable from the date of title whether or not it gives notice, and the seller stays liable until the buyer delivers the signed statement (§ 94.106). No statute says how deposits must be handed over at closing (all Texas codes searched). Transfer or credit the deposits in the purchase contract, have the buyer expressly assume them, hand over your deposit records (§ 92.106) and make sure the statements go out. The general deposit rules are in the security deposit row.

title: Penalties for Mishandling a Deposit
bodyText:
Texas deposit penalties turn on bad faith. If you keep a deposit in bad faith in violation of the deposit rules, you owe $100, plus three times the portion wrongfully withheld, plus the tenant's reasonable attorney's fees (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.109(a)); the multiple is of the amount wrongfully kept, not of the whole deposit. If you fail in bad faith to give the written description and itemized list of deductions, you lose the right to keep any part of the deposit and the right to sue the tenant for damage to the premises, and owe the tenant's attorney's fees (§ 92.109(b)).

Missing the 30-day deadline for the refund or the itemized list creates a presumption of bad faith, and in the tenant's suit you must prove that what you kept was reasonable (§ 92.109(c)-(d)). Your duty to refund or itemize does not start until the tenant gives a written forwarding address (§ 92.107). If you took no deposit, failing to notify the tenant in writing of your claim for damages before reporting it to a credit bureau or debt collector forfeits the claim, unless the tenant never gave you a written forwarding address (§ 92.110).

The same penalties apply to manufactured home lot deposits (§ 94.109). There is no criminal penalty for deposit violations and no penalty tied to how you hold the deposit. A lease cannot waive any of this (§ 92.006(a)). A refund or accounting mailed with a postmark on or before the deadline counts as on time (§ 92.1041).

title: No Posted Deposit Standards Rule
bodyText: No Texas statute requires you to post or give applicants the standards you use to set security deposit amounts, or to apply one standard to every applicant. Texas sets no cap on a deposit, so the amount is your choice. Limits that do apply: you may not discriminate in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental, which include the deposit, because of race, color, religion, sex, familial status, national origin or disability (Tex. Prop. Code §§ 301.021(b), 301.025(b)). When you give out an application you must make available printed notice of your tenant selection criteria and the grounds on which an application may be denied (§ 92.3515(a)); if some approved applicants must pay a larger deposit, for example because of limited credit, say so in those criteria. If you offer a fee in lieu of a deposit, you must also offer a deposit, tell the tenant in writing of both options, of the right to switch to a deposit at any time and of the charges for each option, and may not use the applicant's choice in deciding whether to approve the application (§ 92.111(a)-(b)). A manufactured home lot lease must state the amount of any security deposit (§ 94.053(c)(6)). Applying the same written deposit policy to everyone is the safest course.

title: No Work Card Rule for Senior Housing Staff
bodyText: Texas has no work card, permit or license requirement for employees of housing for older persons, and no staff screening rule that applies only to senior apartments. Housing for older persons matters in Texas law mainly because it is exempt from the fair housing rules on familial status if it is intended for and solely occupied by people 62 or older, or intended and operated for occupancy by at least one person 55 or older per unit, or designed for the elderly under a government program (Tex. Prop. Code § 301.043). For staff at any residential dwelling project, including a house, condominium, apartment building or duplex, Texas lets you check state criminal history records for a job applicant who may need access to dwellings, after making a job offer and with the applicant's authorization, but does not require it (Tex. Health & Safety Code §§ 765.001(6), 765.002(a), 765.003(a), (f)); see the employee screening row. Licensed care facilities such as assisted living are regulated separately and are not covered here.

title: Penalties for Refusing a Service Animal
bodyText: Refusing a tenant with a disability full and equal access to housing because of a service animal is a crime in Texas. A person with a disability who has a service animal is entitled to full and equal access to all housing accommodations offered for rent, and may not be required to pay extra compensation or a deposit for the animal, though the tenant is liable for damage the animal does beyond reasonable wear and tear (Tex. Hum. Res. Code § 121.003(g)-(h)). Anyone who violates those rules, including a company or its agent, commits a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $300 and 30 hours of community service, and the tenant may also sue, with damages conclusively presumed to be at least $300 (§ 121.004). The 60-day notice and cure procedure covers only claims about design or construction standards, not refusing an animal (§ 121.0041(b)). In this law a service animal is a dog specially trained or equipped to help a person with a disability, and housing accommodations exclude a single-family home whose occupants rent out only one room (§ 121.002(1), (3)). Refusing a reasonable accommodation for any assistance animal, including one that is not a trained dog, can also be disability discrimination under the Texas Fair Housing Act (Tex. Prop. Code § 301.025(c)(2)), with actual and punitive damages and attorney's fees in a private suit (§ 301.153) and civil penalties after an administrative hearing (§ 301.112). No other Texas statute makes denying an assistance animal a crime (all Texas codes searched). Federal law (e.g. the Fair Housing Act) may also apply; not reviewed here.

title: Servicemember Tenants in Texas
bodyText: Texas gives servicemember tenants one state lease right and points to federal law for the rest. A tenant who is a servicemember or a servicemember's dependent may end the lease and avoid future rent if the lease was signed before the person entered military service, or if a servicemember signed it while in service and then received orders for a permanent change of station or to deploy with a unit for 90 days or more (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.017(b)). The notice, effective date, refund, separate-document waiver and penalty rules are in the early termination rights row, and the statutory early termination clause keeps your claim to unpaid rent safe (§ 92.017(g)). A member of the Texas military forces (the Texas National Guard and Texas State Guard) ordered to state active duty, or to state training and other duty, is entitled to the same benefits and protections that federal law gives people in federal military service under the federal provisions the statute lists, and may sue in district court for a violation, with damages and attorney's fees (Tex. Gov't Code §§ 437.001(14), 437.213, 437.2131). Every eviction citation must warn, in English and Spanish, that a tenant on active military duty may have special rights under federal law, including the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, or under § 92.017 (Tex. Prop. Code § 24.0051(d)). Texas has no state eviction stay, rent-ceiling stay or application deadline for servicemembers (all Texas codes searched). Check it before evicting or charging a servicemember.

title: Sex Offender Information and Disclosure
bodyText: You have no duty to tell a prospective tenant about registered sex offenders living nearby or at the property. An owner, builder, seller or lessor of single-family residential property, or of any improvement to residential real property, and that person's broker or agent, has no duty to disclose registrants to a prospective lessee, and that rule controls over any other law imposing such a duty (Tex. Code Crim. Proc. art. 62.056(e)). The state registry is public, apart from items such as phone numbers, driver's license and social security numbers and anything identifying the victim, and local law enforcement must release the public information to anyone who asks (art. 62.005(b), (d)); for registrants assigned risk level three, the state mails notice to addresses around where the person will live (art. 62.056(a)). If you share registry information, share only what is public. One duty runs the other way: a group home, including an assisted living or boarding home facility or a supportive or transitional housing facility, must check the registry when a person asks or is assigned to live there and, within three days after a registrant moves in, notify each other resident or the resident's guardian (Tex. Health & Safety Code §§ 325.001-325.004). And you can face a negligence claim if you rent to someone with a reportable sex-offense conviction or adjudication that you knew or should have known about (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.025(b)); see the criminal record row.

title: Renting to Registered Sex Offenders
bodyText: Texas has no statewide rule on where registered sex offenders may live that a landlord must enforce, no crime of leasing to two registrants who live together, and no lease statement or safe harbor about them (all Texas codes searched). The only statewide residence ban is that a registrant may not live on a college or university campus unless assigned risk level one and approved by the institution (Tex. Code Crim. Proc. art. 62.064). A general-law city may by ordinance bar registrants from going in, on or within up to 1,000 feet of a child safety zone such as a school, day-care facility or playground, but the ordinance must exempt a registrant who already lived within that distance before it was adopted, for access to and living in that residence (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code § 341.906). Child safety zones set as conditions of parole or community supervision bind the offender, not you (Tex. Gov't Code § 508.187; Tex. Code Crim. Proc. art. 42A.453). You may screen applicants for criminal history if your printed selection criteria say so (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.3515(a)), and you can face a negligence claim for renting to someone with a reportable conviction you knew or should have known about (§ 92.025(b)). Section 811 project rental assistance units may not house a household member subject to a state lifetime sex offender registration requirement (10 Tex. Admin. Code § 10.624(c)(7)(C)(iii)). Apply any criminal-history policy consistently.

title: No Occupancy Presumption Notice in Texas
bodyText: Texas has no rule that a lease for a single-family home carry a notice about when a tenant's occupancy is presumed lawful, no requirement that a lease be notarized or signed by a licensed property manager for the tenant to be treated as lawfully in possession, and no rule that any notice appear at the top of the first page in larger type. What Texas has instead is a procedure for removing an unauthorized occupant of a residence without an eviction suit; see the squatter removal row. A written lease signed by you and every tenant remains your best proof of who is lawfully in possession.
