Print-size rules in Texas attach to particular notices, such as the 10-point disclosure statement a manufactured home community must give applicants (Tex. Prop. Code § 94.051(3)), not to the lease as a whole.

title: No Shoreline Disclosure for Leases
bodyText: Texas requires no shoreline, beach access or coastal disclosure in a lease (all Texas codes searched). Its coastal notices are for sales, and both expressly exclude leasehold interests. A person who sells or conveys an interest, other than a water, mineral, leasehold or security interest, in property seaward of the Gulf Intracoastal Waterway must put in the sale contract a notice of the public beach easement and the risk that erosion leaves a structure on the public beach; failure lets the buyer terminate and is a deceptive act (Tex. Nat. Res. Code § 61.025). A similar notice applies to sales of property adjoining tidally influenced waters (§ 33.135). The seller's disclosure notice for a home also warns that coastal property may be subject to the Open Beaches Act and Dune Protection Act (Tex. Prop. Code § 5.008(b)). The public's beach access rights do not depend on any notice being given (Tex. Nat. Res. Code §§ 61.025(e), 33.135(e)). If you rent near the Gulf beach, telling tenants about public beach access and the limits on structures and repairs is a sensible courtesy, not a requirement.

title: No Entry-Notice Period to Waive in Texas
bodyText: Texas sets no notice period for a landlord's entry into a rented house or apartment, including entry to show it to prospective tenants or buyers, so there is no statutory notice to waive or shorten and no separate-document rule for a waiver. Your right to enter, and any notice you promise, come from the lease; the library's landlord access clause sets them, and the tenant can rely on what it says. One Texas exception is outside ordinary rentals: in a manufactured home community, you may enter a tenant's manufactured home only if the tenant is present and consents, or has given written consent for a specified date and time, or in an emergency or after abandonment (Tex. Prop. Code § 94.004). Keep showings reasonable and as the lease describes; entry the lease does not authorize can be trespass or a breach of the tenant's right to possession.

title: No Government Shutdown Rent Protection
bodyText: No Texas statute gives a tenant who is a federal or state employee, or anyone else, extra time to pay rent, a defense to eviction, or relief from late fees during a government shutdown or furlough. The ordinary rules apply: you may charge a late fee only if notice of it is in a written lease, it is reasonable, and rent remains unpaid two full days after the date it was originally due (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.019(a)), and the usual notice to vacate and eviction process applies. Offering affected tenants a written payment plan or waiving late fees is a lawful, voluntary choice that can avoid a costly eviction; put any such agreement in writing. The library's summary of other missing rules also notes that no statute gives tenants extra time when government benefit payments are delayed.

title: No Single-Family Zone Leasing Limit
bodyText: No Texas statute limits renting a home in a single-family zone, or requires the owner to live on the lot before renting the home or an accessory unit (all Texas codes searched). Leasing limits come from elsewhere. Your property owners' association's dedicatory instruments may restrict occupancy or leasing, although the association may not require your tenant or applicant to be approved by it or demand the applicant's credit report or rental application (Tex. Prop. Code § 209.016(b), (d)); see the HOA row. City zoning and short-term rental ordinances may limit how a home is used, and a 2025 law that limits city regulation of home-based businesses expressly leaves cities free to regulate short-term rental units (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code § 229.902(d)(2)). Check your city's zoning and rental rules before renting a home or an accessory unit.

title: No Smart Lock Statute in Texas
bodyText: Texas has no statute on smart locks or app-based or biometric entry systems in rentals: nothing requires you to offer a key that needs no app or biometrics, give tenants a privacy policy for the system, or limit the entry data you collect. There is no entry-notice statute either (see the entry-notice row). Existing rules still reach an electronic lock. A required doorknob lock or keyed dead bolt may be operated from outside by a key, card or combination, so a keypad or card lock can serve as one if it meets the bolt, height, strike plate and throw requirements (Tex. Prop. Code §§ 92.151(1), (5), 92.153(a), 92.154). The keyless bolting device must still work only from inside (§ 92.151(6)). A device operated by a key, card or combination must be rekeyed, meaning changed so a different key, card or code is needed, within seven days after each tenant turnover, at your expense (§§ 92.151(10), 92.156(a)); if a tenant leaves in breach of a written lease, you may deduct the reasonable cost from the deposit only if an underlined or bold lease term allows it (§ 92.156(e)). If the system captures a fingerprint, retina or iris scan, voiceprint or hand or face geometry, Texas's biometric law applies to capture "for a commercial purpose", which it does not define; the cautious course is to treat building entry as covered: tell the person and get consent first, do not sell or disclose it except as allowed, protect it, and destroy it within a reasonable time and no later than a year after the purpose ends; each violation can bring a civil penalty of up to $25,000 (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 503.001). Texas consumer data privacy law may also apply to entry data.

title: No Statewide Smoke-Free Housing Rule in Texas
bodyText:
No Texas statute makes the common hallways of an apartment building smoke-free, regulates smoke drifting between units, or applies a smoke-free workplace law to residential buildings, so there is nothing statewide for a lease to waive. The only statewide smoking ban covers a short list of public places: a public school facility, an elevator, an enclosed theater, a library, a museum, a hospital, and certain buses, planes and trains that are public places (Tex. Penal Code § 48.01).

Several Texas cities have their own smoking ordinances, some of which may reach shared indoor areas of multifamily buildings; check yours. Within your property, the lease and rules decide: the library's smoking policy clause lets you ban or limit smoking, including vaping, in the unit and common areas.

title: Late Benefit or Voucher Payments Are No Eviction Defense in Texas
bodyText: No Texas statute or court rule gives a tenant a defense to eviction, a continuance or reinstatement because a Social Security check, another government benefit or a housing-assistance payment arrived late (all Texas codes and the eviction rules searched). A late benefit is handled by the ordinary rules: for nonpayment you give a notice to pay rent or vacate (or a notice to vacate for a tenant already late before that month) and may file when it runs (Tex. Prop. Code § 24.005(a)), and trial cannot be postponed more than seven days without both sides' written agreement (§ 24.0051(g)(3)). Texas deals with assisted rent on appeal. If a government agency pays part of the rent, the justice court sets the agency's portion and the tenant's portion in the judgment, the tenant pays only the tenant's portion into the registry during the appeal, and either side may contest the split within five days after judgment (§ 24.0053(a)-(c)). If the agency stops paying its portion during the appeal, you may ask the county court to make the tenant pay the full rent into the registry to stay in possession; the court must grant it if you prove the agency's portion is owed and unpaid and that you did not cause the agency to stop paying or to pay the wrong amount (§ 24.0054(f)). Federal program rules (for example a voucher payment contract) may bar ending an assisted tenancy for the agency's unpaid share and may require their own notices; they are not reviewed here.

title: No Special District Statement for Leases
bodyText: Texas requires no lease statement about special districts, such as a municipal utility district or public improvement district, and no tenant acknowledgment of a district's rules or assessments (all Texas codes searched). Texas's district notices are for buyers. A person who sells or conveys property in a district that provides water, sewer, drainage or flood control financed by district taxes or bonds, or in a Local Government Code chapter 375 district, must give the purchaser the prescribed notice of district taxes, bonds and assessments before a binding sale contract, and an executory contract of purchase and sale with a performance period of more than six months counts as a sale (Tex. Water Code §§ 49.452(a), (a-1), (f), (i), 49.4521). A seller of property in a public improvement district must give a notice of the assessment, but that rule does not apply to a transfer of only a leasehold interest (Tex. Prop. Code § 5.014(a), (c)(9)), and the water or sewer service area notice to purchasers excludes leasehold interests in the same way (Tex. Water Code § 13.257(c)(11)). If you combine a lease with an option to buy that runs more than six months, giving the district notice at signing is the cautious course (see the required disclosures row).

title: No Sprinkler Disclosure in Texas
bodyText: No Texas statute requires you to tell a tenant whether the building has a fire sprinkler system, when it was last inspected or maintained, or that it has none, and no lease notice or sign about sprinklers is required. Whether a building must have sprinklers is a separate question, covered in the fire sprinkler row. Some state rules limit sprinkler mandates rather than require disclosure; for example, a city may not require a home-based business to install a fire sprinkler system in a single-family detached home or a building with no more than two units (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code § 229.902(b)(3)(B)). If the building has sprinklers, your lease may tell tenants not to hang items from, cover, block or tamper with sprinkler heads, and you should keep inspection records. Telling applicants whether the unit is sprinklered is a lawful courtesy, not a requirement.

title: Leases That Must Be in Writing
bodyText: Texas has two writing rules for longer leases. A lease of real estate for a term longer than one year is not enforceable unless the lease, or a memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by the person to be charged or by someone lawfully authorized to sign for that person (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 26.01(a), (b)(5)). The Property Code adds that a conveyance of an estate for more than one year in land must be in writing and subscribed and delivered by the conveyor or by the conveyor's agent authorized in writing (Tex. Prop. Code § 5.021), so give written authority to any agent who signs a lease longer than one year for you. The statute of frauds also covers any agreement that is not to be performed within one year from the date it is made (§ 26.01(b)(6)), which on its words can reach a one-year lease signed well before its term begins; how courts apply that to leases is case law not reviewed, so put every lease of a year or more in writing, signed by you and every tenant. No statute specifically addresses assigning or surrendering a lease in writing (all Texas codes searched), but an assignment of more than a year's remaining term is safest in a signed writing. A lease binds you and the tenant without being acknowledged or recorded, but an unrecorded lease is void against a later buyer or creditor who pays value without notice of it (Tex. Prop. Code § 13.001); whether a tenant's possession gives notice is case law not reviewed. To record a lease, have it acknowledged or sworn to (§ 12.001(a)). See the lease length row for term limits.

title: Texas Money Limits at a Glance
bodyText: Texas caps few of the amounts you charge a residential tenant. Late fees: notice must be in the written lease, the fee must be reasonable, and you may charge it only after rent has stayed unpaid two full days after it was due; a fee of up to 12 percent of the rent for the rental period (four or fewer units in the structure) or 10 percent (more than four units) counts as reasonable (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.019). Returned checks and electronic payments: a processing fee of at most $30 (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 3.506(b)). Security devices: you may charge only for misuse or damage under an underlined lease term, and no more than a third-party contractor would charge (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.162). Submetered or allocated water: a one-time late penalty of at most 5 percent, and only if the written lease states the percentage (16 Tex. Admin. Code § 24.283(m)). Interest: the general ceiling is 10 percent a year unless another law allows more (Tex. Fin. Code § 302.001(b)). Rent: no cap, and a city may adopt rent control only for a disaster housing emergency with the governor's approval (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code § 214.902). No Texas statute caps a security deposit, an application fee, or a pet deposit, fee or rent (all Texas codes searched). Some state-funded housing has its own limits, such as no late fees in Section 811 units (10 Tex. Admin. Code § 10.624(f)(2)(E)(i)).

title: No Radiator Cover Rule
bodyText: No Texas statute requires you to put covers on steam radiators or other hot heating surfaces, or to give tenants a radiator notice or rider with the lease (all Texas codes searched). The only Texas rules on steam heat are boiler-safety rules: a steam or hot water heating boiler must have a certificate inspection every two years (Tex. Health & Safety Code § 755.025(c)), but a heating boiler in a building used only as a residence with accommodations for no more than four families is exempt from that inspection schedule (§ 755.022(b)). Your general duty is the repair statute: once a tenant who is current on rent gives notice, you must make a diligent effort to repair a condition that materially affects the physical health or safety of an ordinary tenant (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.052(a)). Whether an exposed radiator that could burn a small child meets that test is not settled by statute. Cautious course: if your building has radiators, offer covers where young children live, and keep any boiler on its inspection cycle. City codes may add rules. Nothing needs to be added to the lease.

title: Deaths, Crimes and Other Stigmas
bodyText: No Texas statute requires you to tell an applicant or tenant that someone died in the unit, that a crime happened there, or that a registered sex offender lives nearby, and none deals with so-called stigmatized property in leasing (all Texas codes searched). Texas settles two points. No person is civilly or criminally liable for failing to inquire about, disclose or release information on whether a previous or current occupant had AIDS, an HIV-related illness or HIV infection (Tex. Occ. Code § 1101.802). A licensed real estate broker or sales agent need not inquire about or disclose that information, or whether a death on the property was by natural causes, suicide or an accident unrelated to the property's condition (§ 1101.556); a seller has the same freedom in the seller's disclosure statute (Tex. Prop. Code § 5.008(c)), which applies to sales, not leases. Neither rule covers a death caused by the property's condition, which may point to a defect you should disclose and repair. Never answer a direct question falsely; the Deceptive Trade Practices Act row explains when misleading a tenant can be actionable. Never volunteer an occupant's health information.

title: No Duty to Supply a Stove or Refrigerator
bodyText:
No Texas statute requires you to supply a stove, oven, range or refrigerator in a residential rental. What you include is a lease choice: list the appliances you provide in the library's appliances clause and say who maintains them. Once you supply an appliance, the repair statute covers it like any other part of the dwelling: after notice from a tenant who is current on rent, you must make a diligent effort to repair a condition that materially affects the physical health or safety of an ordinary tenant (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.052(a)).

Whether a broken refrigerator or stove meets that test is not settled by statute, and case law was not reviewed; treat a failure that leaves the tenant unable to store or cook food safely as urgent. You have no duty during the lease to repair a condition the tenant, an occupant, family or a guest caused, other than normal wear and tear (§ 92.052(b)). A city of 1.7 million or more must adopt minimum habitability standards for buildings with three or more rental units (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code § 214.219), and city codes may require cooking or refrigeration equipment.

If you leave an item at the property that you do not provide, the library's items-not-provided clause says so. Never list a device that supplies hot water, or any item whose failure would materially affect the physical health or safety of an ordinary tenant: the repair duty applies to those whatever the lease says (Tex. Prop. Code §§ 92.052, 92.006(c)). Remove a listed item only at the tenant's written request (§ 92.0081(a)).

title: Renting to Students
bodyText: Texas has no student-housing statute for private rentals: nothing gives you a different notice period, deposit rule, academic-year term or group-liability rule because your tenants are students (all Texas codes searched). A student lease is an ordinary residential lease and the Texas rules in this library apply. Points that come up often: you may not let more adults occupy a dwelling than three times the number of bedrooms, unless fair housing law requires more or an adult is seeking temporary sanctuary from family violence for up to a month (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.010); a parent or other guarantor is liable only for the original lease term unless the original lease states a last renewal date and the other terms the statute lists (§ 92.021); and the security-device rules cover a room in a dormitory or rooming house but not housing owned or operated by an accredited college or university (§ 92.152). Colleges and universities are also exempt from the rule against blocking a tenant's telecommunications provider (Tex. Util. Code § 54.259(b)). In housing tax credit and other developments monitored by the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs, the lease or an addendum must require households to report changes in student status, with a narrow exception for some Trust Fund units (10 Tex. Admin. Code § 10.613(d)). Use the library's joint liability clause for roommate groups.

title: Program Inspections in Subsidized Units
bodyText: No Texas statute says what happens when a tenant in a subsidized or voucher unit refuses entry for a program inspection, or makes a refusal a ground for ending the lease (all Texas codes searched). Texas has no general entry-notice statute either, so your right to enter comes from the lease (see the entry rows). Inspections in voucher units are governed by the federal program rules and your contract with the housing authority. In developments monitored by the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs, you must give the Department access to the property and records; the Department inspects the interior of a sample of units, gives you reasonable notice of an onsite inspection or file review so you can notify tenants, and gives at least 48 hours' notice before a follow-up review that needs access to tenant units (10 Tex. Admin. Code § 10.618). What to do: put an inspection cooperation clause in the lease, pass each inspection notice on to tenants in writing, document any refusal, and check the program rules and your contract before treating a refusal as a lease violation. Remember that a tenant's good-faith complaint to a code agency is protected from retaliation (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.331(a)(3)).

title: Subsidy Stopped After a Failed Inspection
bodyText: Whether a housing agency may stop (abate) its share of the rent when a voucher unit fails inspection, and whether you may then collect that share from the tenant, is set by federal program rules and your contract with the agency, not by any Texas statute (all Texas codes searched). Texas law adds these points. On a tenant's repair claim, a court may reduce the rent in proportion to the reduced rental value from the date of the first repair notice until the condition is fixed (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.0563(a)(2)). When rent is subsidized by a government agency, the statute uses the fair market rent, not the tenant's share, for the repair-and-deduct cap (§ 92.0561(b)) and for the one-month part of the retaliation penalty (§ 92.333). After a casualty that leaves the unit partly unusable, rent is reduced in proportion only by court judgment unless the written lease says otherwise (§ 92.054(c)). In a Section 811 Project Rental Assistance unit monitored by the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs, the tenant pays only the tenant rent portion and may not be held responsible for assistance payments (10 Tex. Admin. Code § 10.624(c)(6)). The cautious course: never bill a subsidized tenant for an agency share that was abated or withheld, fix inspection failures within the program's deadlines, and read your assistance contract before charging anything.

title: Late Fees for Subsidized Tenants
bodyText:
Texas's late-fee statute applies to subsidized tenants as it does to everyone: notice of the fee must be in the written lease, the fee must be reasonable, and you may charge it only after any part of the tenant's rent has stayed unpaid two full days after it was due (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.019(a)); see the late-fee rows.

The safe harbor is measured on the amount of rent for the rental period under the lease (§ 92.019(a-1)), and the statute doesn't say whether, for a subsidized tenant, that means the whole contract rent or only the tenant's share. No Texas statute sets a special late-fee rule for subsidized or voucher tenants.

Cautious course: charge a late fee only when the tenant's own share is late, figure the percentage on that share, and never charge the tenant because the housing agency paid late or stopped paying. One state rule is firm: in a Section 811 Project Rental Assistance unit monitored by the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs, you cannot charge fees for late payment of rent (10 Tex. Admin. Code § 10.624(f)(2)(E)(i)).

Federal program rules and HUD lease addenda may limit or bar late fees in other assisted housing.

title: Code Enforcement Orders and Receivership
bodyText: Texas lets cities force repairs of substandard rental buildings and, in serious cases, take management out of your hands. A city may adopt an ordinance setting minimum standards for continued use and occupancy and, after notice and a public hearing, order a building vacated, secured, repaired, removed or demolished and its occupants relocated; you usually get 30 days, and no more than 90 without a detailed plan, and if you don't act the city may do the work and put a lien on the property (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code § 214.001). A home-rule city may also sue in district court for a receiver for property not in substantial compliance with ordinances on fire protection, structural integrity, zoning or refuse, among others (§ 214.003), and a home-rule city or a certified nonprofit housing organization may seek a receiver for property that is a serious and imminent public health or safety hazard (§ 214.0031). A receiver can take control, collect rents, renew and sign leases and make repairs, and keeps control until its costs and any 10 percent fee are repaid; after notice the court may order the property sold. Neither section reaches an owner-occupied single-family home. A court may also appoint a receiver for up to a year for multiunit property found to be a common nuisance (Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 125.046; see the nuisance row). No Texas statute lets tenants petition for a receiver (all Texas codes searched). Answer every code notice promptly.

title: Tenants' Choice of Telephone Provider
bodyText: If a tenant asks for service from a telecommunications utility that holds the city's consent, franchise or permit and any certificate the state requires, you may not prevent or interfere with the utility installing the service facility the tenant requests, discriminate against the utility in installation, terms or compensation, demand or accept an unreasonable payment from the tenant or the utility for allowing it on the property, or discriminate for or against a tenant, including by charging different rent, because of the utility the tenant uses (Tex. Util. Code § 54.259(a)). You may impose conditions reasonably necessary to protect the safety, security, appearance and condition of the property and the safety and convenience of others, reasonably limit when the utility may install, limit the number of utilities if you can show a space constraint, require the utility to indemnify you for damage, make the tenant or utility bear the whole cost of installing, operating or removing the facility, and require reasonable, nondiscriminatory compensation from the utility (§ 54.260). You need not contract for shared tenant services (§ 54.261). The Public Utility Commission enforces these rules, and they don't apply to colleges and universities. No Texas statute governs cable television, internet-only or satellite access to rental property in the same way (all Texas codes searched).

title: Tenants at Will and by Sufferance
bodyText: Texas statutes use, but don't define, the terms tenant at will and tenant by sufferance (all Texas codes searched). They appear in the eviction chapter. A tenant at will or by sufferance, including an occupant at the time of a foreclosure of a lien superior to the tenant's lease, who refuses to give up possession on written demand commits a forcible detainer, so the remedy is an eviction suit (Tex. Prop. Code § 24.002). Before filing you must give at least three days' written notice to vacate, unless a written lease or agreement sets a shorter or longer period (§ 24.005(b)), delivered by one of the statutory methods (§ 24.005(f-3)). Someone who pays rent by the month may instead be a month-to-month tenant, and that tenancy ends only on the termination notice: the later of the date in the notice or one month after it is given, unless you both signed an agreement setting a different period (§ 91.001); see the month-to-month row. Which category an occupant is in is decided by case law. Cautious course: if the occupant has paid rent for a regular period, give the termination notice for that period and then the notice to vacate before filing. A foreclosure buyer who chooses not to continue the lease must give a residential tenant who is current at least 30 days' written notice to vacate (§ 24.005(b)).

title: When a Tenant Files for Bankruptcy
bodyText: What happens to a lease, to rent arrears and to an eviction when a tenant files for bankruptcy is governed by federal bankruptcy law, including its automatic stay and its rules on keeping or rejecting a lease. No Texas statute makes a tenant's bankruptcy a ground for ending a residential lease, sets a procedure for an eviction after the tenant files, or limits a lease clause that treats bankruptcy as a default, and the Texas eviction rules don't address it either (all Texas codes and the Texas Rules of Civil Procedure searched). The one Texas rule tying bankruptcy to a lease concerns your bankruptcy, not the tenant's: the tenant's claim to the security deposit takes priority over the claim of any of your creditors, including a trustee in bankruptcy (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.103(c)). What to do: when you learn a tenant has filed, stop collection and eviction steps and get advice before you send a notice, file or continue an eviction, or apply the deposit. Don't rely on a lease clause that ends the lease because of bankruptcy.

title: Protecting Tenants' Personal Information
bodyText: No Texas statute bars a landlord in general from sharing tenant information, but Texas business privacy laws reach the personal data you collect from applicants and tenants. You must use reasonable procedures to protect sensitive personal information you collect or keep in the regular course of business, such as a name together with a Social Security number, driver's license number, or an account number with its access code, and you must shred, erase or otherwise make unreadable records containing it that you won't keep (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §§ 521.002, 521.052). If computerized data with that information is breached, notify each affected person without unreasonable delay and within 60 days, and notify the attorney general within 30 days if at least 250 Texans are affected (§ 521.053); penalties are steep (§ 521.151). You may not require an applicant's Social Security number unless you adopt, make available and follow a privacy policy saying how personal information is collected, used, protected, accessed and disposed of (§ 501.052), and you may not make a Social Security number available to the public (§ 501.001). Information a tenant gives you to end a lease after sexual assault, other listed sexual offenses or stalking may be shared only for a legitimate or customary business purpose or as the law requires (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.0161(j)). Larger businesses may also fall under the Texas Data Privacy and Security Act, which does not apply to a small business as the federal Small Business Administration defines it, except that a small business may not sell sensitive personal data without the consumer's prior consent (§§ 541.002(a)(3), 541.107).

title: Flags, Signs and Displays by Tenants
bodyText: No Texas statute gives a residential tenant a right against you to display a flag, sign, banner or decoration, or limits your neutral rules on displays (all Texas codes searched). Texas's display rules bind property owners' associations. An association may not bar an owner from displaying the United States flag, the Texas flag or an armed forces flag, though it may regulate flagpoles, flag size, lighting and location (Tex. Prop. Code § 202.012); it may not bar a property owner from installing a solar energy device except in the listed cases (§ 202.010); and it may not bar a property owner or resident from displaying religious items motivated by sincere religious belief, with exceptions for items that threaten safety, violate other law, are patently offensive or sit on common property (§ 202.018). The flag and solar rules protect the owner, so in an association community they protect you, not your tenant; only the religious-display rule names residents. Political signs are covered in the political-access row and religious items in the religious-display row. Keep your own display rules written, neutral and evenly enforced, because fair housing law bars discrimination in rental terms because of religion or national origin (see the fair housing row).

title: Housing Your Employees
bodyText: Texas has no general statute on housing your own employees: nothing requires a disclosure of occupancy and vacating terms, ends an employee's right to stay when the job ends, or creates a separate removal route for a resident manager or caretaker (all Texas codes searched). If an employee occupies a unit under a written or oral agreement for its use and occupancy, the residential tenancy chapter applies: it covers landlords and tenants of residential rental property, and a tenant is a person a lease authorizes to occupy a dwelling to the exclusion of others (Tex. Prop. Code §§ 92.001, 92.002). After the job ends, an occupant who won't leave is removed by an eviction suit after written notice to vacate (§§ 24.002, 24.005); whether the occupant is a tenant, a tenant at will or something else depends on the arrangement and on case law. So put the housing terms in a written agreement separate from the employment terms, including what happens when the job ends and the notice period, which the parties may set by written agreement (§ 24.005(b)). One licensing rule applies: a facility used for more than three days as living quarters for two or more seasonal, temporary or migrant families, or three or more such workers, needs a license from the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs, whether or not rent is paid (Tex. Gov't Code §§ 2306.921, 2306.922).

title: Claims on a Tenant's Insurance
bodyText: No Texas statute governs claims between you and a tenant's insurer: nothing bars you from asking a tenant to claim on the tenant's renter's insurance for damage the tenant caused, requires the tenant's written permission before you claim on the tenant's policy, or says whether a tenant's policy may pay for repairs that are your duty (all Texas codes searched). Texas rules shape the answer anyway. Your duty to repair conditions that materially affect health or safety can't be waived or shifted to the tenant except in the narrow ways the statute allows (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.006(c)-(f); see the non-waivable terms row), so don't make a tenant's policy fund those repairs. After an insured casualty such as fire, smoke, hail or explosion, your repair period does not begin until you receive the insurance proceeds (§ 92.054(a)). You have no duty during the lease to repair damage the tenant, an occupant, family or a guest caused, other than normal wear and tear (§ 92.052(b)), so you may look to the tenant for those costs, and the tenant may claim on the tenant's own policy. The flood notice already warns tenants that most tenant insurance policies do not cover flood loss (§ 92.0135(b)). For renter's insurance requirements, see the renter's insurance row.

title: Online Tenant Portals
bodyText:
No Texas statute regulates tenant portals or bars a lease term requiring rent, requests or signatures through one. Texas's electronic transactions law sets the limits. It applies only between parties who have each agreed to deal electronically, and a party who agreed may refuse to conduct other transactions electronically; that right can't be waived by agreement (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 322.005(b), (c)).

An electronic record or signature has the same effect as paper (§ 322.007), and a written notice a law requires may go electronically only if the recipient can keep and print it (§ 322.008(a)). Statutory notices keep their own methods: a notice to vacate may be sent electronically only if the parties agreed in writing (Tex. Prop. Code § 24.005(f-3)(4)); deposit-refund notices may go by e-mail if you and the tenant have already communicated by e-mail, for a lease entered into or renewed on or after September 1, 2025 (§ 92.113); and a tenant's repair notice goes to the person or place where rent is normally paid (§ 92.052(a)(1)).

You must accept timely cash rent unless the written lease requires payment by check, money order or another traceable or negotiable instrument (§ 92.011(a)); whether a portal-only payment term meets that is unsettled. So offer the portal as a convenience, keep the lease's notice methods open, and use the library's optional portal clause. Leases for designated units in developments subject to the 2025 federal HOME rule, monitored by the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs, must give tenants more than one way to reach the owner and management, such as in person, by phone, by e-mail or through a portal (10 Tex. Admin. Code § 10.613(o)(3)(B)).

title: Records You Must Keep and Share
bodyText: Texas has no general rule requiring you to keep a rent ledger, give a tenant a payment history on request, or attach a ledger to a nonpayment notice (all Texas codes searched). Specific record duties do apply. If you accept cash rent, give a written receipt and enter the payment date and amount in a record book you keep (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.011(b)). Keep accurate records of all security deposits (§ 92.106). If a tenant asks whether a late fee is owed and how much, you must answer in writing by any established means you regularly use for written communication with the tenant, though not answering does not erase a late fee owed (§ 92.0191). If you change towing or parking rules in a multiunit complex, you must be able to prove the tenant received the change, for example by certified mail or a file note of the time, place, method and who delivered it (§ 92.0131(d)). Protect records with applicants' and tenants' personal information and destroy them securely when you discard them (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §§ 72.004, 521.052; see the confidential information row); a business record a Texas law requires you to keep may be destroyed after three years unless another law sets a different period (§ 72.002). Developments monitored by the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs have tenant-file rules, including a full tenant ledger in Section 811 units (10 Tex. Admin. Code § 10.624(c)(3)).

title: Tenant Organizations
bodyText: You may not retaliate against a tenant because the tenant establishes, attempts to establish or participates in a tenant organization (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.331(a)(4)). For six months after that activity you may not, because of it, file an eviction (except on the grounds the statute always allows), deprive the tenant of the use of the premises, decrease services, raise the rent, end the lease, or in bad faith interfere materially with the tenant's lease rights (§ 92.331(b)). Delinquent rent, intentional damage or threats, serious lease breaches and certain holdovers remain valid grounds (§ 92.332(b)). A tenant who proves retaliation recovers one month's rent plus $500, actual damages, court costs and attorney's fees, less any rent owed; for a subsidized tenant the penalty uses fair market rent (§ 92.333). In a multifamily development owned by a public facility corporation that claims the property-tax exemption, every lease must also state that you won't retaliate against the tenant or the tenant's guests for tenant-organization activity, and the tenant can't waive it (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code § 303.0425(i)(1), (j)); see the good-cause rows. No Texas statute gives apartment tenants a right to meet in common areas, post or hand out literature, or have an organization recognized (all Texas codes searched); only manufactured home communities have a meetings rule (§ 94.006). Apply your common-area and solicitation rules evenly so they can't be seen as targeting organizers.

title: Tenant Rights Statements
bodyText: Texas has no general requirement that you give tenants a state-prepared statement or summary of tenant rights, attach one to the lease, or get a signed acknowledgment of one (all Texas codes searched). The attorney general's office publishes renter's rights information on its website that you may share, but no statute requires it. What Texas requires instead is specific language in the lease, such as notice of the tenant's repair remedies in underlined or bold print and the early-termination statements (see the lease content row), and specific notices for specific events, such as a description of the tenant's rights in a notice that submetered electricity will be disconnected (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.008(h)(3)(B)(vi)). One program rule does require a rights brochure: the owner of a development monitored by the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs must post the Department's Tenant Rights and Resources Guide in the leasing office and give it to each household during the application process and after changes to amenities or services, and a household representative must sign a certification of receipt no more than 120 days before the initial lease is signed; a late guide is cured by giving it and getting the signed certification, and the guide must say whether the site is in the 100-year floodplain (10 Tex. Admin. Code § 10.613(l)).

title: Tenant Duties Under Texas Statutes
bodyText:
Texas has no statute listing a residential tenant's general duties, such as keeping the unit clean, disposing of waste or using fixtures reasonably; those come from the lease, so use the library's tenant maintenance and no-disturbance clauses. Texas statutes do set these specific duties. The tenant may not sublet during the term without your prior consent (Tex. Prop. Code § 91.005).

The tenant may not withhold the last month's rent on the ground that the deposit covers it; a tenant who does is presumed to act in bad faith and owes three times the rent withheld plus attorney's fees (§ 92.108). You need not refund the deposit or itemize deductions until the tenant gives a written forwarding address (§ 92.107).

A tenant who withholds rent, or repairs and deducts, outside the repair statute owes your actual damages, and after your written warning a bad-faith tenant owes one month's rent plus $500 (§ 92.058). The tenant may not remove, rekey or alter a security device without your permission, except under the repair-and-deduct remedy (§ 92.163).

A tenant who removes a smoke alarm's battery without replacing it, or knowingly disconnects or intentionally damages the alarm, owes your damages, unless they come from your failure to repair the alarm within a reasonable time after the tenant asked; and if the lease has the required underlined or bold notice and the tenant ignores your seven-day written notice, owes one month's rent plus $100, costs and fees (§ 92.2611).

To use the repair remedies the tenant must give notice and be current on rent (§ 92.052(a)). Damage the tenant causes is the tenant's cost (see the tenant-caused damage row).

title: Changing Lease Terms or Rules
bodyText:
Texas has no general rule on how much notice you must give to change a lease term, rule or fee. During a fixed term, change a term only as the lease allows or with the tenant's agreement. For a month-to-month tenancy, a change the tenant won't accept works through the termination notice: at least one month for a monthly tenancy unless you both signed an agreement setting a different period (Tex. Prop. Code § 91.001); see the month-to-month and rent-increase rows.

Two rule changes have their own notice. You must give prior written notice of a rule or policy change not in the lease that will affect a tenant's personal property outside the dwelling, in person or by mail, and you owe the tenant any expense your failure causes (§ 92.013). In a multiunit complex, a mid-term change to towing or parking rules needs written notice before the tenant must comply and can't take effect before the 14th day after delivery, except in a construction or utility emergency; it must apply to all tenants in the complex and rest on necessity, safety or security, construction needs or other tenants' parking rights, or be adopted with the tenant's written consent; a violation costs $100 plus towing and storage costs and fees (§ 92.0131(d)-(f)).

A rent increase within six months after a tenant's protected act can be retaliation (§ 92.331(b)(4)). In Section 811 units, a tenant rent increase needs at least 30 days' notice (10 Tex. Admin. Code § 10.624(g)(2)).

title: No Tenant-Purchase Exemption Notice
bodyText: Some places give tenants a right to buy their building before it is sold and require owners of exempt buildings to tell tenants about the exemption before they sign. Texas has neither: no statute gives residential tenants a general right to purchase or a right of first refusal when you sell, and none requires a notice that a property is exempt from such a right (all Texas codes searched). The nearest Texas rule covers certain housing tax credit developments whose land use restriction agreement gives a qualified entity a right of first refusal: the owner must notify the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs and the tenants of an intent to sell after the compliance period (Tex. Gov't Code § 2306.6726(a)); see the tax credit sale notice row. A Texas residential lease therefore needs no tenant-purchase exemption statement.

title: Notice Before Selling a Tax Credit Property
bodyText: Texas gives residential tenants no general right to buy their building or right of first refusal when you sell, and no general duty to tell tenants you intend to sell (all Texas codes searched). One program rule applies. If you own a housing tax credit development whose land use restriction agreement gives a qualified entity a right of first refusal, and you intend to sell after the federal compliance period, you must notify the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs and the tenants of your intent to sell (Tex. Gov't Code § 2306.6726(a)). After the Department posts the notice, for the first 60 days you may negotiate only with certain community housing development organizations (or, in some cases, a housing authority or its public facility corporation), in the next 60 days also with qualifying nonprofits and tenant organizations, and in the last 60 days with any qualified entity; from the 181st day you may sell to anyone if no qualified entity offers a price the Department finds reasonable (§ 2306.6726(b), (c)). The rule applies only to a right of first refusal in a land use restriction agreement. Owners of some Department-funded developments must also give the Department 12 months' notice before selling or opting out of a Section 8 contract (§ 2306.185(f)). Check your agreement and the Department's rules before marketing such a property.

title: No Expiry Date on Texas Tenant Law
bodyText: Texas's residential tenancy statutes carry no sunset or dated repeal: no section of the Property Code's landlord-tenant, eviction or manufactured home community chapters says it expires or is repealed on a set date. Texas's Sunset Act reviews and abolishes state agencies, not tenant protections (for example Tex. Gov't Code § 325.015). What changes Texas tenant law is amendment, and recent amendments have been large. The 2025 eviction overhaul, effective January 1, 2026, rewrote the notice-to-vacate section, including how the notice must be delivered (Tex. Prop. Code § 24.005(f-3)), and added a new English and Spanish citation warning where you seek summary disposition (§ 24.0051(e)). So instead of diarying an expiry date, check for amendments after each regular and called legislative session, and look at the history line under each section you rely on. The library's rows on Texas eviction notices and procedure carry the 2026 rules.

title: Leases in Another Language
bodyText: Texas does not require an ordinary residential lease, or any lease disclosure, to be translated, even when you negotiate in another language, and sets no type-size rule tied to a translation (all Texas codes searched). Three narrower rules involve another language. First, a lease combined with an option to buy is treated as an executory contract for conveyance (Tex. Prop. Code § 5.062(a)(2)). If the negotiations were conducted primarily in a language other than English, you must provide a copy in that language of all written documents relating to the transaction, including the contract and required notices (§ 5.068). That rule does not apply to a lease-option of three years or less where the parties have not been in an executory contract for the property for more than three years (§ 5.062(f)), and the subchapter does not apply at all if the contract provides for a deed within 180 days (§ 5.062(c)). Second, if you are the customer on a master-metered, non-submetered electric or gas account at a property with at least 10 dwellings and you receive a disconnection notice, your notice to residents must include the statutory text in English and Spanish (§ 92.302(b)). Third, every eviction citation carries court warnings in English and Spanish (§ 24.0051(d), (e)); the court issues it. Cautious course when you negotiate in another language: offer a courtesy translation, and say in the lease which version controls.

title: Trespass Warnings at Texas Rental Property
bodyText: You can use Texas's criminal trespass law to bar a non-tenant from your property. A person commits criminal trespass by entering or staying on another's property, including residential land or a building, without effective consent after having notice that entry was forbidden, or after receiving notice to depart and not leaving (Tex. Penal Code § 30.05(a)). Notice can be oral or written communication by the owner or someone with apparent authority to act for the owner, fencing, or signs at the property or building entrance that intruders are likely to see (§ 30.05(b)(2)); there is no required form. Trespass in a habitation is a Class A misdemeanor; most other trespass is Class B (§ 30.05(d)). At a rental, be careful: the unit is in the tenant's possession, and whether you can bar a guest the tenant invites, from the unit or from common areas the tenant uses, turns on effective consent, a case-law question not reviewed here. Cautious course: give a written warning naming the person, the date, the areas covered and the reason, keep a copy, tell the tenant, and call the police rather than removing anyone yourself. You may not bar a tenant or guest from lawfully possessing a firearm in the unit, in a vehicle in tenant parking, or on the way between them (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.026; Penal Code § 30.05(f-2)). For an intruder who was never your tenant, use the sheriff-removal procedure in Property Code chapter 24B (see the library's squatter row); knowingly presenting a fake lease or deed to enter or stay is a Class A misdemeanor (Penal Code § 32.56). Anyone who was ever your tenant must be evicted (§ 24B.001(3)(A)).

title: No Truth-in-Renting Act in Texas
bodyText: Texas has no truth-in-renting law: no state-published statement of landlord and tenant rights that every landlord must hand out, and no statute that voids a lease or penalizes you merely because a clause misstates tenants' rights (all Texas codes searched; the Texas Administrative Code mostly not held). Texas covers the same ground in other ways. The Deceptive Trade Practices Act reaches residential leasing, because its goods include real property leased for use (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 17.45(1)), and its list of deceptive acts includes representing that an agreement confers rights, remedies or obligations it does not have, or that the law prohibits (§ 17.46(b)(12)). A tenant who relied on such a term to the tenant's detriment can sue for damages and attorney's fees (§ 17.50(a)(1), (b), (d)). Many Property Code sections also void a lease term that waives them, for example the late-fee, lockout and utility-cutoff rules (Tex. Prop. Code §§ 92.019(d), 92.0081(j), 92.008(g)). The library's rows on the Deceptive Trade Practices Act, lease terms Texas voids, plain-language rules and tenant rights guides give the details. What to do: keep any clause that restates the law accurate, and take out any term a Texas statute voids rather than leaving it in the lease.

title: Charging Separately for Parking in Texas
bodyText: No Texas statute requires you to rent or price parking separately from the dwelling, or stops you from including it in the rent or charging for it separately. So the lease decides: say whether parking is included, which space or area the tenant may use, and any separate charge (the library's parking and assigned parking space clauses). If you charge separately, state the amount in the lease, because Texas's debt-collection law bars collecting a fee the lease does not expressly authorize (the library's row on fees your lease must state). Three Texas rules touch parking. If you issue a parking permit, it must run for the whole lease term, and you may not end or suspend it before the tenant's right of possession ends (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.0132). In a multiunit complex you must give tenants your towing and parking rules (the library's parking rules rows). And since September 1, 2025, a city of more than 150,000 people in a county of more than 300,000 may not require a multifamily development of three or more units, or a mixed-use residential development, to provide more than one parking space per dwelling unit (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code §§ 218.001, 218.002, 218.102(a)(2)). That limits what a developer must build, not how you price the spaces.

title: Unconscionable Lease Terms in Texas
bodyText: Texas has no unconscionability rule written for ordinary residential leases. Several statutes use the word, and only some can reach a rental of housing. The Uniform Commercial Code rule that lets a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable lease clause (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 2A.108) covers leases of goods only; that chapter does not apply to a lease of real estate (§ 2A.102), and the sales-chapter version covers transactions in goods (§§ 2.102, 2.302). The Deceptive Trade Practices Act does reach residential leases, because its goods include real property leased for use (§ 17.45(1)). A tenant may sue for any unconscionable action or course of action (§ 17.50(a)(3)), meaning an act or practice that, to the tenant's detriment, takes advantage of the tenant's lack of knowledge, ability, experience or capacity to a grossly unfair degree (§ 17.45(5)). That targets your conduct rather than a clause as such; a winning tenant recovers economic damages, up to three times if you acted knowingly, plus attorney's fees (§ 17.50(b), (d)). For a manufactured home community lot lease, any illegal or unconscionable provision is void, and the rest of the lease survives (Tex. Prop. Code § 94.053(e)). A court also may not enforce an arbitration agreement that was unconscionable when made (Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 171.022). Whether a court will refuse an unconscionable term in an ordinary house or apartment lease under common law is case law, not reviewed here, so draft terms that are plainly fair.

title: Interest on Unpaid Rent and Charges
bodyText: No Texas statute sets interest on a tenant's unpaid rent or other lease charges in particular (all Texas codes searched). General rules apply, with one trap. Treat interest on late rent as a late fee: the late-fee section covers any fee, charge or other sum of money the lease requires when rent is not paid on time, and an initial fee plus daily charges count as one fee (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.019(b), (e)). So it needs notice in a written lease, may start only once rent is two full days late, and together with any late fee should stay within the 10 or 12 percent safe harbor, or you risk $100 plus three times the amount collected plus attorney's fees (§ 92.019(a), (a-1), (c)). For other sums, a creditor that has not agreed on interest may charge legal interest of six percent a year from the 30th day after the amount is due (Tex. Fin. Code § 302.002); whether that reaches a tenant's unpaid repair charges or damages is case law, not reviewed. An agreed rate generally may not exceed 10 percent a year (§ 302.001(b)). A judgment earns interest at the lease rate, capped at 18 percent, if the lease provides for interest, and otherwise at the prime-based rate, between 5 and 15 percent (§§ 304.002, 304.003). This library offers no interest clause for Texas because of the late-fee overlap; if you add one, limit it to non-rent sums at 10 percent a year or less, after advice. Your damages claim can also be lost through deposit mistakes (the library's deposit penalty row).

title: Leases From Life Tenants and Trustees in Texas
bodyText: Texas has no civil-law usufruct, and no Texas statute says what happens to a residential lease granted by someone who holds the property only for life (all Texas codes searched). Limited ownership still arises in Texas. When a person dies without a will leaving a spouse and children, the surviving spouse takes a life estate in one-third of the person's separate land, with the remainder going to the children (Tex. Est. Code § 201.002(b)(3)), and a will or deed can create a life estate too. A life tenant who keeps real property originally conveyed to the life tenant is subject to the common-law duties of a life tenant (Tex. Prop. Code § 5.009(b)). Trusts work differently: a trustee may lease trust real property for any term, and the lease may run beyond the duration of the trust (§ 113.011). Whether a lease from a life tenant survives the life tenant's death, and what the remainder owners may then do, is common law, not reviewed here. Cautious course: before you sign a lease as, or with, a limited owner, check the recorded title and any probate order, have everyone with a present or future interest sign the lease or consent in writing, and keep the term short if they won't. A lease longer than one year must be in writing and signed (the library's row on leases that must be in writing).

title: Limits on What You Charge for Utilities
bodyText:
When you pass a utility bill on to tenants, Texas caps the charge in most multiunit settings. Water and wastewater at an apartment house of five or more units, a condominium or a manufactured home rental community: submetered bills may not exceed the utility's cost per gallon plus taxes and surcharges, apart from a service charge of up to 9 percent at an apartment house or manufactured home community (none for tax-credit units or Section 8 voucher holders).

Allocated bills may not exceed the actual charges to you, apart from a late fee of up to 5 percent (Tex. Water Code §§ 13.501(1), 13.503(b), (c), 13.5031(a); the library's water billing row). Submetered electricity at an apartment house of more than five units, a condominium or a mobile home park: no more than the utility's cost per kilowatt hour, and no extra charges beyond what the provider bills you (Tex. Util. Code §§ 184.011(1), 184.014(b)(1); 16 Tex. Admin. Code § 25.142(d)(1)(F)).

Allocated master-metered electricity, or central heating, cooling or hot water costs, at a building of two or more units: no more than the actual charge to you (Util. Code §§ 184.051(1), 184.052(b)(2)(A)). Breaking the electricity rules costs three times the overcharge, a penalty of one month's rent unless the mistake was unintentional and in good faith, and attorney's fees (§ 184.071).

Submetered gas may not be resold for profit (§ 124.002(b)(1)). In those buildings a fixed utility allowance with the tenant paying any overage is an allocation that must follow these rules, so the library offers no allowance clause for Texas. Outside them, for example a house with the account in your name, no statute caps the charge: bill only the actual cost, as the lease states.

title: Dividing a Shared Utility Bill Among Tenants
bodyText: Texas lets you divide a master-metered utility bill among tenants only on regulated terms in most multiunit buildings. Water and wastewater: an owner of an apartment house of five or more units, a manufactured home rental community or a multiple use facility, or a condominium manager, may allocate master-metered costs only under Public Utility Commission rules. The lease must clearly describe how the allocation is calculated and state the average unit monthly bill for the previous calendar year, you may not charge more than the actual charges to you, and you must keep the records open to tenants (Tex. Water Code § 13.5031(a)). You must also register with the PUC before billing (16 Tex. Admin. Code § 24.277(a)), and you may not switch from submetering to allocation without PUC approval (Water Code § 13.502(e); the library's water rows). Electricity and central systems: at an apartment house of two or more units, allocating master-metered electricity, or central air conditioning, heating, hot water or chilled water costs, must follow PUC rules, with the same lease description, average-bill statement, actual-cost cap and records (Tex. Util. Code §§ 184.051, 184.052). That PUC rule is not held here, so read it before you allocate. The gas statute provides only for submetering under Railroad Commission rules (§ 124.002). In buildings outside these rules, such as a duplex sharing a water meter, the lease controls: state the formula and charge no more than the bill (all Texas codes searched). Never cut off service over an unpaid share; only submetered or allocated electricity may be interrupted, under strict rules (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.008(b), (h)).

title: Utility Deposits
bodyText: Who refunds a utility deposit depends on whose deposit it is. If the account is in the tenant's name, the deposit is between the tenant and the utility. Water and sewer utilities under the Public Utility Commission's customer rules must promptly refund a deposit with interest after service is disconnected, or once a residential customer has paid 18 consecutive bills on time, and may not require you, as landlord, to guarantee the tenant's deposit or monthly bill as a condition of service (16 Tex. Admin. Code §§ 24.151, 24.159(e), (h)). A city may set its own utility deposits (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code § 552.0025(c)); electric deposit rules are not held here. An unclaimed utility deposit is generally presumed abandoned a year after the refund check was payable or the customer last made contact (Tex. Prop. Code § 72.1017(b)). If you bill tenants for submetered or allocated utilities, your water bills to tenants may not pass on any deposit, disconnect, reconnect or late fee the utility charged you (16 Tex. Admin. Code § 24.281(a)), and a submetered electric bill may not include a deposit, except a deposit of up to one-sixth of estimated annual billing from a tenant on a level or average payment plan, which earns interest (§ 25.142(d)(1)(F), (d)(7)(D)). Any other money you take to secure the tenant's utility payments is a security deposit (Prop. Code § 92.102), so list it with the deposit and refund or account for it within 30 days after the tenant surrenders the premises (§ 92.103(a); the library's deposit rows).

title: Utility Disclosures With the Lease
bodyText:
Texas has no general rule that a lease disclose utility costs, which utilities serve the unit, or past bills. Utility disclosures are required only when you bill tenants for a utility yourself. Submetered or allocated water at an apartment house of five or more units, a condominium or a manufactured home rental community: the lease must carry the PUC-required statements, including the average, highest and lowest monthly bills for the previous year, and you must give the tenant a copy of the PUC rules when the lease is discussed (16 Tex. Admin. Code § 24.279(a), (b); the library's water billing clause).

Submetered electricity at an apartment house of more than five units, a condominium or a mobile home park: the lease must state that the unit is submetered, that common-area electricity is your responsibility and that billing disputes are between you and the tenant, and you must give the tenant a copy of the PUC rule or an approved summary when the lease is signed (16 Tex. Admin. Code § 25.142(d); the library's submetered electricity clause).

Allocated master-metered or central system electricity at a building of two or more units: the lease must contain a clear written description of the allocation method and the previous calendar year's average monthly bill (Tex. Util. Code §§ 184.051(1), 184.052(b)(1); 16 Tex. Admin. Code § 25.141(e); the library's allocated electricity clause).

You may change the method only after 90 days' notice. A manufactured home community lot lease must disclose any incorporated submetering addendum (Tex. Prop. Code § 94.053(c)(13)). In every lease, say who pays each utility (the library's utilities clauses).

title: Copies of a Tenant's Utility Shutoff Notices
bodyText: No Texas statute lets you, as owner, authorize a utility to tell you when a tenant's service is about to be disconnected, or lets a tenant name you to receive copies of shutoff notices (all Texas codes searched). Whether a utility will copy a third party is a matter for the Public Utility Commission's electric customer-protection rules and each utility's tariff, and for city-owned utilities and cooperatives their own policies. Those electric rules are not held here; the PUC water rules held here have no third-party notice provision (16 Tex. Admin. Code § 24.167). What Texas law does provide runs the other way. If you are the customer on a master-metered, non-submetered electric or gas account for an apartment, a condominium, or one or more buildings with at least 10 dwellings, you must give each tenant written notice by mail to the tenant's preferred mailing address or by hand within five days after you receive a disconnection notice, with your contact information, the tenant's remedies under § 92.301 and the statutory text in English and Spanish, and, if the property is in a city, send the same notice to the city by certified mail, unless you pay the bill and avoid the disconnection (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.302(a)-(d)). Covered electric providers and gas utilities must notify a city that has registered a representative at least 10 days before disconnecting such a property for nonpayment (Tex. Util. Code §§ 17.202, 104.352). Cautious course: ask the tenant, in the lease or separately, to share any shutoff notice with you, and ask the utility whether it offers third-party notification. The library's utility continuity clause already bars the tenant from letting service lapse.

title: Utilities Kept in Your Name
bodyText:
If a utility account stays in your name, Texas puts the risk of your nonpayment on you. If the lease says you furnish and pay for water, gas or electricity and the utility cuts off, or gives notice it will cut off, service because you didn't pay, the tenant may pay the utility and deduct it from rent, end the lease, and recover damages and attorney's fees (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.301; the library's row on falling behind on utilities you pay).

At an apartment, a condominium, or one or more buildings with at least 10 dwellings on a master-metered, non-submetered electric or gas service, you must notify each tenant by mail or hand delivery within five days after receiving a disconnection notice, in English and Spanish, with your contact information and the § 92.301 remedies, and, if the property is in a city, notify the city by certified mail (§ 92.302), and covered electric and gas providers must warn a registered city at least 10 days before disconnecting the property (Tex. Util. Code §§ 17.202, 104.352).

You may not interrupt service you furnish except for bona fide repairs, construction or an emergency (Prop. Code § 92.008(b)). Some rules help keep accounts out of your name. A water district may not require an individually metered unit's service to be connected in the landlord's name when the tenant applies (Tex. Water Code § 54.2051). A PUC-regulated water utility may not require you to guarantee a tenant's deposit or bill, or disconnect a customer for a previous occupant's unpaid bill (16 Tex. Admin. Code §§ 24.159(e), 24.167(c)(1)).

A city utility lien does not reach bills for service in a tenant's name after you tell the city the property is a rental (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code § 552.0025(e); the library's city lien row). No Texas statute lets tenants seek a receiver over your unpaid utility bill.

title: When the Tenant Does Not Transfer Utilities
bodyText:
No Texas statute lets you cut off a utility left in your name because the tenant did not transfer it, or sets a deadline for the tenant to put utilities in its own name. The general rule controls instead. You may not interrupt or cause the interruption of water, wastewater, gas or electric service you furnish to a tenant as an incident of the tenancy or by other agreement, except for bona fide repairs, construction or an emergency, and the same goes for service the tenant pays for directly (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.008(a), (b)).

A violation lets the tenant recover possession or end the lease, plus actual damages, one month's rent plus $1,000, attorney's fees and court costs, less any delinquent rent or other sums the tenant owes you, and a lease term waiving the rule is void (§ 92.008(f), (g)). Closing your account so that service stops while the tenant is in possession risks counting as causing an interruption.

Cautious course: require the tenant to open its own accounts by the start date (the library's utilities clause), arrange the changeover with the utility for that date and tell the tenant in writing beforehand, and if the tenant has not opened an account, keep yours open, bill the tenant the actual charges under the lease and treat the failure as a lease default.

To keep a city utility lien off your property for service connected in the tenant's name, notify the city that the property is a rental (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code § 552.0025(e)); the notice does not protect you for service left in your own name; and a water district may not insist that an individually metered unit's service be in your name (Tex. Water Code § 54.2051).

title: No Landlord Incentive for Renting to Veterans
bodyText: Texas offers a private landlord no tax credit, fee waiver or other incentive for renting to a veteran, and no state law requires or regulates a veterans' rent discount or preference in private housing (all Texas codes searched). Veteran status is not among the bases in the Texas Fair Housing Act's rental section, which lists race, color, religion, sex, familial status and national origin (Tex. Prop. Code § 301.021(a); the library's fair housing row covers the rest of that Act). The veteran rules that do exist sit elsewhere. A city or county may not ban refusing a tenant because the tenant's rent comes partly from a federal housing assistance program, but that limit does not affect a local rule prohibiting refusal to rent to a military veteran because of the veteran's lawful source of income, so check your city's ordinances (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code § 250.007(a), (b); the library's voucher row). State veteran money goes through the Texas Veterans Commission, which makes grants to address veterans' needs (Tex. Gov't Code § 434.017(c)), and housing authorities in counties of more than 500,000 may develop housing for veterans (Tex. Loc. Gov't Code § 392.067). Servicemember tenants have their own lease rights (the library's servicemember row). You may offer a voluntary veterans' discount; offer it on the same terms to every eligible veteran. Federal law (e.g. the Fair Housing Act) may also apply; not reviewed here.

title: Accepting Rent After a Notice in Texas
bodyText: No Texas statute or court rule decides whether accepting rent after you give a notice to vacate, or after you learn of a breach, waives the notice or the breach (all Texas codes and the Rules of Civil Procedure searched). The answer rests on case law. The one related statute runs the other way: a tenant who pays a late fee does not waive the tenant's own late-fee rights (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.019(e)). The cautious course: once you have given a notice to vacate, don't accept rent for any period after the notice unless you intend to continue the tenancy; if a payment arrives, return it promptly or accept it only with a written statement that acceptance does not waive the notice, the breach or your right to possession. If you do accept rent and want to keep the eviction alive, give a fresh notice to vacate before filing. Partial payments raise the same question.

title: Hot Water Temperature
bodyText: Texas sets a minimum, not a maximum, for hot water. Your repair duty covers a failure to provide and maintain in good operating condition a device to supply hot water of at least 120 degrees Fahrenheit, once the tenant gives notice and is current on rent, whether or not the shortfall affects health or safety (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.052(a)(3)(B)); the tenant's statutory repair remedies then apply (the library's repair rows). No Texas statute sets a maximum water heater setting, or requires you to set or check the temperature at each new tenancy. Large water heaters are regulated as boilers. A potable water heater, meaning one with heat input over 200,000 Btu per hour or holding more than 120 gallons (Tex. Health & Safety Code § 755.001(18)), must be registered with the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation and hold a current certificate of operation (§ 755.021), with a certificate inspection every three years (§ 755.025(d)). Heating boilers used to heat buildings used only as residences for not more than four families are exempt from that inspection (§ 755.022(b)); whether the exemption reaches a water heater is unclear, so ask the Department. Cautious course: set unit water heaters at or just above 120 degrees, which meets the minimum and limits scalding risk, check the setting at turnover, and act promptly on a no-hot-water complaint.

title: Waterbeds in Texas Rentals
bodyText: No Texas statute deals with waterbeds or other water-filled furniture in rentals: nothing gives a tenant a right to have one, limits what you may require (such as insurance or an added deposit), or sets installation standards (all Texas codes searched). So it is a lease matter. The library's Use of Property and Common Areas clause, which carries Texas, bars a waterbed or other water-filled furniture without your prior written consent. If you consent, put your conditions in writing, for example a liner, professional installation, a floor-load limit and liability coverage. Any extra money you take to secure the tenant's performance is a security deposit, whatever you call it (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.102), so the refund and itemization rules apply to it (the library's deposit rows); Texas sets no cap on its amount (the library's deposit cap row). Damage from a waterbed the tenant brings in is a condition caused by the tenant, which you have no duty to repair during the lease unless it is normal wear and tear (§ 92.052(b)), and which you may charge against the deposit under the deposit rules. Federal law on reasonable accommodations (for example a medical need for a particular bed) may also apply; not reviewed here.

title: No Window Guard Rule in Texas
bodyText: No Texas statute requires window guards, window stops or other fall-prevention devices in rentals, or a window-guard notice in the lease. Texas window rules deal with security and escape instead. Without waiting for a request, you must equip each exterior window with a window latch, at your expense, and keep it operable while a tenant is in possession (Tex. Prop. Code § 92.153(a)(1), (c), (h); the library's security device rows). If you install security bars on a door or window of a bedroom, the bars on at least one door or window in that bedroom must have an interior release mechanism, or at least one bedroom window or door to the outside must open for emergency escape or rescue (Tex. Health & Safety Code § 756.082). Where a building wall is part of a pool yard enclosure, each window in a wall built before 1994 needs a latch and secured screens, ground-floor windows in a newer wall must be permanently closed, and the windows of units inside the pool yard must meet the same rules (§§ 757.007, 757.008; the library's pool row). If you add window guards or stops anyway, choose ones that release from inside without a key or special knowledge, so they don't block an escape route that the security-bar rule or your local fire code protects.

title: Notices That Must Be in Writing
bodyText:
Texas has no general rule that every lease notice be in writing; writing is required notice by notice. These must be written:
- The notice to vacate before an eviction, at least three days unless the lease sets another period (Tex. Prop. Code § 24.005(a))
- The advance notice before changing locks for unpaid rent, and the notice you post on the door when you do (§ 92.0081(c), (d))
- Both electricity termination notices before and at an interruption of submetered or allocated electricity (§ 92.008(h))
- A tenant's notice ending the lease for family violence or military service (§§ 92.016(c)(3), 92.017(c)(1))
- The tenant's forwarding address, without which your deposit refund and itemization duties do not start (§ 92.107(a))
- A tenant's request that you mail notices to a primary residence elsewhere, plus any change of that address (§ 92.012(a), (b)).

Two common notices need not be written under the statutes: notice ending a month-to-month tenancy (§ 91.001), and a tenant's repair request, which must be written only if a written lease requires it (§ 92.052(d)). A requirement that the tenant give advance notice of surrender as a condition of the deposit refund works only if it is underlined or in bold in the lease (§ 92.103(b)). The library's notices clause asks for written notice throughout; still act on an oral repair request (the library's repair notice row).

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Texas follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 3.311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 1.308(b)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Texas's landlord-tenant statutes impose no general duty of good faith of the kind in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (Tex. Prop. Code chs. 91 and 92 searched); good faith appears only in specific rules. Courts in many states read a covenant of good faith and fair dealing into every contract, a lease included; whether and how Texas's courts do is case law, so act as if the duty applies. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.
